docs.text: Data Analytics ¶ Learn to turn a business question into a recommendation you can defend, using Python, clear charts and real analytical habits. Welcome! I'm Aayush, your facilitator for this training programme. We will explore and explain data from five areas of a business: retail and e-commerce, finance, operations, marketing and HR. Along the way you will also practise on sports, technology, government and other datasets. This site is still being built Right now you will find the Foundations section, the course roadmap and the first Python lessons. More lessons, cases and a Tableau section are on their way. The business cases and the lesson template are previews. They are not ready-to-run assignments yet. Course at a glance ¶ Live, hands-on classes. Demonstrations, guided practice and independent work, plus practice between sessions. Spreadsheet basics are enough. No coding experience is assumed. Session 1 starts from the very beginning. Python in your browser. You run every lesson in Google Colab: nothing to install, and every result on these pages comes from the same code you run. Synthetic and public data only. Never private workplace data. Portfolio and briefing. You finish with a practical portfolio and an executive briefing grounded in checked evidence. Tableau later. A separate Tableau section will show how to build the same analyses as interactive dashboards. Where to start ¶ Work through these pages in order: Foundations : why data analytics and clear presentation matter, with real examples. Learning roadmap : what each stage of the course covers. Setup and practice : getting started with Google Colab and keeping notes. Analytical workflow : the seven steps we use in every analysis. Business cases : the five business problems you will solve. Session 1 lecture : why data analytics matters, then its lab on Python and Colab basics. How we will practise ¶ Every topic follows the same rhythm: Watch a short demonstration. Run the working code yourself, step by step. Change a few lines to answer a related question on your own. Debug a deliberate mistake. Recommend an action to a stakeholder. One habit to build from day one Before you trust a chart, check three things: what each row means, how the metric is defined, and what evidence supports the number. You will never be asked to write programs from scratch. Each lesson gives you working code to read, run and then modify. Instructor solutions are shared separately after each practice round. docs.text: Business case previews ¶ Five business problems, one for each department. Each case teaches a core skill and a common mistake to catch. Previews, not assignments yet These are proposed case themes. Individual files have not been released yet. We combine selected Tableau sample datasets with synthetic (made-up) teaching data. Meridian Commerce is a proposed fictional company used only for the synthetic cases. Real datasets keep their own context, units and dates. The five core cases ¶ Retail ¶ Decision: Which customer segment deserves a closer investigation? You will practise: what a row means, distinct orders, average order value, Sales and Profit, ratios, discounts, customers, trends and the limits of a returns list. Mistake to catch: treating order lines as orders. Finance ¶ Decision: Which departments need a spending review? You will practise: budget versus actual, time periods, reconciliation and whether a cost difference is favourable. Mistake to catch: repeating a monthly budget on every transaction row. Operations ¶ Decision: Where should delivery reliability improve? You will practise: promised dates, overdue open shipments, distributions, median and mean. Mistake to catch: dropping undelivered shipments from the service measure. Marketing ¶ Decision: Which campaigns need closer evaluation before budget moves? You will practise: weighted funnel rates, cost per conversion, return on ad spend and the limits of attribution. Mistake to catch: averaging percentages that have different denominators. HR ¶ Decision: How is the workforce changing, and which comparisons are fair? You will practise: historical headcount, turnover, cohorts, tenure and recruitment timelines. All employee records are synthetic. Mistake to catch: dividing past exits by the current headcount. What every case includes ¶ Stakeholder brief : the decision and why it matters Data dictionary : what each field means Metric definitions : exact formulas and scope Worked example : a guided walk-through Exercises : guided and independent practice Debugging task : find and fix a mistake Recommendation challenge : advise the stakeholder Validation checkpoints : confirm your numbers Each case also has an optional pandas connection. Instructor answers are supplied separately. Combining evidence across departments ¶ Before combining findings, explain any differences in grain, period and units. Within the synthetic company, marketing-attributed revenue is a view of the same retail revenue. Do not count it twice. Separate catalog datasets do not describe that fictional company. A good recommendation weighs trade-offs. It does not add incompatible KPIs together. Additional practice choices ¶ You will also be able to practise on topics beyond the five departments: Topic Example dataset Sports World Cup match results Technology Mobile operating-system usage (a data-quality exercise), start-up funding Government US construction spending, US home sales Other Science, education and entertainment datasets These are transfer exercises: the same process, with source-specific definitions and checks. They fit into your existing practice time or optional extensions. The five core cases remain the foundation of your portfolio. Every dataset is reviewed first A dataset appearing in a catalog does not tell us what each row means, which calculations it supports or whether it can be shared. Each lesson will give you the exact reviewed file and dictionary, or instructions to download it from the source, before you use it.

docs.text: Learning roadmap ¶ The course has sixteen Python sessions, followed by a Tableau section. Every session has two parts: a Lecture that teaches the theory with worked examples, and a Lab where you practise it yourself on real and synthetic data. This is the planned sequence Lecture and lab materials are released only after they have been checked. Sessions marked with a link already have draft material. How each session works ¶ Lecture. A short recap quiz, then the theory, explained with examples and questions where you predict the answer before seeing it. It ends with a worked case in code. Lab. Three levels of practice in a Colab notebook: Guided: step-by-step, everyone together. Independent: the same skill applied to a new question. Challenge: a harder problem or a deliberate mistake to debug. You keep the evidence from every lab in your portfolio. Part A: Thinking with data ¶ Session Lecture Lab 1. Why data analytics matters Why data analytics matters : the four levels of analytics, decision-driven questions, and why statistics alone can mislead Python, Colab and always plotting your data : recreate Anscombe's quartet and the Datasaurus 2. Data, grain and the DataFrame Data, grain and the DataFrame : types of data, tidy data, grain and keys, data dictionaries, data quality Can we trust the sales table? 3. Cleaning and preparing data Cleaning and preparing data : missing data, duplicates, outliers, dates, joins and their pitfalls, reshaping Clean World Cup and mobile-OS data; merge tables safely Part B: Describing and measuring ¶ Session Lecture Lab 4. Descriptive statistics and distributions Descriptive statistics and distributions : centre, spread, percentiles, skew, outliers, histograms and box plots Distributions of order value and shipping time; median vs mean house prices 5. Metrics and KPIs Metrics and KPIs : designing metrics, ratios of totals, weighted rates, Simpson's paradox Which segment deserves a closer look? ; the Berkeley admissions paradox 6. Visualisation principles Visualisation principles : choosing charts, perception, data-ink, Gestalt, colour and accessibility ( Designing clear visuals ) Redesign bad charts; one-, two- and many-variable views Part C: Relationships, change and uncertainty ¶ Session Lecture Lab 7. Time series and trends Time series and trends : trend and seasonality, month-on-month vs year-on-year, moving averages Trends, returns and a decision dashboard ; construction spending 8. Correlation and regression Correlation, confounding, simple linear regression, residuals Discount vs profit; advertising spend vs revenue 9. Sampling, uncertainty and experiments Samples and populations, confidence intervals, A/B tests, practical vs statistical significance Simulate sampling; bootstrap a confidence interval; analyse an A/B test Part D: Business cases ¶ Session Lecture Lab 10. Finance Budget vs actual, variance, reconciliation Find the spending that needs review 11. Operations Service levels, open shipments, delay distributions Measure delivery reliability fairly 12. Marketing Funnels, weighted conversion, cost per acquisition, attribution limits Compare campaigns and judge an experiment 13. HR Headcount, turnover, cohorts, fairness and privacy Track workforce change correctly Part E: Communicating and bringing it together ¶ Session Lecture Lab 14. Dashboards and storytelling Audience, the big idea, dashboard design, the Challenger case ( Storytelling with data ) Build a decision dashboard and a three-slide story 15. Capstone studio Combining evidence across departments, validation, trade-offs Build your capstone analysis with coaching 16. Executive briefings Presenting to executives and handling questions Present, give and receive critique, revise Part F: Tableau ¶ Session Lecture Lab T1. Tableau fundamentals How Tableau thinks: dimensions, measures, aggregation Rebuild earlier views ( draft ) T2. Calculations and KPIs Calculated fields, distinct counts, table calculations Rebuild the segment KPIs and growth measures T3. Dashboards in Tableau Layout, filters, actions, accessibility Rebuild your decision dashboard T4. Publishing and portfolio Tableau Public and privacy Your Tableau portfolio piece What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of the course you should be able to: Turn a business request into a clear question with a decision, population, period and measure. Load, inspect, clean and reshape data in Python, keeping a record of every change. Describe data with the right statistics and charts, and explain distributions, outliers and skew. Define metrics precisely and avoid the common traps. Measure relationships and change over time, and explain what correlation and regression can and cannot show. Express uncertainty with confidence intervals and simple experiments. Design clear charts and dashboards, and tell a decision-focused story. Apply all of this to retail, finance, operations, marketing and HR, and defend a recommendation to executives. Rebuild key analyses in Tableau. How you will be assessed ¶ Theory quizzes at the start of each lecture help you check your understanding. They are for feedback. Your lab portfolio collects your evidence from every session and covers all five business areas. Your capstone combines findings from at least three areas into a dashboard and an executive briefing. Feedback rewards correct reasoning, careful checking and honest statements of uncertainty, not only attractive charts. Extra practice topics ¶ Selected datasets from the Tableau sample-data catalog give you practice in sports, technology, government and more. Each keeps its own real dates, units and context.

docs.text: Setup and practice ¶ What you need before you start, how to run the lessons in Google Colab, how to stay safe with data, and how to keep a simple evidence log. What you need ¶ A computer with a modern web browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari) A Google account, to use Google Colab A way to receive course files and submit your work Before teaching starts We will confirm devices, accessibility needs and the submission channel with everyone. Nothing needs to be installed for the Python lessons. Open a lesson in Google Colab ¶ Every Python lesson page has an Open in Colab button near the top. Click Open in Colab . The lesson notebook opens in Google Colab; sign in with your Google account if asked. Run the cells from top to bottom: click a cell and press Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive , so your changes are kept. The notebook opens with the facilitator's outputs already visible. Running it yourself replaces them with your own results. The first code cell in each lesson downloads the course data from Tableau's sample-data page and checks that it is exactly the version the lesson was written for. If it prints a warning, tell your facilitator. If something goes wrong Choose Runtime → Restart session and run all . This runs everything again from the top and fixes most problems. New to Python? Start with the Session 1 lab: Python, Colab and always plotting your data . Keep your data safe ¶ Only use course data Use only the datasets supplied for this course. Never upload private employer, customer or employee files to Colab or any other online tool. Notebooks you save in Google Drive are private to you unless you choose to share them. Check the sharing setting before sending a link to anyone. If something does not work ¶ No internet or no Google account Follow the demonstration or pair with a classmate, and keep writing your metric and checking notes. Run the notebook yourself later, once access is back. Tableau (later) ¶ A separate Tableau section will come later in the course. You do not need Tableau for the Python lessons. When we reach that section, you will install Tableau Desktop Public Edition from the official Tableau Public page . Anything you publish to Tableau Public is public Published workbooks and their data can be seen by anyone. Hiding an item on your profile does not make it private. Tableau Public also lets you save workbooks on your own computer, so publishing online is optional. Keep an evidence log ¶ For every task, write down a few short notes. They make your portfolio much easier to build. Record Example prompt Data release Which file and version did I use? Question What decision is this for? Grain What does one row represent? Date window and filters Which records are included? Metric definition What is the numerator and denominator? Checks How did I confirm the number is right? Chart and recommendation What should the stakeholder do next? Save your notebook and your notes together. When two numbers disagree Compare their populations and denominators before changing the chart.

docs.text: From business question to recommendation ¶ A useful analysis supports a decision. A chart becomes trustworthy when its population, calculations and limitations are clear. We follow the same seven steps in every lesson and case. The seven steps ¶ 1. Business question ¶ Ask: Who must decide what, and by when? Keep: the decision and a one-sentence question. 2. Data understanding ¶ Ask: What does each row represent? What is missing? Keep: the grain, keys, units, data dictionary and scope. 3. Preparation ¶ Ask: What changes are needed, and could someone else repeat them? Keep: an untouched copy of the original data and a log of every change. 4. Analysis ¶ Ask: Which comparison or metric actually answers the question? Keep: the metric definition, filters and calculation. 5. Validation ¶ Ask: Do totals reconcile? Can I explain any odd values? Keep: a manual spot check, count and total checks, and edge cases. 6. Visualization ¶ Ask: Can the audience see the important comparison at a glance? Keep: a labelled chart showing the period, units and population. 7. Recommendation ¶ Ask: What action follows, and what is still uncertain? Keep: an action linked to evidence, one caveat and a follow-up measure. A worked example ¶ Why are orders falling? A manager asks: "Why are orders falling?" The data file has one row per order line , so a single order with three products takes up three rows. Counting rows would count lines , not orders. First, define what an order is, which period to look at and which orders are eligible. Then count distinct order IDs in that population. Compare the result with an order-level summary before reading anything into the trend. The same care applies elsewhere in the course: a budget repeated on every row after a join undelivered shipments left out of a service calculation campaign percentages averaged without their volumes past staff exits divided by today's headcount When a result looks wrong ¶ Work through these checks in order: Grain and keys Date filters Missing values Join or relationship behaviour Aggregation Then write down why the wrong answer was tempting and what evidence supports the corrected one. A plausible number is not a checked number Looking reasonable is not the same as being validated. Association is not causation ¶ A pattern in the data can tell you where to look . It does not prove that a discount, campaign, carrier or HR policy caused a result. When a decision depends on cause and effect, recommend a follow-up comparison or a test.

docs.text: Why data analytics matters ¶ Every organisation makes decisions. Data analytics is the discipline of making those decisions with evidence instead of guesswork, and of explaining that evidence so other people act on it. Before we write any code or build any charts, this Foundations section answers a simple question: why bother? You will see how analysis has changed real outcomes, how numbers can mislead, and why the way we present evidence matters as much as the evidence itself. What is data analytics? ¶ Data analytics turns raw records into answers to business questions. It usually works at four levels: Level Question it answers Everyday example Descriptive What happened? Sales fell 8% last quarter. Diagnostic Why did it happen? The fall came almost entirely from one region after a competitor opened. Predictive What is likely to happen next? If nothing changes, the region will lose a further 5% next quarter. Prescriptive What should we do about it? Test a local loyalty offer in that region before changing national prices. This course focuses mostly on the first two levels, done properly : a clear question, trustworthy data, correct calculations, honest charts and a recommendation a manager can act on. Real stories where data changed the outcome ¶ A map that changed how we think about disease (London, 1854) ¶ During a cholera outbreak in Soho, physician John Snow investigated where the victims lived and where they drew their water. The cases clustered around one public water pump on Broad Street. At the time, most experts blamed "bad air". Snow persuaded the local authorities to remove the pump's handle. His famous dot map of the deaths, drawn shortly afterwards, became the classic demonstration that cholera spreads through water, though it took years for that view to be widely accepted. Lesson A simple, well-chosen picture of the data can overturn what "everyone knows". A chart that reformed hospitals (1850s) ¶ After the Crimean War, Florence Nightingale showed with her "rose" diagrams that far more soldiers died of preventable disease in hospitals than of battle wounds. Her charts were designed for politicians, not statisticians, and helped drive major sanitary reforms. Lesson Analysis only changes things when the people who decide can understand it. Winning on a small budget (baseball, 2002) ¶ The Oakland Athletics , with one of the lowest payrolls in Major League Baseball, used statistics such as on-base percentage to find undervalued players. They competed with teams spending far more. The story became the book and film Moneyball , and data-driven scouting spread across sport. Lesson Measuring the right thing can matter more than having the most money. Preparing for a hurricane (retail, 2004) ¶ Before a hurricane reached Florida, Walmart analysts looked at what shoppers had bought before earlier storms. Alongside torches and water, sales of strawberry Pop-Tarts and beer reportedly jumped well above normal. Stores were stocked accordingly. Lesson Past patterns can guide practical, everyday operational decisions. When big data got it wrong (public health, 2008–2015) ¶ Google Flu Trends tried to estimate flu levels from search queries. It worked for a while, then missed the 2009 swine-flu pandemic and badly overestimated later flu seasons, and was shut down. People's search habits and Google's own search algorithms changed, and the model was not re-checked against official flu data often enough. Lesson More data is not automatically better data. Every result still needs validation. Where you meet analytics every day ¶ Banking: a card payment is flagged as possible fraud because it does not fit your normal pattern. Streaming and shopping: recommendations are based on what similar customers watched or bought. Transport: ride-hailing prices rise when demand outstrips available drivers. Healthcare: hospitals plan staff rotas using predicted admission levels. Workplaces: HR teams track hiring time and staff turnover to spot problems early. Why presentation is part of analysis ¶ An analysis that nobody understands has no effect. The most important finding in a report can be lost in a cluttered table, a misleading chart or a slide with too much text. Good analysts therefore do three jobs: Find what is true in the data. Check that it really is true. Show it so the right person understands it quickly and acts on it. The rest of this Foundations section covers each of these. docs.text: Every organisation makes decisions. Data analytics is the discipline of making those decisions with evidence instead of guesswork, and of explaining that evidence so other people act on it. Before we write any code or build any charts, this Foundations section answers a simple question: why bother? You will see how analysis has changed real outcomes, how numbers can mislead, and why the way we present evidence matters as much as the evidence itself.
docs.title: Why data analytics matters

docs.text: Data analytics turns raw records into answers to business questions. It usually works at four levels: Level Question it answers Everyday example Descriptive What happened? Sales fell 8% last quarter. Diagnostic Why did it happen? The fall came almost entirely from one region after a competitor opened. Predictive What is likely to happen next? If nothing changes, the region will lose a further 5% next quarter. Prescriptive What should we do about it? Test a local loyalty offer in that region before changing national prices. This course focuses mostly on the first two levels, done properly : a clear question, trustworthy data, correct calculations, honest charts and a recommendation a manager can act on.

docs.text: During a cholera outbreak in Soho, physician John Snow investigated where the victims lived and where they drew their water. The cases clustered around one public water pump on Broad Street. At the time, most experts blamed "bad air". Snow persuaded the local authorities to remove the pump's handle. His famous dot map of the deaths, drawn shortly afterwards, became the classic demonstration that cholera spreads through water, though it took years for that view to be widely accepted. docs.text: How statistics can mislead ¶ Numbers feel objective, but the same data can support very different stories depending on how it is summarised, compared and drawn. Learn the common traps so you never fall into them, and can spot them in other people's work. In 1954, Darrell Huff wrote a short, famous book called How to Lie with Statistics . Its point was not to teach lying. It was to show readers how easily numbers mislead, often by accident. The traps below are the ones you will meet most often at work. 1. Correlation is not causation ¶ Two things that move together are correlated . That does not mean one causes the other. A classic example: in many cities, ice cream sales and crime both rise in summer and fall in winter. Plot one against the other and you see a strong relationship. Does ice cream cause crime? Of course not. Both are plausibly driven by a third factor, warm weather , when more people are outside. The chart uses synthetic data made up for illustration. The hidden third factor is called a confounder . Whenever you see two things moving together, ask: Could a third factor be driving both? Could the cause run the other way? Could it be coincidence, especially if I searched through many variables? Spurious correlations If you compare enough unrelated series, some will match by pure chance. Tyler Vigen's Spurious Correlations project collects amusing examples, such as films featuring a particular actor tracking the number of swimming-pool drownings in the same years. At work "Customers who used our app spent 30% more." Perhaps the app made them spend more. Or perhaps the customers who already spent the most were the ones who bothered to download the app. Only a fair comparison or a test can tell you which. 2. Simpson's paradox: the total can reverse the parts ¶ In 1973, the University of California, Berkeley, looked at graduate admissions. Overall, 44% of men but only 35% of women were admitted. It looked like clear bias against women. But when the figures were split by department, the picture changed. The chart and table show the six largest departments; the overall row covers all departments. Department Men admitted Women admitted A 62% 82% B 63% 68% C 37% 34% D 33% 35% E 28% 24% F 6% 7% All departments (overall) 44% 35% What happened? Women applied mostly to departments that were very competitive for everyone (C to F). Men applied mostly to departments that admitted many applicants (A and B). The overall rate mixed together very different groups. The lesson Before comparing two overall rates, check whether the groups being compared have a different mix underneath. A total can tell the opposite story to every one of its parts. 3. Misleading axes ¶ The same two numbers can look dramatically different depending on where the axis starts. Synthetic data for illustration. Bar charts should start at zero, because we judge bars by their length. Line charts may start elsewhere, because we judge lines by their slope, but label the axis clearly. Watch for two different y-axes on one chart. They let the author make any two lines appear to move together. 4. Cherry-picked time windows ¶ Choose the start and end dates carefully and almost any trend can be made to look like growth or decline. "Sales up 40% since March!" (March was the worst month in five years.) "Complaints halved this quarter!" (Last quarter included a one-off system outage.) Synthetic data for illustration. The left chart is true, but the right chart shows the real story: March was an unusual low, and sales have been falling for five years. Ask Why does the chart start and end there ? What does the longer history look like? 5. Which average? ¶ The word "average" can mean different things: The mean adds everything up and divides by the count. The median is the middle value when everything is sorted. If a few values are extremely large, the mean is pulled upward. Imagine nine employees earning 40,000 and one director earning 1,000,000. The mean salary is 136,000; the median is 40,000. Both are "the average salary", but only one describes a typical employee. Synthetic data for illustration. Which to use Use the median for things with a few very large values, such as salaries, house prices or delivery delays. Report both when the difference matters. 6. Percentages without the base ¶ "Complaints rose 200%!" sounds alarming. From 1 to 3, it is not. From 10,000 to 30,000, it is a crisis. Synthetic data for illustration. Notice that the two charts look exactly the same. Only the axis numbers reveal how different the situations are. Always ask for the count behind a percentage. Be wary of averaging percentages from groups of very different sizes. You will meet this trap in the marketing case. 7. Survivorship bias ¶ As the story is usually told, during the Second World War analysts studied bombers returning from missions and mapped where they had been hit. The obvious idea was to add armour where the bullet holes were. The statistician Abraham Wald pointed out the flaw: these were the planes that survived . Planes hit in other places, such as the engines, never came back to be counted. The armour belonged where the returning planes had no holes. Simplified illustration, not real wartime data. At work Surveying only current customers about why they like you tells you nothing about why others left. Studying only successful projects hides the reasons projects fail. A checklist for any number you are shown ¶ Before you trust a figure, ask: Compared to what? A number without a comparison means little. Who or what is included? Which records, which dates, which filters? What is the denominator? Out of how many? Could something else explain it? A confounder, a different mix, chance? How is it drawn? Where does the axis start? Is the time window fair? Try it yourself ¶ Exercise 1: name the confounder For each claim, suggest a third factor that could explain the link: Towns with more fire engines have more fire damage. Employees who attend more training get promoted more often. Stores with more staff have more customer complaints. Exercise 2: fix the chart Find a chart in a news article or a company report. Check where its axis starts, which time period it covers and whether the counts behind its percentages are shown. Rewrite its headline so it is fair. Exercise 3: spot the paradox A sales manager says: "Team A's overall conversion rate is lower than Team B's, so Team A is weaker." What extra breakdown would you ask for before agreeing?

docs.text: Statistics are not enough ¶ Averages, spreads and correlations are useful summaries. But very different data can produce exactly the same summary numbers. The only safe habit is to look at the data as well. Anscombe's quartet ¶ In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe created four small datasets. Each has eleven points. Look at their summary statistics: Statistic Dataset I Dataset II Dataset III Dataset IV Mean of x 9.0 9.0 9.0 9.0 Mean of y 7.50 7.50 7.50 7.50 Variance of x 11.0 11.0 11.0 11.0 Variance of y 4.13 4.13 4.12 4.12 Correlation of x and y 0.816 0.816 0.816 0.817 Best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500x y = 3.00 + 0.500x y = 3.00 + 0.500x y = 3.00 + 0.500x If you only read this table, you would say the four datasets are the same. Now look at them: Dataset What the picture shows What the statistics hide I A loose, roughly straight-line relationship Nothing. This is the case the summary describes well. II A smooth curve The relationship is not a straight line at all. III A perfect straight line, except for one outlier A single unusual point drags the trend line. IV Almost all points share one x value; one extreme point creates the "trend" Remove that one point and every x is the same, so there is no trend left to measure. The lesson Summary statistics compress data. Compression throws information away. A chart lets you see what was thrown away. The raw data, if you want to plot it yourself x (I, II, III) y I y II y III x IV y IV 10 8.04 9.14 7.46 8 6.58 8 6.95 8.14 6.77 8 5.76 13 7.58 8.74 12.74 8 7.71 9 8.81 8.77 7.11 8 8.84 11 8.33 9.26 7.81 8 8.47 14 9.96 8.10 8.84 8 7.04 6 7.24 6.13 6.08 8 5.25 4 4.26 3.10 5.39 19 12.50 12 10.84 9.13 8.15 8 5.56 7 4.82 7.26 6.42 8 7.91 5 5.68 4.74 5.73 8 6.89 The Datasaurus Dozen ¶ In 2017, researchers Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice took the idea further. Starting from a dinosaur drawing made of data points (originally created by Alberto Cairo), they nudged points step by step into new shapes while keeping the summary statistics nearly identical, to about two decimal places. Every one of these thirteen datasets has: mean of x ≈ 54.3 and mean of y ≈ 47.8 standard deviation of x ≈ 16.8 and of y ≈ 26.9 correlation between x and y between −0.06 and −0.07 A report that said "x and y are essentially unrelated, centred around 54 and 48" would be technically correct for all of them, including the dinosaur. Data source Datasaurus Dozen data from the open-source datasauRus package (MIT licence), based on Matejka and Fitzmaurice, Same Stats, Different Graphs , ACM CHI 2017. What this means at work ¶ You will rarely meet a dinosaur in a sales report. But you will meet the same problems in everyday forms: An average hides two very different groups. Average delivery time looks fine, because most deliveries are fast while a few customers wait weeks. One outlier drives the trend. A single huge order makes a quiet month look like growth. A relationship is curved, not straight. Discounts raise sales up to a point, then only cut profit. Rule of thumb Never report a summary number you have not also looked at in a chart, at least once, yourself. Try it yourself ¶ Exercise 1: predict, then check Cover the Anscombe chart above. Using only the statistics table, sketch what you think each dataset looks like. Then uncover the chart. Which of your sketches was furthest off, and why? Exercise 2: find a hidden shape at work Think of a number you see regularly in your job, for example average monthly sales or average response time. Write down two different situations that would produce the same average but would need different decisions . Exercise 3: in Python (after Lesson 0) In a new Colab notebook, recreate Dataset II and compare its statistics with a chart: import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt d = pd . DataFrame ({ "x" : [ 10 , 8 , 13 , 9 , 11 , 14 , 6 , 4 , 12 , 7 , 5 ], "y" : [ 9.14 , 8.14 , 8.74 , 8.77 , 9.26 , 8.10 , 6.13 , 3.10 , 9.13 , 7.26 , 4.74 ], }) print ( d . mean ()) print ( "Correlation:" , d [ "x" ] . corr ( d [ "y" ])) d . plot ( kind = "scatter" , x = "x" , y = "y" , title = "Anscombe dataset II" ) plt . show () Then replace the y values with Dataset III from the table above. The printed statistics barely change. Does the chart?

docs.text: Storytelling with data ¶ A correct analysis that nobody understands changes nothing. Storytelling with data means shaping evidence into a clear message, for a specific audience, that leads to a decision. The Challenger disaster: right data, wrong presentation ¶ On 28 January 1986 , the space shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch, killing all seven crew. The investigation found that rubber O-ring seals in a booster rocket had failed. They had become stiff in the unusually cold weather: the air temperature at launch was about 36°F (2°C) , far colder than any previous launch. The night before, engineers at the contractor Morton Thiokol were worried. They had data on O-ring damage from earlier flights and recommended not launching below 53°F, the coldest temperature previously flown. In a tense teleconference, their recommendation was challenged, managers reversed it, and the launch went ahead. What did the data show? ¶ Discussion that night focused on flights where O-rings had been damaged , the view later highlighted by the Rogers Commission investigation. Looked at alone, those flights do not show an obvious temperature pattern: damage appeared at both cool and warm temperatures. The picture changes completely when you include the flights with no damage: What you see Only damaged flights All 23 flights Pattern with temperature Unclear Every flight below 65°F had O-ring damage Launches near 36°F None None. Challenger was far outside all experience Every launch below 65°F had damage. Most warm launches had none. And Challenger would launch more than 15 degrees colder than anything ever tried. Two views of the lesson Edward Tufte argued in Visual Explanations (1997) that the engineers' charts failed to show this relationship clearly. Others have pointed out that the engineers did raise temperature as the key concern, and that the decision was also shaped by schedule and organisational pressure. Both views lead to the same lesson for analysts: when the stakes are high, the evidence must be presented so the risk is impossible to miss. Data source O-ring data for the 23 flights before Challenger: UCI Machine Learning Repository, Challenger USA Space Shuttle O-Ring dataset (erosion or blow-by version), based on Draper (1995) and Dalal, Fowlkes and Hoadley (1989). What makes a data story ¶ The ideas in this section draw on Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic's book Storytelling with Data (2015), paraphrased for this course. A data story is not a decorated chart. It has three parts: Context: who is the audience, what do they already know, and what decision do they face? Evidence: the few charts and numbers that matter, checked and clearly drawn. Action: what you recommend, what is uncertain, and how success will be measured. Start with the "big idea" ¶ Before building any chart, write your main message in one sentence that: states your point of view, says what is at stake, and is written for your audience. docs.text: On 28 January 1986 , the space shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch, killing all seven crew. The investigation found that rubber O-ring seals in a booster rocket had failed. They had become stiff in the unusually cold weather: the air temperature at launch was about 36°F (2°C) , far colder than any previous launch. The night before, engineers at the contractor Morton Thiokol were worried. They had data on O-ring damage from earlier flights and recommended not launching below 53°F, the coldest temperature previously flown. In a tense teleconference, their recommendation was challenged, managers reversed it, and the launch went ahead.
docs.title: The Challenger disaster: right data, wrong presentation

docs.text: Discussion that night focused on flights where O-rings had been damaged , the view later highlighted by the Rogers Commission investigation. Looked at alone, those flights do not show an obvious temperature pattern: damage appeared at both cool and warm temperatures. The picture changes completely when you include the flights with no damage: What you see Only damaged flights All 23 flights Pattern with temperature Unclear Every flight below 65°F had O-ring damage Launches near 36°F None None. Challenger was far outside all experience Every launch below 65°F had damage. Most warm launches had none. And Challenger would launch more than 15 degrees colder than anything ever tried. Two views of the lesson Edward Tufte argued in Visual Explanations (1997) that the engineers' charts failed to show this relationship clearly. Others have pointed out that the engineers did raise temperature as the key concern, and that the decision was also shaped by schedule and organisational pressure. Both views lead to the same lesson for analysts: when the stakes are high, the evidence must be presented so the risk is impossible to miss. Data source O-ring data for the 23 flights before Challenger: UCI Machine Learning Repository, Challenger USA Space Shuttle O-Ring dataset (erosion or blow-by version), based on Draper (1995) and Dalal, Fowlkes and Hoadley (1989).

docs.text: Types of analysis: one, two or many variables ¶ Most questions start with one variable, then ask how it relates to a second, and finally how several factors work together. Each step needs different summaries and different charts. Synthetic data for illustration. Univariate analysis: one variable at a time ¶ Question: What does this one variable look like? You describe its centre (mean, median), spread (range, standard deviation) and shape (symmetric, skewed, any outliers). Kind of variable Good summaries Good charts Numbers (sales, days, age) Mean, median, minimum, maximum, spread Histogram, box plot Categories (region, product type) Counts and percentages Bar chart sorted by size Dates Counts per day, week or month Line chart over time Business examples: How long do deliveries usually take, and how long do the slowest ones take? Which product category sells most often? How many customer complaints arrive each week? Watch for A skewed shape. In the histogram above, most orders arrive within 1 to 5 days, but a long tail stretches past two weeks. The median (3 days) describes a typical order better than the mean (about 4 days), which the slow tail pulls upward. Bivariate analysis: two variables together ¶ Question: How does one variable change with another? The two variables are… Good summaries Good charts Number and number Correlation, trend line Scatter plot Category and number Mean or median per group Bar chart, box plot per group Category and category Counts in a cross-table Heat map, stacked or grouped bar Date and number Change over time Line chart Business examples: Does higher advertising spend go with higher revenue? Do some regions have longer delivery times than others? Which customer segments buy which product categories? Remember A relationship between two variables is a correlation , not proof of cause. See How statistics can mislead . Multivariate analysis: three or more variables ¶ Question: Does the relationship change when we account for something else? You add a third variable by using colour , size , small multiples (one small chart per group) or filters . Business examples: Does the link between ad spend and revenue differ by sales channel? Do delivery times by region change once we separate standard and express shipping? Is a profit drop explained by a change in the product mix? The second and third panels show exactly the same points. Colouring by channel in the third panel shows that "Store" tends to sit above the others at the same spend, on average. That pattern is invisible in the two-variable chart. Rule of thumb Add one variable at a time. If a chart needs a long explanation, split it into small multiples instead. What is the typical order value? Do larger discounts go with lower profit? Does the discount–profit relationship differ between furniture and office supplies? How many orders were placed each month? docs.text: Designing clear visuals ¶ A good chart lets the reader see the important comparison in seconds. That depends on removing what does not help, and on using what we know about how the eye and brain read pictures. The data-ink ratio ¶ Information designer Edward Tufte suggested a simple test. Of all the ink on a chart, how much actually shows data ? Everything else (heavy gridlines, borders, shading, 3D effects, decorative colours) is non-data ink. Tufte called unnecessary decoration chartjunk . Aim: increase the share of ink that carries data, without removing anything the reader needs. Synthetic data for illustration. What changed between the two versions: Removed the background shading, borders and hatching. Removed the gridlines and the value axis, and wrote the values directly on the bars. Sorted the bars, so the ranking is obvious. Used colour once , to point at the bar that matters. Turned the bars horizontal , so labels are easy to read. Do not overdo it Removing axis labels, units or context to make a chart "clean" makes it less useful. The goal is clarity, not minimalism. Pre-attentive attributes: what the eye sees first ¶ Some visual differences are noticed almost instantly, before we consciously think. These are called pre-attentive attributes . They include colour, size, position, orientation and boldness. Try it: count the number 3 in the top grid, then in the bottom grid. The bottom grid takes a second. The top one takes much longer. The only difference is one attribute: colour. Use this deliberately Make most of the chart grey, then use one strong colour or bold label for the thing you want the reader to see. If everything is highlighted, nothing is. Gestalt principles: how we group things ¶ Our brains automatically group what we see. Designers use these Gestalt principles to make related items look related. Principle What it means Use it in a chart or dashboard Proximity Things close together seem related Put related charts next to each other; leave space between unrelated ones Similarity Things that look alike (colour, shape) seem related Use the same colour for the same category on every chart Enclosure Things inside a shared border or shaded area seem grouped Shade a time period, such as a promotion, on a line chart Connection Things joined by a line seem related Lines connect points in a time series; avoid lines between unrelated categories Closure We complete incomplete shapes in our minds Charts rarely need full borders; the eye fills them in Continuity We follow smooth paths Align charts and labels so the eye flows across the page Colour with purpose ¶ One colour for one meaning. If "East" is blue in one chart, keep it blue in every chart. Grey for context, colour for focus. Do not rely on colour alone. Around one in twelve men has some colour-vision deficiency. Add labels or patterns too. Avoid rainbow palettes for numbers. Use light-to-dark shades of one colour for "more" and "less". Avoid red and green as the only difference. It is the most common pair people cannot tell apart. A clean-chart checklist ¶ Does the title say what the reader should notice, not just what is plotted? Are axes labelled with units, and do bars start at zero? Is everything that is not data as light as possible? Is colour used only where it means something? Can someone who cannot see colour still read it? Would a sorted table or a single number be clearer than a chart? Try it yourself ¶ Exercise 1: declutter Take a chart from a recent report at work, or any chart from the news. List every element that is not data. For each, decide: keep , lighten or remove . Sketch the improved version. Exercise 2: one highlight Sketch a bar chart of five products where only one product needs attention. Use grey for four bars and one colour for the fifth. Write a title that tells the reader what to notice. Exercise 3: spot the Gestalt Open any dashboard you use at work. Find one place where proximity or similarity helps you, and one place where it confuses you.

docs.text: Session 1 lab: Python, Colab and always plotting your data ¶ Learn just enough Python to run every notebook in this course, then use it to recreate the lecture's main lesson yourself: summary statistics are not enough, so always plot your data. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . How this lab works ¶ Part Level What you do A. Guided practice Core Follow step by step: Colab, variables, lists, tables, filters, groups and a chart B. Independent tasks Core and Stretch Use the same skills on a new question: Anscombe's quartet and your own analytical question C. Challenge Challenge Investigate the Datasaurus Dozen Core tasks are for everyone and are enough for your portfolio. Stretch tasks are for when you finish early. Challenge tasks are optional and need more reasoning. How the course uses code Every notebook gives you working code with explanations. You read it, run it, then change a few lines in the exercises. You will not be asked to write programs from scratch. Evidence you keep: your Anscombe statistics table and plots with a two-sentence lesson, and one workplace decision rewritten as an analytical question. Part A: Guided practice (Core) ¶ A1. Google Colab in two minutes ¶ Google Colab is a free website for running Python notebooks. You need a Google account. Go to colab.research.google.com , or use the Open in Colab button above. To open a file you downloaded, choose File → Upload notebook and select the .ipynb file. A notebook is made of cells . Text cells explain; code cells run. Click inside a code cell and press Shift + Enter to run it. The result appears underneath. Run cells from top to bottom . Later cells use results from earlier ones. If something goes wrong Choose Runtime → Restart session and run all . This starts again from the top and fixes most problems. A2. Values and variables ¶ A variable is a name for a value. The = sign stores the value under that name. price = 120 quantity = 3 total = price * quantity total 360 The last line of a cell is shown as the output. You can also use print to show several things. discount = 0.10 print ( "Total before discount:" , total ) print ( "Total after discount:" , total * ( 1 - discount )) Total before discount: 360 Total after discount: 324.0 Text goes inside quotes, and a list holds several values in square brackets. segment = "Consumer" monthly_sales = [ 120 , 95 , 140 , 180 ] print ( segment , "sales in four months:" , monthly_sales ) print ( "Total:" , sum ( monthly_sales )) print ( "Number of months:" , len ( monthly_sales )) Consumer sales in four months: [120, 95, 140, 180] Total: 535 Number of months: 4 Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # Change the numbers in the list, then run the cell again. monthly_sales = [ 120 , 95 , 140 , 180 ] print ( "Average monthly sales:" , sum ( monthly_sales ) / len ( monthly_sales )) Average monthly sales: 133.75 A3. Tables with pandas ¶ pandas is the Python library analysts use for tables. A table in pandas is called a DataFrame . We first import the library, then build a small made-up table of five orders. import pandas as pd orders = pd . DataFrame ({ "order_id" : [ "A1" , "A2" , "A3" , "A4" , "A5" ], "region" : [ "North" , "South" , "North" , "East" , "South" ], "sales" : [ 250.0 , 120.0 , 90.0 , 310.0 , 180.0 ], "items" : [ 3 , 1 , 2 , 4 , 2 ], }) orders .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } order_id region sales items 0 A1 North 250.0 3 1 A2 South 120.0 1 2 A3 North 90.0 2 3 A4 East 310.0 4 4 A5 South 180.0 2 Each row is one order. Each column has a name. A4. Select, filter, add up, count ¶ Select one column with its name in square brackets: orders [ "sales" ] 0 250.0 1 120.0 2 90.0 3 310.0 4 180.0 Name: sales, dtype: float64 Add up or average a column: print ( "Total sales:" , orders [ "sales" ] . sum ()) print ( "Average sales per order:" , orders [ "sales" ] . mean ()) Total sales: 950.0 Average sales per order: 190.0 Filter rows with a condition. This keeps only orders from the North region: north = orders [ orders [ "region" ] == "North" ] north .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } order_id region sales items 0 A1 North 250.0 3 2 A3 North 90.0 2 Count how many rows, and how many different values a column has: print ( "Number of orders:" , len ( orders )) print ( "Number of different regions:" , orders [ "region" ] . nunique ()) Number of orders: 5 Number of different regions: 3 Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # Change "North" to "South" and run again. How many South orders are there, # and what are their total sales? selected = orders [ orders [ "region" ] == "North" ] print ( len ( selected ), "orders, total sales" , selected [ "sales" ] . sum ()) 2 orders, total sales 340.0 A5. Group and summarise ¶ groupby splits the table into groups and summarises each one. Here: total sales for each region. sales_by_region = orders . groupby ( "region" )[ "sales" ] . sum () sales_by_region region East 310.0 North 340.0 South 300.0 Name: sales, dtype: float64 agg computes several summaries for each group at once. Each line inside it reads: new column name = (column to use, summary to compute) . You will use this pattern in Part B. orders . groupby ( "region" ) . agg ( orders = ( "order_id" , "count" ), total_sales = ( "sales" , "sum" ), average_sales = ( "sales" , "mean" ), ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } orders total_sales average_sales region East 1 310.0 310.0 North 2 340.0 170.0 South 2 300.0 150.0 A6. docs.text: A variable is a name for a value. The = sign stores the value under that name. price = 120 quantity = 3 total = price * quantity total 360 The last line of a cell is shown as the output. docs.text: pandas is the Python library analysts use for tables. A table in pandas is called a DataFrame . We first import the library, then build a small made-up table of five orders. import pandas as pd orders = pd . DataFrame ({ "order_id" : [ "A1" , "A2" , "A3" , "A4" , "A5" ], "region" : [ "North" , "South" , "North" , "East" , "South" ], "sales" : [ 250.0 , 120.0 , 90.0 , 310.0 , 180.0 ], "items" : [ 3 , 1 , 2 , 4 , 2 ], }) orders .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } order_id region sales items 0 A1 North 250.0 3 1 A2 South 120.0 1 2 A3 North 90.0 2 3 A4 East 310.0 4 4 A5 South 180.0 2 Each row is one order. Each column has a name. Useful first checks: print ( "Rows and columns:" , orders . shape ) print ( orders . dtypes ) Rows and columns: (5, 4) order_id object region object sales float64 items int64 dtype: object dtypes shows each column's type: object means text, int64 whole numbers, float64 decimals.

docs.text: Select one column with its name in square brackets: orders [ "sales" ] 0 250.0 1 120.0 2 90.0 3 310.0 4 180.0 Name: sales, dtype: float64 Add up or average a column: print ( "Total sales:" , orders [ "sales" ] . sum ()) print ( "Average sales per order:" , orders [ "sales" ] . mean ()) Total sales: 950.0 Average sales per order: 190.0 Filter rows with a condition. docs.text: groupby splits the table into groups and summarises each one. Here: total sales for each region. sales_by_region = orders . groupby ( "region" )[ "sales" ] . sum () sales_by_region region East 310.0 North 340.0 South 300.0 Name: sales, dtype: float64 agg computes several summaries for each group at once. Each line inside it reads: new column name = (column to use, summary to compute) . You will use this pattern in Part B. orders . groupby ( "region" ) . agg ( orders = ( "order_id" , "count" ), total_sales = ( "sales" , "sum" ), average_sales = ( "sales" , "mean" ), ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } orders total_sales average_sales region East 1 310.0 310.0 North 2 340.0 170.0 South 2 300.0 150.0

docs.text: pandas can draw a chart directly from a summary. kind="barh" makes horizontal bars. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt sales_by_region . sort_values () . plot ( kind = "barh" , title = "Sales by region (made-up data)" ) plt . xlabel ( "Sales" ) plt . ylabel ( "" ) plt . show () Your turn: change the code in the next cell and run it again. # Change "sales" to "items" to chart the number of items per region instead. # Then change the title to match. orders . groupby ( "region" )[ "sales" ] . sum () . sort_values () . plot ( kind = "barh" , title = "Sales by region" ) plt . show () A scatter plot shows two numbers for each row: one along the bottom, one up the side. docs.text: Session 1 lecture: Why data analytics matters ¶ Data analytics means making decisions with evidence instead of guesswork, and explaining that evidence so people act on it. This lecture shows why that matters, how an analysis is organised, and why you must always look at the data, not only its summary numbers. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . What you will be able to do ¶ Name the four levels of analytics and give a business example of each. Explain, with a real story, how data changed a decision and how it can fail. Turn a vague request into a question with a decision , population , period and measure . Show with code why summary statistics are not enough, using Anscombe's quartet and the Datasaurus Dozen. Name the most common ways numbers mislead. This lecture uses the Foundations pages as its reading. In the Lab you practise the Python behind every demonstration here. How to use the questions in this notebook Predict, then reveal boxes ask you to guess before running the next cell. Write your guess down first: being wrong is how you learn what to check. Check your understanding boxes are short questions to answer in your own words. Part 1: What is data analytics? ¶ Data analytics turns raw records into answers to business questions. It works at four levels, each building on the one before. Level Question it answers Everyday example Descriptive What happened? Sales fell last quarter. Diagnostic Why did it happen? The fall came almost entirely from one region after a competitor opened. Predictive What is likely to happen next? If nothing changes, that region will keep losing sales. Prescriptive What should we do about it? Test a local loyalty offer in that region before changing national prices. Most of this course works at the first two levels, done properly : a clear question, trustworthy data, correct calculations, honest charts and a recommendation a manager can act on. Later sessions add uncertainty and simple prediction. Check your understanding Which level is each statement? "Deliveries in the North got slower because the new carrier skips Saturday collections." "We expect about 400 returns in December." "Move the slow carrier's routes to the faster one for one month and measure the effect." "We shipped 12,000 parcels in October." Part 2: Real stories where data changed the outcome ¶ Each story teaches one habit you will use in every session. Read the full versions in Why data analytics matters . Story What happened The habit it teaches John Snow , London, 1854 Mapping cholera deaths showed them clustered around one water pump. Its handle was removed. A simple, well-chosen picture can overturn what "everyone knows". Florence Nightingale , 1850s Her diagrams showed most soldiers died of preventable disease in hospitals, not of wounds. Analysis only changes things when decision-makers understand it. Moneyball , baseball, 2002 A low-budget team found undervalued players by measuring on-base percentage. Measuring the right thing can matter more than having the most money. Walmart , hurricane, 2004 Sales patterns before earlier storms guided what to stock before a new one. Past patterns can guide everyday operational decisions. Google Flu Trends , 2008–2015 Estimating flu from searches worked, then failed badly and was shut down. More data is not automatically better data. Every result needs validation. Predict, then reveal Four of these stories are successes; one is a failure. Before reading the last row, ask yourself: what could make a model that once worked stop working? Then read the last row and the full story in Foundations. Check your understanding Snow and Nightingale both drew their evidence. Why might a chart persuade a decision-maker when a table of the same numbers does not? Part 3: From question to recommendation ¶ Every analysis in this course follows the same seven steps. The full version is in the analytical workflow . Step Ask Keep as evidence 1. Business question Who must decide what, and by when? The decision and a one-sentence question 2. Data understanding What does each row represent? What is missing? Grain, keys, units, scope 3. Preparation What changes are needed, and can someone repeat them? Untouched original data and a change log 4. Analysis Which comparison or metric answers the question? Metric definition, filters, calculation 5. Validation Do totals reconcile? Can I explain odd values? Spot checks, count and total checks 6. Visualisation Can the audience see the key comparison at a glance? A labelled chart with period, units and population 7. Recommendation What action follows, and what is still uncertain? Action, one caveat, a follow-up measure Step 1 in detail: a question you can answer ¶ A manager says: "Sales feel uneven across our customer groups." That is a feeling, not a question. A question you can answer with data names four things: Part Ask yourself Example Decision What will someone do differently? Choose one customer segment to investigate next month Population Which records count? All order lines in the sales table Period Which dates? Orders placed in 2023, 2024 and 2025 Measure What will we compare? Total sales by customer segment "Which customer segment had the highest total sales for orders placed in 2023–2025, so we can choose one segment to investigate next month?" Check your understanding A colleague asks: "Is the new website working?" Which of the four parts are missing? Suggest one value for each. Part 4: Always plot your data — Anscombe's quartet ¶ In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe made four small datasets to make one point. We build them in code, compute their summary statistics, and only then look at them. The code below stores all four datasets in one table. Each row is one point: which set it belongs to ( set ), and its x and y values. import pandas as pd # Anscombe's quartet (1973): four small datasets, eleven points each. x = [ 10 , 8 , 13 , 9 , 11 , 14 , 6 , 4 , 12 , 7 , 5 ] anscombe = pd . concat ([ pd . DataFrame ({ "set" : "I" , "x" : x , "y" : [ 8.04 , 6.95 , 7.58 , 8.81 , 8.33 , 9.96 , 7.24 , 4.26 , 10.84 , 4.82 , 5.68 ]}), pd . DataFrame ({ "set" : "II" , "x" : x , "y" : [ 9.14 , 8.14 , 8.74 , 8.77 , 9.26 , 8.10 , 6.13 , 3.10 , 9.13 , 7.26 , 4.74 ]}), pd . DataFrame ({ "set" : "III" , "x" : x , "y" : [ 7.46 , 6.77 , 12.74 , 7.11 , 7.81 , 8.84 , 6.08 , 5.39 , 8.15 , 6.42 , 5.73 ]}), pd . DataFrame ({ "set" : "IV" , "x" : [ 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 19 , 8 , 8 , 8 ], "y" : [ 6.58 , 5.76 , 7.71 , 8.84 , 8.47 , 7.04 , 5.25 , 12.50 , 5.56 , 7.91 , 6.89 ]}), ], ignore_index = True ) print ( "Rows, columns:" , anscombe . shape ) anscombe . head () Rows, columns: (44, 3) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } set x y 0 I 10 8.04 1 I 8 6.95 2 I 13 7.58 3 I 9 8.81 4 I 11 8.33 Now the summary statistics for each set. groupby("set") splits the table into the four sets; agg computes several summaries for each one. summary = anscombe . groupby ( "set" ) . agg ( mean_x = ( "x" , "mean" ), mean_y = ( "y" , "mean" ), sd_x = ( "x" , "std" ), sd_y = ( "y" , "std" ), ) summary [ "correlation" ] = anscombe . groupby ( "set" )[[ "x" , "y" ]] . apply ( lambda d : d [ "x" ] . corr ( d [ "y" ])) summary . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } mean_x mean_y sd_x sd_y correlation set I 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 II 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 III 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 IV 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 Finally, the straight line that best fits each set. np.polyfit(x, y, 1) returns the slope and the intercept of that line. import numpy as np for name , points in anscombe . groupby ( "set" ): slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], 1 ) print ( f "Set { name : >3 } : best-fit line y = { intercept : .2f } + { slope : .3f } x" ) Set I: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Set II: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Set III: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Set IV: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Predict, then reveal Read the outputs above. The four sets share their means, spreads, correlation and best-fit line. Sketch what you think a scatter plot of each set looks like. Will the four pictures be similar? Then run the next cell. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 2 , 2 , figsize = ( 8 , 6.5 ), sharex = True , sharey = True ) line_x = np . array ([ 2 , 20 ]) for ax , ( name , points ) in zip ( axes . flat , anscombe . groupby ( "set" )): slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], 1 ) ax . plot ( line_x , intercept + slope * line_x , color = "#d95f02" , linewidth = 2 ) ax . scatter ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], s = 40 , color = "#1f78b4" , zorder = 3 ) ax . set_title ( f "Set { name } " ) for ax in axes [ 1 ]: ax . set_xlabel ( "x" ) for ax in axes [:, 0 ]: ax . set_ylabel ( "y" ) fig . suptitle ( "Same statistics, same trend line, four different stories" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Set What the picture shows What the statistics hide I A loose, roughly straight-line relationship Nothing: the summary describes it well II A smooth curve The relationship is not a straight line III A perfect line except for one outlier One unusual point drags the trend line IV Almost every point has the same x; one far point creates the "trend" Remove that point and there is no trend to measure Remember Summary statistics compress data, and compression throws information away. A chart shows you what was thrown away. Plot first, then summarise. Check your understanding In set IV, what happens to the correlation if the one point far to the right is a data-entry error and you remove it? Why can you not even compute it? Part 5: The Datasaurus Dozen ¶ In 2017 Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice pushed Anscombe's idea further. Starting from a dinosaur drawn with data points, they nudged the points step by step into twelve other shapes while keeping the summary statistics almost identical. The next cell downloads their data from a fixed public address and checks the file's fingerprint, so everyone gets exactly the same version. import hashlib import io import urllib.request import pandas as pd # The Datasaurus Dozen (Matejka and Fitzmaurice, 2017), from the open-source # datasauRus package (MIT licence). The link points to one fixed version, and the # fingerprint check confirms we got exactly that file. DATASAURUS_URL = ( "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jumpingrivers/datasauRus/" "94f3c3a82660e256b84f70961f50dc0e216757de/inst/extdata/DatasaurusDozen-Long.tsv" ) DATASAURUS_SHA256 = "c8c4792c3ed15238ba07dad6ab778adc79d72e3e1324ead4d8c1ae52849780f8" file_bytes = urllib . request . urlopen ( DATASAURUS_URL ) . read () assert hashlib . sha256 ( file_bytes ) . hexdigest () == DATASAURUS_SHA256 , "Unexpected file: ask your instructor." dozen = pd . read_csv ( io . BytesIO ( file_bytes ), sep = " \t " ) print ( "Rows, columns:" , dozen . shape ) print ( "Datasets:" , dozen [ "dataset" ] . nunique ()) dozen . head () Rows, columns: (1846, 3) Datasets: 13 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } dataset x y 0 dino 55.3846 97.1795 1 dino 51.5385 96.0256 2 dino 46.1538 94.4872 3 dino 42.8205 91.4103 4 dino 40.7692 88.3333 Predict, then reveal The table has thirteen datasets. Their names ( dino , star , circle , …) are a hint. First look at the statistics in the next cell. Would you have guessed the datasets had different shapes from these numbers alone? dozen_summary = dozen . groupby ( "dataset" ) . agg ( mean_x = ( "x" , "mean" ), mean_y = ( "y" , "mean" ), sd_x = ( "x" , "std" ), sd_y = ( "y" , "std" ), ) dozen_summary [ "correlation" ] = dozen . groupby ( "dataset" )[[ "x" , "y" ]] . apply ( lambda d : d [ "x" ] . corr ( d [ "y" ])) dozen_summary . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } mean_x mean_y sd_x sd_y correlation dataset away 54.27 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.06 bullseye 54.27 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.07 circle 54.27 47.84 16.76 26.93 -0.07 dino 54.26 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.06 dots 54.26 47.84 16.77 26.93 -0.06 h_lines 54.26 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.06 high_lines 54.27 47.84 16.77 26.94 -0.07 slant_down 54.27 47.84 16.77 26.94 -0.07 slant_up 54.27 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.07 star 54.27 47.84 16.77 26.93 -0.06 v_lines 54.27 47.84 16.77 26.94 -0.07 wide_lines 54.27 47.83 16.77 26.94 -0.07 x_shape 54.26 47.84 16.77 26.93 -0.07 Now draw one small scatter plot per dataset. Charts like this, one per group on the same axes, are called small multiples . import matplotlib.pyplot as plt names = dozen [ "dataset" ] . unique () fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 3 , 5 , figsize = ( 12 , 7 ), sharex = True , sharey = True ) for ax in axes . flat : ax . set_visible ( False ) for ax , name in zip ( axes . flat , names ): points = dozen [ dozen [ "dataset" ] == name ] ax . set_visible ( True ) ax . scatter ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], s = 8 ) ax . set_title ( name . replace ( "_" , " " )) fig . suptitle ( "The Datasaurus Dozen: one scatter plot per dataset" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () A report saying "x and y are essentially unrelated, centred around the same values" would be true for every panel, including the dinosaur. At work You will rarely meet a dinosaur in a sales report. You will meet the same problem in everyday forms: an average delivery time that hides a group of customers waiting weeks; one huge order that makes a quiet month look like growth; two stores with the same average sales but very different patterns. See Statistics are not enough . Check your understanding Why are the thirteen panels drawn with the same axes? What could go wrong if each panel chose its own axis range? Part 6: A preview of how numbers mislead ¶ Numbers feel objective, but the same data can tell very different stories depending on how it is summarised and drawn. Here is one trap, live. Both charts below show the same two numbers . products = [ "Product A" , "Product B" ] satisfaction = [ 96 , 98 ] # made-up percentages fig , ( left , right ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 9 , 3.5 )) left . bar ( products , satisfaction , color = "#1f78b4" ) left . set_ylim ( 95 , 98.5 ) left . set_title ( "Axis starts at 95" ) right . bar ( products , satisfaction , color = "#1f78b4" ) right . set_ylim ( 0 , 100 ) right . set_title ( "Axis starts at 0" ) for ax in ( left , right ): ax . set_ylabel ( "Satisfied customers (%)" ) fig . suptitle ( "Same data, two impressions (made-up numbers)" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () We judge bars by their length , so bar charts should start at zero. On the left, Product B looks several times better; on the right you see the truth: two products almost the same. The full list of traps is in How statistics can mislead . Later sessions return to each one with real data. Trap One-line warning Where we meet it again Correlation is not causation Two things moving together may share a hidden cause Correlation and regression Simpson's paradox A total can reverse the story of every part Metrics and KPIs Misleading axes Where the axis starts changes the impression Visualisation principles Cherry-picked time windows The chosen start and end dates can create any trend Time series and trends Which average? Mean and median can tell different stories Descriptive statistics Percentages without the base "Up 200%" means little without the counts Marketing case Survivorship bias The records you see may be only the survivors Business cases A checklist for any number you are shown Compared to what? Who or what is included? What is the denominator? Could something else explain it? How is it drawn? Summary ¶ Analytics answers four kinds of question: what happened, why, what next and what to do. Good analysis starts from a decision , and a good question names a decision, population, period and measure. The seven-step workflow keeps evidence at each step so someone else can check your work. Different data can share identical summary statistics. Always plot your data. Numbers mislead through causation claims, mixing groups, axes, time windows, averages, missing bases and survivors. Quiz ¶ Answer these in your own words. We go through them at the start of the next lecture. Name the four levels of analytics, and give a one-line business example of the diagnostic level. Google Flu Trends worked for a while and then failed. Give one reason, and the habit this teaches. Rewrite "How are our stores doing?" as an analytical question that names a decision, population, period and measure. Two datasets have the same mean, standard deviation and correlation. Can you conclude they look alike? What should you do? In Anscombe's set III, what single feature of the data changes the best-fit line? Why should a bar chart's value axis start at zero, while a line chart's axis may not? A report says "Customers who used our app spent 30% more." Give one explanation other than "the app made them spend more". In the seven-step workflow, what is the difference between analysis and validation ? Independent: recreate the Anscombe statistics and plots yourself, and rewrite a workplace decision as an analytical question. DataFrame ({ "set" : "IV" , "x" : [ 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 19 , 8 , 8 , 8 ], "y" : [ 6.58 , 5.76 , 7.71 , 8.84 , 8.47 , 7.04 , 5.25 , 12.50 , 5.56 , 7.91 , 6.89 ]}), ], ignore_index = True ) print ( "Rows, columns:" , anscombe . shape ) anscombe . head () Rows, columns: (44, 3) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } set x y 0 I 10 8.04 1 I 8 6.95 2 I 13 7.58 3 I 9 8.81 4 I 11 8.33 Now the summary statistics for each set. groupby("set") splits the table into the four sets; agg computes several summaries for each one. summary = anscombe . groupby ( "set" ) . agg ( mean_x = ( "x" , "mean" ), mean_y = ( "y" , "mean" ), sd_x = ( "x" , "std" ), sd_y = ( "y" , "std" ), ) summary [ "correlation" ] = anscombe . groupby ( "set" )[[ "x" , "y" ]] . apply ( lambda d : d [ "x" ] . corr ( d [ "y" ])) summary . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } mean_x mean_y sd_x sd_y correlation set I 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 II 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 III 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 IV 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 Finally, the straight line that best fits each set. np.polyfit(x, y, 1) returns the slope and the intercept of that line. import numpy as np for name , points in anscombe . groupby ( "set" ): slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], 1 ) print ( f "Set { name : >3 } : best-fit line y = { intercept : .2f } + { slope : .3f } x" ) Set I: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Set II: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Set III: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Set IV: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Predict, then reveal Read the outputs above. The four sets share their means, spreads, correlation and best-fit line. Sketch what you think a scatter plot of each set looks like. Will the four pictures be similar? Then run the next cell. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 2 , 2 , figsize = ( 8 , 6.5 ), sharex = True , sharey = True ) line_x = np . array ([ 2 , 20 ]) for ax , ( name , points ) in zip ( axes . flat , anscombe . groupby ( "set" )): slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], 1 ) ax . plot ( line_x , intercept + slope * line_x , color = "#d95f02" , linewidth = 2 ) ax . scatter ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], s = 40 , color = "#1f78b4" , zorder = 3 ) ax . set_title ( f "Set { name } " ) for ax in axes [ 1 ]: ax . set_xlabel ( "x" ) for ax in axes [:, 0 ]: ax . set_ylabel ( "y" ) fig . suptitle ( "Same statistics, same trend line, four different stories" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Set What the picture shows What the statistics hide I A loose, roughly straight-line relationship Nothing: the summary describes it well II A smooth curve The relationship is not a straight line III A perfect line except for one outlier One unusual point drags the trend line IV Almost every point has the same x; one far point creates the "trend" Remove that point and there is no trend to measure Remember Summary statistics compress data, and compression throws information away. A chart shows you what was thrown away. Plot first, then summarise. Check your understanding In set IV, what happens to the correlation if the one point far to the right is a data-entry error and you remove it? Why can you not even compute it?
