docs.text: Session 3 lecture: Cleaning and preparing data ¶ Real data arrives with gaps, repeats, odd values, numbers stored as text and tables that do not quite fit together. Cleaning is not tidying up: every fix is a decision that can change the answer, so you make it deliberately and write it down. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . Recap quiz ¶ Start by answering the quiz at the end of the Session 2 lecture, 02_data_and_grain_lecture.md . Write your answers down before the discussion. What you will be able to explain ¶ Why the raw data is never overwritten, and what a cleaning log records. Three reasons data goes missing , and when to drop, flag or keep a missing value. The difference between a duplicate and a legitimate repeat . Why an outlier is something to investigate, not something to delete. How to turn numbers and dates stored as text into real numbers and dates, safely. Join types and cardinality , and how a join can silently multiply rows. How to reshape a table between wide and long. Part Topic 1 Raw data and the cleaning log 2 Missing data 3 Duplicates 4 Outliers 5 Text, numbers, dates and encodings 6 Joins and cardinality 7 Reshaping 8 Worked case: World Cup attendance How to use this notebook When you see Predict, then reveal , write your guess first and only then run the cell. Every demonstration uses a small made-up table, so you can see the whole problem at once. The worked case at the end uses real data. Run the next cell first. It loads the libraries, sets the chart style and defines fetch , which downloads a file and checks it is exactly the version this lecture was written for. import hashlib import io import urllib.request import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd def fetch ( url , expected_sha256 ): """Download a file into memory and check its SHA-256 fingerprint.""" with urllib . request . urlopen ( url ) as response : data = response . read () if hashlib . sha256 ( data ) . hexdigest () != expected_sha256 : print ( "WARNING: this file has changed since the course was written:" , url ) print ( "Your numbers may differ from the lecture. Ask your facilitator." ) return data pd . set_option ( "display.float_format" , " {:,.2f} " . format ) plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 8 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.prop_cycle" : plt . cycler ( color = [ "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]), "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) print ( "Setup complete." ) Setup complete. Part 1: Raw data and the cleaning log ¶ Two rules come before any cleaning technique. Never overwrite the raw data. Read the original file, clean a copy in code, and keep the original exactly as it arrived. If a decision turns out wrong, you can rerun from the start. Log every change. A cleaning log records what changed, why, and how many rows or values it affected. A reader who sees your result can then see exactly how you got there. Step What changed Why Rows before Rows after Check 1 Removed exact duplicate rows Same match loaded twice … … Match count equals the official count 2 Converted attendance text to numbers Stored with dots as thousands separators … … No values lost; totals plausible In pandas, the habit looks like this: clean = raw.copy() , then change clean , and print a row count after every step. Remember Cleaning code is part of the analysis. If you fix something by hand in a spreadsheet, nobody (including you next month) can repeat it. Part 2: Missing data ¶ A blank cell is not just an empty space: why it is empty decides what you can safely do with it. There are three broad reasons. Type Plain meaning Example Risk if you just ignore the blanks Missing completely at random (MCAR) Blanks happen by chance, unrelated to anything A scanner randomly fails on some parcels Fewer rows, but averages stay fair Missing at random (MAR) Blanks depend on another column you can see One warehouse never records delivery times Averages lean towards the warehouses that do record Missing not at random (MNAR) Blanks depend on the missing value itself Very late deliveries are the ones nobody logs Averages are biased, and the data cannot show it The made-up example below has 200 deliveries. We know every true delivery time, then hide some of them in two different ways. rng = np . random . default_rng ( 3 ) true_days = rng . gamma ( shape = 3 , scale = 1.5 , size = 200 ) . round ( 1 ) deliveries = pd . DataFrame ({ "delivery_days" : true_days }) # MCAR: hide 25% of values purely at random. random_blank = rng . random ( 200 ) < 0.25 deliveries [ "recorded_mcar" ] = deliveries [ "delivery_days" ] . mask ( random_blank ) # MNAR: the later the delivery, the more likely nobody recorded it. late_blank = rng . random ( 200 ) < ( deliveries [ "delivery_days" ] / deliveries [ "delivery_days" ] . max ()) deliveries [ "recorded_mnar" ] = deliveries [ "delivery_days" ] . mask ( late_blank ) deliveries . head ( 8 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } delivery_days recorded_mcar recorded_mnar 0 11.40 11.40 NaN 1 5.10 5.10 NaN 2 3.00 3.00 3.00 3 0.80 0.80 0.80 4 2.20 2.20 2.20 5 4.60 NaN NaN 6 3.30 3.30 3.30 7 1.90 NaN 1.90 Predict, then reveal ¶ Both recorded columns have some values hidden. pandas skips blanks when it computes a mean. Which recorded mean will be close to the true mean, and which will be too low? summary = pd . DataFrame ({ "values_present" : deliveries . notna () . sum (), "mean_days" : deliveries . mean (), }) summary .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } values_present mean_days delivery_days 200 4.79 recorded_mcar 143 4.65 recorded_mnar 132 4.00 The randomly hidden column keeps a fair average, because the blanks are a random sample. The second column loses mostly the late deliveries, so its average looks better than reality, and nothing in the recorded data warns you. Drop, flag or keep? ¶ Choice What you do Use it when Drop Remove rows with the blank Blanks are few and plausibly random, and you report how many you dropped Flag Add a column such as delivery_missing = 1 and keep the row The fact that a value is missing is itself information Keep as missing Leave NaN , let each calculation skip it, and say so Most of the time: it is honest and reversible Fill (impute) Replace the blank with an estimate Only with a stated method and a reason; never silently, never with 0 unless 0 is true pandas makes flagging and counting easy: deliveries [ "mnar_missing" ] = deliveries [ "recorded_mnar" ] . isna () . astype ( int ) print ( "Missing values:" , deliveries [ "mnar_missing" ] . sum (), "of" , len ( deliveries )) print ( "Share missing: " , f " { deliveries [ 'mnar_missing' ] . mean () : .0% } " ) Missing values: 68 of 200 Share missing: 34% Check your understanding 1 A customer survey asks for household income. The income question is left blank more often by people with very high incomes. Which type of missingness is this? What happens to the average income if you simply drop the blanks, and what would you write in your report? A common mistake Filling blanks with 0 ( fillna(0) ) turns "we do not know" into "it was zero". A missing sales figure is not zero sales, and a missing delivery time is not a same-day delivery. Part 3: Duplicates ¶ A duplicate is the same real-world event recorded more than once: a file loaded twice, a form submitted twice. A legitimate repeat is two real events that happen to look alike: a customer who really did buy the same item twice on one day. The difference is not visible from the values alone. You decide using the grain and the keys from Session 2. lines = pd . DataFrame ({ "line_id" : [ 101 , 102 , 103 , 103 , 104 ], "order_id" : [ "A1" , "A1" , "A2" , "A2" , "A3" ], "product" : [ "Pen" , "Pen" , "Desk" , "Desk" , "Lamp" ], "quantity" : [ 1 , 1 , 1 , 1 , 2 ], }) lines .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } line_id order_id product quantity 0 101 A1 Pen 1 1 102 A1 Pen 1 2 103 A2 Desk 1 3 103 A2 Desk 1 4 104 A3 Lamp 2 Predict, then reveal ¶ How many rows does duplicated() mark, and are they all mistakes? Look at line_id and order_id before you run the cell. print ( "Exact duplicate rows: " , lines . duplicated () . sum ()) print ( "Repeats ignoring line_id: " , lines . duplicated ( subset = [ "order_id" , "product" , "quantity" ]) . sum ()) lines [ lines . duplicated ( keep = False )] Exact duplicate rows: 1 Repeats ignoring line_id: 2 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } line_id order_id product quantity 2 103 A2 Desk 1 3 103 A2 Desk 1 Line 103 appears twice with every value equal, including its own key. That is a true duplicate: the same line loaded twice. Remove one copy. Lines 101 and 102 share the order and product but have different line IDs . Two pens on two lines is a legitimate repeat. Removing one would lose a real sale. Check pandas What it finds Exact duplicate rows df.duplicated() Rows equal in every column Repeats on chosen columns df.duplicated(subset=[...]) Rows equal on the columns that define one real event Is the key unique? df["key"].is_unique Whether the primary key can be trusted Show all copies df[df.duplicated(keep=False)] Both the first copy and its repeats, to inspect Remove exact duplicates df.drop_duplicates() Keeps the first copy of each Check your understanding 2 A payments table has two rows with the same customer, amount and date, but different payment_id values. Are they duplicates? What extra information would you look for before deciding? Part 4: Outliers ¶ An outlier is a value far from the rest. Some are errors (a typing slip adds a zero). Some are real and important (one huge corporate order). Detecting an outlier is mechanical; deciding what it means is not. A common rule flags values more than 1.5 × IQR beyond the quartiles. The IQR (interquartile range) is the distance between the 25th and 75th percentiles; you will meet it properly in Session 4. order_values = pd . Series ( [ 42 , 55 , 38 , 61 , 47 , 53 , 49 , 58 , 44 , 51 , 4900 , 1250 ], index = [ f "O { i : 02d } " for i in range ( 1 , 13 )], name = "order_value" , ) q1 , q3 = order_values . quantile ([ 0.25 , 0.75 ]) iqr = q3 - q1 low , high = q1 - 1.5 * iqr , q3 + 1.5 * iqr print ( f "Flag values below { low : ,.1f } or above { high : ,.1f } " ) order_values [( order_values < low ) | ( order_values > high )] Flag values below 27.5 or above 77.5 O11 4900 O12 1250 Name: order_value, dtype: int64 Predict, then reveal ¶ Two orders are flagged. Suppose a check with the sales team shows that O11 was typed as 4900 instead of 49.00, and O12 is a genuine bulk order from a school. What happens to the average if you delete both, and what if you fix only the error? fixed = order_values . copy () fixed [ "O11" ] = 49.00 # confirmed typing error, corrected with a logged reason pd . Series ({ "Average, raw" : order_values . mean (), "Average, both outliers deleted" : order_values . drop ([ "O11" , "O12" ]) . mean (), "Average, error fixed, real order kept" : fixed . mean (), "Median, raw" : order_values . median (), }) Average, raw 554.00 Average, both outliers deleted 49.80 Average, error fixed, real order kept 149.75 Median, raw 52.00 dtype: float64 Deleting both outliers hides a real customer and understates the business. Fixing only the confirmed error gives the honest figure. Notice also that the median hardly moves: it resists extreme values, which is why it suits skewed data (Session 4). Situation Action Confirmed error with a known correct value Fix it, log the old and new value and the evidence Impossible value (negative age, date in the future) and no correction available Set to missing and flag it Real but extreme Keep it; consider reporting the median too, or showing results with and without it Not sure Keep it, flag it, and ask the data owner Check your understanding 3 A shipping table has one shipment that took 210 days. Give one explanation that makes it an error and one that makes it real. What would you do before your report goes out? Part 5: Text, numbers, dates and encodings ¶ Files often store numbers and dates as text . pandas then cannot add them up, sort them correctly or compare them with dates. Numbers with thousands separators ¶ Many countries write one million and a half as 1.500.000 and use the comma for decimals. Python reads a dot as a decimal point. attendance_text = pd . Series ([ "590.549" , "1.045.246" , "363.000" , "819.810" ], name = "attendance" ) naive = pd . to_numeric ( attendance_text , errors = "coerce" ) careful = pd . to_numeric ( attendance_text . str . replace ( "." , "" , regex = False )) pd . DataFrame ({ "text" : attendance_text , "naive" : naive , "careful" : careful }) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } text naive careful 0 590.549 590.55 590549 1 1.045.246 NaN 1045246 2 363.000 363.00 363000 3 819.810 819.81 819810 Predict, then reveal (look at the output above) ¶ The naive conversion reads 590.549 as five hundred and ninety, and it cannot read 1.045.246 at all, so errors="coerce" silently turned it into NaN . The careful version removes the dots first, so every value becomes a whole number. errors="coerce" is useful, but always count how many values became NaN : each one is a value you just lost. Dates written as text ¶ 03/04/2024 is the 3rd of April in most of the world and March 4th in the United States. Tell pandas the format instead of letting it guess. date_text = pd . Series ([ "03/04/2024" , "15/04/2024" , "28/02/2024" ]) day_first = pd . to_datetime ( date_text , format = " %d /%m/%Y" ) print ( day_first . dt . strftime ( " %d %B %Y" ) . tolist ()) month_first = pd . to_datetime ( date_text , format = "%m/ %d /%Y" , errors = "coerce" ) print ( "Values that fail as month/day/year:" , month_first . isna () . sum ()) ['03 April 2024', '15 April 2024', '28 February 2024'] Values that fail as month/day/year: 2 Encodings and stray spaces ¶ Text is stored as bytes, and the encoding says how to turn bytes into letters. When a file is saved in one encoding and read in another, letters such as ô or é come out as strange symbols. If the symbol is the Unicode replacement character, the original letter is lost : you can only restore it from outside knowledge. Invisible spaces cause a quieter problem: "Paris " and "Paris" look identical on screen but count as two different cities. cities = pd . Series ([ "Paris" , "Paris " , " Lyon" , "Lyon" , "Malm \ufffd " ]) print ( "Different values before strip:" , cities . nunique ()) print ( "Different values after strip: " , cities . str . strip () . nunique ()) print ( "Values containing the replacement character:" , cities . str . contains ( " \ufffd " ) . sum ()) Different values before strip: 5 Different values after strip: 3 Values containing the replacement character: 1 Problem Detect Fix Numbers stored as text df.dtypes shows object pd.to_numeric , after removing separators; count new NaN s Dates stored as text object type; odd sorting pd.to_datetime(..., format=...) Leading or trailing spaces (s != s.str.strip()).sum() s.str.strip() Broken characters s.str.contains("\ufffd") Flag; correct from a trusted list, never by guessing Different spellings of one thing value_counts() A documented mapping, e.g. {"IR Iran": "Iran"} Check your understanding 4 After pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce") a column of 5,000 prices has 37 NaN values that were not there before. What do you do next, and what goes in the cleaning log? Part 6: Joins and cardinality ¶ A join ( merge in pandas) puts columns from two tables side by side by matching a key. Two choices decide the result. 1. Which rows to keep ( how ) how= Keeps "inner" Only keys found in both tables "left" Every row of the left table; blanks where the right has no match "right" Every row of the right table "outer" Every key from either table 2. Cardinality: how many matches each key has Cardinality Meaning Example Row count after a left join One-to-one Each key once on both sides Employee ↔ employee contract Unchanged Many-to-one Many left rows share one right row Order lines → region manager Unchanged One-to-many One left row matches many right rows Order → its lines Grows Many-to-many Keys repeat on both sides Orders by region × campaigns by region Multiplies orders = pd . DataFrame ({ "order_id" : [ "A1" , "A2" , "A3" , "A4" ], "region" : [ "North" , "North" , "South" , "East" ], "sales" : [ 100 , 250 , 80 , 120 ], }) managers = pd . DataFrame ({ "region" : [ "North" , "South" , "West" ], "manager" : [ "Asha" , "Ben" , "Chen" ], }) joined = orders . merge ( managers , on = "region" , how = "left" , validate = "many_to_one" , indicator = True ) print ( "Rows before:" , len ( orders ), "| rows after:" , len ( joined )) joined Rows before: 4 | rows after: 4 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } order_id region sales manager _merge 0 A1 North 100 Asha both 1 A2 North 250 Asha both 2 A3 South 80 Ben both 3 A4 East 120 NaN left_only indicator=True adds a _merge column showing where each row found a match: East has no manager ( left_only ), and the manager for West has no orders, so that row does not appear in a left join. validate="many_to_one" makes pandas check that each region appears only once in managers . Predict, then reveal: the row explosion ¶ North changed manager during the year, so someone adds a second North row to the managers table. Sales are then totalled from the joined table. What happens to total Sales? managers_history = pd . DataFrame ({ "region" : [ "North" , "North" , "South" , "West" ], "manager" : [ "Asha" , "Dev" , "Ben" , "Chen" ], }) exploded = orders . merge ( managers_history , on = "region" , how = "left" ) print ( "Rows before:" , len ( orders ), "| rows after:" , len ( exploded )) print ( "Total sales before the join:" , orders [ "sales" ] . sum ()) print ( "Total sales after the join: " , exploded [ "sales" ] . sum ()) Rows before: 4 | rows after: 6 Total sales before the join: 550 Total sales after the join: 900 Each North order now matches two manager rows, so it appears twice and its sales are counted twice. No error appears. This is the most common way joins go wrong. validate turns the silent mistake into a loud one: try : orders . merge ( managers_history , on = "region" , how = "left" , validate = "many_to_one" ) except pd . errors . MergeError as problem : print ( "MergeError:" , problem ) MergeError: Merge keys are not unique in right dataset; not a many-to-one merge Remember: three checks for every join Before: is the key unique on the side that should be unique? ( df["key"].is_unique ) During: validate= with the cardinality you expect, and indicator=True to see unmatched rows. After: compare row counts and one total (such as Sales) before and after. Check your understanding 5 You left-join 6,000 order lines to a product table on product_id and get 6,240 rows. What does that tell you about the product table? Which validate value would have caught it? Part 7: Reshaping ¶ The same numbers can be laid out wide (one column per month, easy to read) or long (one row per item per month, easy to filter, group and chart). Session 2 called the long layout tidy . wide = pd . DataFrame ({ "store" : [ "Central" , "Harbour" ], "Jan" : [ 120 , 95 ], "Feb" : [ 130 , 101 ], "Mar" : [ 125 , 110 ], }) long = wide . melt ( id_vars = "store" , var_name = "month" , value_name = "sales" ) long .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } store month sales 0 Central Jan 120 1 Harbour Jan 95 2 Central Feb 130 3 Harbour Feb 101 4 Central Mar 125 5 Harbour Mar 110 back_to_wide = long . pivot ( index = "store" , columns = "month" , values = "sales" )[[ "Jan" , "Feb" , "Mar" ]] print ( "Same total before and after reshaping:" , wide [[ "Jan" , "Feb" , "Mar" ]] . sum () . sum () == back_to_wide . sum () . sum ()) back_to_wide Same total before and after reshaping: True .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } month Jan Feb Mar store Central 120 130 125 Harbour 95 101 110 Function Direction Typical use melt wide → long Columns that are really values of a variable (months, years, products) pivot long → wide A readable table for a report pivot_table long → wide, with a summary When pairs repeat and need adding up A quick total before and after reshaping catches lost or duplicated values. Check your understanding 6 long.pivot(...) raises an error saying the index contains duplicate entries. What does that tell you about the long table, and which function would you use instead? Part 8: Worked case — World Cup attendance ¶ The World Cup results workbook from Tableau's sample-data page has a sheet called WorldCups , with one row per tournament since 1930. We want total attendance per tournament. About the data The workbook was compiled for Sports Viz Sundays 2018 and is published in Tableau's sample-data catalog. We download it from that source for learning; we do not redistribute it, and the course does not claim a licence for it. WORLD_CUP_URL = "https://public.tableau.com/app/sample-data/world_cup_results.xlsx" WORLD_CUP_SHA256 = "dbad641c16c914c14fef0c95bf6f918fa5d2746671e4dc269b6a1ec3e2a3cc45" world_cup_bytes = fetch ( WORLD_CUP_URL , WORLD_CUP_SHA256 ) cups = pd . read_excel ( io . BytesIO ( world_cup_bytes ), sheet_name = "WorldCups" ) cups [[ "Year" , "Country" , "MatchesPlayed" , "Attendance" ]] . head ( 8 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Year Country MatchesPlayed Attendance 0 1930 Uruguay 18 590.55 1 1934 Italy 17 363 2 1938 France 18 375.70 3 1950 Brazil 22 1.045.246 4 1954 Switzerland 26 768.61 5 1958 Sweden 35 819.81 6 1962 Chile 32 893.17 7 1966 England 32 1.563.135 Step 1: Profile the column ¶ The Attendance values look like numbers with dots. Check what Python actually stored in each cell. print ( "Column type:" , cups [ "Attendance" ] . dtype ) cups [ "Attendance" ] . map ( lambda value : type ( value ) . __name__ ) . value_counts () Column type: object Attendance str 14 float 5 int 1 Name: count, dtype: int64 The column mixes text and numbers . Excel stored the big values (two dots) as text, but read values with one dot as decimal numbers : 590.549 became five hundred and ninety point five (pandas shows it rounded as 590.55 ), and 375.700 lost its trailing zeros to become 375.7 . Step 2: Predict, then reveal ¶ If you just convert the column with pd.to_numeric , what will the 1930 value be, and how many values will fail? naive = pd . to_numeric ( cups [ "Attendance" ], errors = "coerce" ) print ( "Values that failed:" , naive . isna () . sum (), "of" , len ( cups )) naive . head ( 4 ) Values that failed: 14 of 20 0 590.55 1 363.00 2 375.70 3 NaN Name: Attendance, dtype: float64 Step 3: A careful conversion ¶ Each kind of cell needs its own rule: Text such as "1.045.246" : remove the dots. Numbers such as 590.549 or 375.7 : these were thousands, so multiply by 1,000 and round. def parse_attendance ( value ): if isinstance ( value , str ): return int ( value . replace ( "." , "" )) return int ( round ( value * 1000 )) cups [ "attendance" ] = cups [ "Attendance" ] . map ( parse_attendance ) cups [ "attendance_per_match" ] = cups [ "attendance" ] / cups [ "MatchesPlayed" ] cups [[ "Year" , "Attendance" , "attendance" , "attendance_per_match" ]] . head ( 8 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Year Attendance attendance attendance_per_match 0 1930 590.55 590549 32,808.28 1 1934 363 363000 21,352.94 2 1938 375.70 375700 20,872.22 3 1950 1.045.246 1045246 47,511.18 4 1954 768.61 768607 29,561.81 5 1958 819.81 819810 23,423.14 6 1962 893.17 893172 27,911.62 7 1966 1.563.135 1563135 48,847.97 Step 4: Check the result is plausible ¶ A conversion can run without errors and still be wrong. Plot attendance per match : if any value were off by a factor of 1,000, it would stand out at once. ax = cups . plot ( x = "Year" , y = "attendance_per_match" , kind = "bar" , legend = False , title = "Average attendance per match, each World Cup 1930–2014" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Spectators per match" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () What the worked case shows The problem was invisible in the first five rows and only appeared when we profiled the types . The fix needed a reason for each rule (why multiply by 1,000), which belongs in the cleaning log. A plausibility chart is a cheap final check: no bar is a thousand times too small. In the lab you clean the match-level sheet of the same workbook, where the problem is duplicated matches rather than text numbers. Summary ¶ Keep the raw file untouched; clean a copy in code and log every change with before and after counts. Ask why data is missing before you drop or fill anything. Missing is not zero. Duplicates are judged against the grain and keys. Identical-looking rows can be real. Outliers are investigated, not deleted: fix confirmed errors, keep real extremes. Parse text numbers and dates with explicit rules, and count every value that fails. Know the cardinality of every join; use validate= , indicator=True and row-count checks. melt and pivot reshape tables; check totals before and after. Quiz ¶ Answer these at the start of the next lecture. Write your answers before the discussion. Explain the difference between data missing at random and not at random , with a business example of each. Why is fillna(0) usually wrong for a missing sales value? Two rows in a table are identical in every column except their ID. Are they duplicates? What decides it? Give two different actions you might take for an outlier, and when each is right. What does pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce") do to a value it cannot parse, and why must you count those values? A left join increases the number of rows. What does that tell you about the right-hand table? What does validate="many_to_one" check, and what happens if the check fails? Name two things a cleaning log should record for every step. Lab briefing ¶ In the Lab you will: clean the World Cup match results: find duplicated matches, check them against the official tournament totals, and fix text problems; diagnose missing dates in a mobile operating system usage file and decide which part of it can be trusted; join the three sheets of the Superstore workbook with every check from Part 6; debug a colleague's join that inflates sales. Bring your evidence log. Continue with the Session 3 lab .

docs.text: Why the raw data is never overwritten, and what a cleaning log records. Three reasons data goes missing , and when to drop, flag or keep a missing value. The difference between a duplicate and a legitimate repeat . Why an outlier is something to investigate, not something to delete. How to turn numbers and dates stored as text into real numbers and dates, safely. Join types and cardinality , and how a join can silently multiply rows. How to reshape a table between wide and long. Every demonstration uses a small made-up table, so you can see the whole problem at once. The worked case at the end uses real data. Run the next cell first. It loads the libraries, sets the chart style and defines fetch , which downloads a file and checks it is exactly the version this lecture was written for. import hashlib import io import urllib.request import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd def fetch ( url , expected_sha256 ): """Download a file into memory and check its SHA-256 fingerprint.""" with urllib . request . urlopen ( url ) as response : data = response . read () if hashlib . sha256 ( data ) . hexdigest () != expected_sha256 : print ( "WARNING: this file has changed since the course was written:" , url ) print ( "Your numbers may differ from the lecture. Ask your facilitator." ) return data pd . set_option ( "display.float_format" , " {:,.2f} " . format ) plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 8 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.prop_cycle" : plt . cycler ( color = [ "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]), "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) print ( "Setup complete." ) Setup complete.

docs.text: Two rules come before any cleaning technique. Never overwrite the raw data. Read the original file, clean a copy in code, and keep the original exactly as it arrived. If a decision turns out wrong, you can rerun from the start. Log every change. A cleaning log records what changed, why, and how many rows or values it affected. A reader who sees your result can then see exactly how you got there. Step What changed Why Rows before Rows after Check 1 Removed exact duplicate rows Same match loaded twice … … Match count equals the official count 2 Converted attendance text to numbers Stored with dots as thousands separators … … No values lost; totals plausible In pandas, the habit looks like this: clean = raw.copy() , then change clean , and print a row count after every step. Remember Cleaning code is part of the analysis. If you fix something by hand in a spreadsheet, nobody (including you next month) can repeat it.
docs.title: Part 1: Raw data and the cleaning log

docs.text: A blank cell is not just an empty space: why it is empty decides what you can safely do with it. There are three broad reasons. Type Plain meaning Example Risk if you just ignore the blanks Missing completely at random (MCAR) Blanks happen by chance, unrelated to anything A scanner randomly fails on some parcels Fewer rows, but averages stay fair Missing at random (MAR) Blanks depend on another column you can see One warehouse never records delivery times Averages lean towards the warehouses that do record Missing not at random (MNAR) Blanks depend on the missing value itself Very late deliveries are the ones nobody logs Averages are biased, and the data cannot show it The made-up example below has 200 deliveries. We know every true delivery time, then hide some of them in two different ways. rng = np . random . default_rng ( 3 ) true_days = rng . gamma ( shape = 3 , scale = 1.5 , size = 200 ) . round ( 1 ) deliveries = pd . DataFrame ({ "delivery_days" : true_days }) # MCAR: hide 25% of values purely at random. random_blank = rng . random ( 200 ) < 0.25 deliveries [ "recorded_mcar" ] = deliveries [ "delivery_days" ] . mask ( random_blank ) # MNAR: the later the delivery, the more likely nobody recorded it. late_blank = rng . random ( 200 ) < ( deliveries [ "delivery_days" ] / deliveries [ "delivery_days" ] . max ()) deliveries [ "recorded_mnar" ] = deliveries [ "delivery_days" ] . mask ( late_blank ) deliveries . head ( 8 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } delivery_days recorded_mcar recorded_mnar 0 11.40 11.40 NaN 1 5.10 5.10 NaN 2 3.00 3.00 3.00 3 0.80 0.80 0.80 4 2.20 2.20 2.20 5 4.60 NaN NaN 6 3.30 3.30 3.30 7 1.90 NaN 1.90
docs.title: Part 2: Missing data

docs.text: Both recorded columns have some values hidden. pandas skips blanks when it computes a mean. Which recorded mean will be close to the true mean, and which will be too low? summary = pd . DataFrame ({ "values_present" : deliveries . notna () . sum (), "mean_days" : deliveries . mean (), }) summary .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } values_present mean_days delivery_days 200 4.79 recorded_mcar 143 4.65 recorded_mnar 132 4.00 The randomly hidden column keeps a fair average, because the blanks are a random sample. The second column loses mostly the late deliveries, so its average looks better than reality, and nothing in the recorded data warns you.
docs.title: Predict, then reveal

docs.text: Choice What you do Use it when Drop Remove rows with the blank Blanks are few and plausibly random, and you report how many you dropped Flag Add a column such as delivery_missing = 1 and keep the row The fact that a value is missing is itself information Keep as missing Leave NaN , let each calculation skip it, and say so Most of the time: it is honest and reversible Fill (impute) Replace the blank with an estimate Only with a stated method and a reason; never silently, never with 0 unless 0 is true pandas makes flagging and counting easy: deliveries [ "mnar_missing" ] = deliveries [ "recorded_mnar" ] . isna () . astype ( int ) print ( "Missing values:" , deliveries [ "mnar_missing" ] . sum (), "of" , len ( deliveries )) print ( "Share missing: " , f " { deliveries [ 'mnar_missing' ] . mean () : .0% } " ) Missing values: 68 of 200 Share missing: 34% Check your understanding 1 A customer survey asks for household income. The income question is left blank more often by people with very high incomes. Which type of missingness is this? What happens to the average income if you simply drop the blanks, and what would you write in your report? A common mistake Filling blanks with 0 ( fillna(0) ) turns "we do not know" into "it was zero". A missing sales figure is not zero sales, and a missing delivery time is not a same-day delivery.
docs.title: Drop, flag or keep?

docs.text: A duplicate is the same real-world event recorded more than once: a file loaded twice, a form submitted twice. A legitimate repeat is two real events that happen to look alike: a customer who really did buy the same item twice on one day. The difference is not visible from the values alone. You decide using the grain and the keys from Session 2. lines = pd . DataFrame ({ "line_id" : [ 101 , 102 , 103 , 103 , 104 ], "order_id" : [ "A1" , "A1" , "A2" , "A2" , "A3" ], "product" : [ "Pen" , "Pen" , "Desk" , "Desk" , "Lamp" ], "quantity" : [ 1 , 1 , 1 , 1 , 2 ], }) lines .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } line_id order_id product quantity 0 101 A1 Pen 1 1 102 A1 Pen 1 2 103 A2 Desk 1 3 103 A2 Desk 1 4 104 A3 Lamp 2
docs.title: Part 3: Duplicates

docs.text: How many rows does duplicated() mark, and are they all mistakes? Look at line_id and order_id before you run the cell. print ( "Exact duplicate rows: " , lines . duplicated () . sum ()) print ( "Repeats ignoring line_id: " , lines . duplicated ( subset = [ "order_id" , "product" , "quantity" ]) . sum ()) lines [ lines . duplicated ( keep = False )] Exact duplicate rows: 1 Repeats ignoring line_id: 2 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } line_id order_id product quantity 2 103 A2 Desk 1 3 103 A2 Desk 1 Line 103 appears twice with every value equal, including its own key. That is a true duplicate: the same line loaded twice. Remove one copy. Lines 101 and 102 share the order and product but have different line IDs . Two pens on two lines is a legitimate repeat. Removing one would lose a real sale. Check pandas What it finds Exact duplicate rows df.duplicated() Rows equal in every column Repeats on chosen columns df.duplicated(subset=[...]) Rows equal on the columns that define one real event Is the key unique? df["key"].is_unique Whether the primary key can be trusted Show all copies df[df.duplicated(keep=False)] Both the first copy and its repeats, to inspect Remove exact duplicates df.drop_duplicates() Keeps the first copy of each Check your understanding 2 A payments table has two rows with the same customer, amount and date, but different payment_id values. Are they duplicates? What extra information would you look for before deciding?
docs.title: Predict, then reveal

docs.text: An outlier is a value far from the rest. Some are errors (a typing slip adds a zero). Some are real and important (one huge corporate order). Detecting an outlier is mechanical; deciding what it means is not. A common rule flags values more than 1.5 × IQR beyond the quartiles. The IQR (interquartile range) is the distance between the 25th and 75th percentiles; you will meet it properly in Session 4. order_values = pd . Series ( [ 42 , 55 , 38 , 61 , 47 , 53 , 49 , 58 , 44 , 51 , 4900 , 1250 ], index = [ f "O { i : 02d } " for i in range ( 1 , 13 )], name = "order_value" , ) q1 , q3 = order_values . quantile ([ 0.25 , 0.75 ]) iqr = q3 - q1 low , high = q1 - 1.5 * iqr , q3 + 1.5 * iqr print ( f "Flag values below { low : ,.1f } or above { high : ,.1f } " ) order_values [( order_values < low ) | ( order_values > high )] Flag values below 27.5 or above 77.5 O11 4900 O12 1250 Name: order_value, dtype: int64
docs.title: Part 4: Outliers

docs.text: Two orders are flagged. Suppose a check with the sales team shows that O11 was typed as 4900 instead of 49.00, and O12 is a genuine bulk order from a school. What happens to the average if you delete both, and what if you fix only the error? fixed = order_values . copy () fixed [ "O11" ] = 49.00 # confirmed typing error, corrected with a logged reason pd . Series ({ "Average, raw" : order_values . mean (), "Average, both outliers deleted" : order_values . drop ([ "O11" , "O12" ]) . mean (), "Average, error fixed, real order kept" : fixed . mean (), "Median, raw" : order_values . median (), }) Average, raw 554.00 Average, both outliers deleted 49.80 Average, error fixed, real order kept 149.75 Median, raw 52.00 dtype: float64 Deleting both outliers hides a real customer and understates the business. Fixing only the confirmed error gives the honest figure. Notice also that the median hardly moves: it resists extreme values, which is why it suits skewed data (Session 4). Situation Action Confirmed error with a known correct value Fix it, log the old and new value and the evidence Impossible value (negative age, date in the future) and no correction available Set to missing and flag it Real but extreme Keep it; consider reporting the median too, or showing results with and without it Not sure Keep it, flag it, and ask the data owner Check your understanding 3 A shipping table has one shipment that took 210 days. Give one explanation that makes it an error and one that makes it real. What would you do before your report goes out?

docs.text: Files often store numbers and dates as text . pandas then cannot add them up, sort them correctly or compare them with dates.

docs.text: Many countries write one million and a half as 1.500.000 and use the comma for decimals. Python reads a dot as a decimal point. attendance_text = pd . Series ([ "590.549" , "1.045.246" , "363.000" , "819.810" ], name = "attendance" ) naive = pd . to_numeric ( attendance_text , errors = "coerce" ) careful = pd . to_numeric ( attendance_text . str . replace ( "." , "" , regex = False )) pd . DataFrame ({ "text" : attendance_text , "naive" : naive , "careful" : careful }) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } text naive careful 0 590.549 590.55 590549 1 1.045.246 NaN 1045246 2 363.000 363.00 363000 3 819.810 819.81 819810
docs.title: Numbers with thousands separators

docs.text: The naive conversion reads 590.549 as five hundred and ninety, and it cannot read 1.045.246 at all, so errors="coerce" silently turned it into NaN . The careful version removes the dots first, so every value becomes a whole number. errors="coerce" is useful, but always count how many values became NaN : each one is a value you just lost.

docs.text: 03/04/2024 is the 3rd of April in most of the world and March 4th in the United States. Tell pandas the format instead of letting it guess. date_text = pd . Series ([ "03/04/2024" , "15/04/2024" , "28/02/2024" ]) day_first = pd . to_datetime ( date_text , format = " %d /%m/%Y" ) print ( day_first . dt . strftime ( " %d %B %Y" ) . tolist ()) month_first = pd . to_datetime ( date_text , format = "%m/ %d /%Y" , errors = "coerce" ) print ( "Values that fail as month/day/year:" , month_first . isna () . sum ()) ['03 April 2024', '15 April 2024', '28 February 2024'] Values that fail as month/day/year: 2

docs.text: Text is stored as bytes, and the encoding says how to turn bytes into letters. When a file is saved in one encoding and read in another, letters such as ô or é come out as strange symbols. If the symbol is the Unicode replacement character, the original letter is lost : you can only restore it from outside knowledge. Invisible spaces cause a quieter problem: "Paris " and "Paris" look identical on screen but count as two different cities. cities = pd . Series ([ "Paris" , "Paris " , " Lyon" , "Lyon" , "Malm \ufffd " ]) print ( "Different values before strip:" , cities . nunique ()) print ( "Different values after strip: " , cities . str . strip () . nunique ()) print ( "Values containing the replacement character:" , cities . str . contains ( " \ufffd " ) . sum ()) Different values before strip: 5 Different values after strip: 3 Values containing the replacement character: 1 Problem Detect Fix Numbers stored as text df.dtypes shows object pd.to_numeric , after removing separators; count new NaN s Dates stored as text object type; odd sorting pd.to_datetime(..., format=...) Leading or trailing spaces (s != s.str.strip()).sum() s.str.strip() Broken characters s.str.contains("\ufffd") Flag; correct from a trusted list, never by guessing Different spellings of one thing value_counts() A documented mapping, e.g. {"IR Iran": "Iran"} Check your understanding 4 After pd.to_numeric(..., errors="coerce") a column of 5,000 prices has 37 NaN values that were not there before. What do you do next, and what goes in the cleaning log?

docs.text: A join ( merge in pandas) puts columns from two tables side by side by matching a key. Two choices decide the result. 1. Which rows to keep ( how ) how= Keeps "inner" Only keys found in both tables "left" Every row of the left table; blanks where the right has no match "right" Every row of the right table "outer" Every key from either table 2. Cardinality: how many matches each key has Cardinality Meaning Example Row count after a left join One-to-one Each key once on both sides Employee ↔ employee contract Unchanged Many-to-one Many left rows share one right row Order lines → region manager Unchanged One-to-many One left row matches many right rows Order → its lines Grows Many-to-many Keys repeat on both sides Orders by region × campaigns by region Multiplies orders = pd . DataFrame ({ "order_id" : [ "A1" , "A2" , "A3" , "A4" ], "region" : [ "North" , "North" , "South" , "East" ], "sales" : [ 100 , 250 , 80 , 120 ], }) managers = pd . DataFrame ({ "region" : [ "North" , "South" , "West" ], "manager" : [ "Asha" , "Ben" , "Chen" ], }) joined = orders . merge ( managers , on = "region" , how = "left" , validate = "many_to_one" , indicator = True ) print ( "Rows before:" , len ( orders ), "| rows after:" , len ( joined )) joined Rows before: 4 | rows after: 4 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } order_id region sales manager _merge 0 A1 North 100 Asha both 1 A2 North 250 Asha both 2 A3 South 80 Ben both 3 A4 East 120 NaN left_only indicator=True adds a _merge column showing where each row found a match: East has no manager ( left_only ), and the manager for West has no orders, so that row does not appear in a left join. validate="many_to_one" makes pandas check that each region appears only once in managers .
docs.title: Part 6: Joins and cardinality

docs.text: North changed manager during the year, so someone adds a second North row to the managers table. Sales are then totalled from the joined table. What happens to total Sales? managers_history = pd . DataFrame ({ "region" : [ "North" , "North" , "South" , "West" ], "manager" : [ "Asha" , "Dev" , "Ben" , "Chen" ], }) exploded = orders . merge ( managers_history , on = "region" , how = "left" ) print ( "Rows before:" , len ( orders ), "| rows after:" , len ( exploded )) print ( "Total sales before the join:" , orders [ "sales" ] . sum ()) print ( "Total sales after the join: " , exploded [ "sales" ] . sum ()) Rows before: 4 | rows after: 6 Total sales before the join: 550 Total sales after the join: 900 Each North order now matches two manager rows, so it appears twice and its sales are counted twice. No error appears. This is the most common way joins go wrong. validate turns the silent mistake into a loud one: try : orders . merge ( managers_history , on = "region" , how = "left" , validate = "many_to_one" ) except pd . errors . MergeError as problem : print ( "MergeError:" , problem ) MergeError: Merge keys are not unique in right dataset; not a many-to-one merge Remember: three checks for every join Before: is the key unique on the side that should be unique? ( df["key"].is_unique ) During: validate= with the cardinality you expect, and indicator=True to see unmatched rows. After: compare row counts and one total (such as Sales) before and after. Check your understanding 5 You left-join 6,000 order lines to a product table on product_id and get 6,240 rows. What does that tell you about the product table? Which validate value would have caught it?

docs.text: The Attendance values look like numbers with dots. Check what Python actually stored in each cell. print ( "Column type:" , cups [ "Attendance" ] . dtype ) cups [ "Attendance" ] . map ( lambda value : type ( value ) . __name__ ) . value_counts () Column type: object Attendance str 14 float 5 int 1 Name: count, dtype: int64 The column mixes text and numbers . docs.text: Each kind of cell needs its own rule: Text such as "1.045.246" : remove the dots. Numbers such as 590.549 or 375.7 : these were thousands, so multiply by 1,000 and round. def parse_attendance ( value ): if isinstance ( value , str ): return int ( value . replace ( "." , "" )) return int ( round ( value * 1000 )) cups [ "attendance" ] = cups [ "Attendance" ] . map ( parse_attendance ) cups [ "attendance_per_match" ] = cups [ "attendance" ] / cups [ "MatchesPlayed" ] cups [[ "Year" , "Attendance" , "attendance" , "attendance_per_match" ]] . head ( 8 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Year Attendance attendance attendance_per_match 0 1930 590.55 590549 32,808.28 1 1934 363 363000 21,352.94 2 1938 375.70 375700 20,872.22 3 1950 1.045.246 1045246 47,511.18 4 1954 768.61 768607 29,561.81 5 1958 819.81 819810 23,423.14 6 1962 893.17 893172 27,911.62 7 1966 1.563.135 1563135 48,847.97

Plot attendance per match : if any value were off by a factor of 1,000, it would stand out at once. ax = cups . plot ( x = "Year" , y = "attendance_per_match" , kind = "bar" , legend = False , title = "Average attendance per match, each World Cup 1930–2014" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Spectators per match" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () What the worked case shows The problem was invisible in the first five rows and only appeared when we profiled the types . docs.text: Session 4 lecture: Descriptive statistics and distributions ¶ One number never describes a column. This lecture shows how to summarise a variable with the right centre, the right spread and an honest picture of its shape, and how to tell a real extreme value from a mistake. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . Recap quiz ¶ Before we start, answer the quiz at the end of the Session 3 lecture . Write short answers; we discuss them together. What you will be able to explain ¶ When the mean , the median or the mode is the right "typical value". How range , IQR , standard deviation and percentiles describe spread, and which ones resist extreme values. What skew and a long tail are, and how to spot them from the mean and median alone. How to read a histogram , a box plot and an ECDF , and what each can hide. What a z-score says, and why the normal curve is a reference , not an assumption. How the IQR rule flags unusual values, and why we flag them instead of deleting them. This lecture builds on How statistics can mislead , especially the section on averages. In the Lab you apply every idea to the retail orders and to US house prices. How to use the questions in this notebook Predict, then reveal boxes ask you to guess before running the next cell. Write your guess down first. Check your understanding boxes are short questions to answer in your own words. Run the setup cell first. Later we also use numpy , Python's library for numbers, to simulate small example datasets. A fixed seed makes the "random" numbers the same every time you run the notebook, so your output matches everyone else's. # Course data setup. Run this cell first; you do not need to understand it yet. # It downloads the Superstore sample from Tableau's website, checks it is the # exact version this course was written for, and prepares the order-lines table. import hashlib import os import urllib.request import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd SOURCE_URL = "https://public.tableau.com/app/sample-data/sample_-_superstore.xls" EXPECTED_SHA256 = "5045ed4fec49cae2cc0dfc5ab0d204ba09efa767fe00c996822499e8cc42fbbd" SOURCE_FILE = os . environ . get ( "COURSE_XLS_PATH" , "sample_-_superstore.xls" ) try : import xlrd # noqa: F401 (needed to read .xls files) except ImportError : import subprocess import sys subprocess . check_call ([ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-q" , "xlrd" ]) if not os . path . exists ( SOURCE_FILE ): urllib . request . urlretrieve ( SOURCE_URL , SOURCE_FILE ) with open ( SOURCE_FILE , "rb" ) as f : digest = hashlib . sha256 ( f . read ()) . hexdigest () if digest != EXPECTED_SHA256 : print ( "WARNING: Tableau has changed this sample file since the course was written." ) print ( "Your numbers will differ from the lesson. Ask your facilitator for the course copy." ) def load_orders (): """Return one row per order line, orders placed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31.""" raw = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Orders" ) returns = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Returns" ) # Orders with more than one Customer ID (a known data issue), found before filtering. ids_per_order = raw . groupby ( "Order ID" )[ "Customer ID" ] . nunique () conflict_orders = set ( ids_per_order [ ids_per_order > 1 ] . index ) in_scope = ( raw [ "Order Date" ] >= "2023-01-01" ) & ( raw [ "Order Date" ] < "2026-01-01" ) df = raw . loc [ in_scope ] . copy () df = df . rename ( columns = { "Row ID" : "row_id" , "Order ID" : "order_id" , "Order Date" : "order_date" , "Ship Date" : "ship_date" , "Ship Mode" : "ship_mode" , "Customer ID" : "customer_id" , "Segment" : "segment" , "Country/Region" : "country_region" , "Region" : "region" , "Category" : "category" , "Sub-Category" : "sub_category" , "Product ID" : "product_id" , "Product Name" : "product_name" , "Sales" : "sales" , "Quantity" : "quantity" , "Discount" : "discount" , "Profit" : "profit" , }) df [ "returned_order_flag" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( set ( returns [ "Order ID" ])) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( conflict_orders ) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_analysis_eligible" ] = 1 - df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] df [ "order_to_ship_days" ] = ( df [ "ship_date" ] - df [ "order_date" ]) . dt . days df [ "order_month" ] = df [ "order_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "M" ) . dt . to_timestamp () columns = [ "row_id" , "order_id" , "order_date" , "ship_date" , "ship_mode" , "customer_id" , "segment" , "country_region" , "region" , "category" , "sub_category" , "product_id" , "product_name" , "sales" , "quantity" , "discount" , "profit" , "returned_order_flag" , "customer_analysis_eligible" , "customer_order_conflict" , "order_to_ship_days" , "order_month" , ] return df [ columns ] . sort_values ( "row_id" ) . reset_index ( drop = True ) pd . set_option ( "display.float_format" , " {:,.2f} " . format ) plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 8 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.prop_cycle" : plt . cycler ( color = [ "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]), "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) print ( "Setup complete." ) Setup complete. import numpy as np rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 42 ) df = load_orders () print ( "Order lines:" , len ( df )) Order lines: 6815 Part 1: The centre — mean, median and mode ¶ There are three common answers to "what is a typical value?": Measure How it is found Good for Mean (average) Add all values, divide by how many Totals and planning: mean × count = total Median The middle value once values are sorted "A typical case" when a few values are extreme Mode The most frequent value Categories, and counts with few possible values Predict, then reveal: one very large salary ¶ A small team has nine salaries. Then the company owner, who pays themself far more, is added to the list. Predict, then reveal When the owner is added, which moves more: the mean or the median ? Write down your guess, then run the next cell. team = pd . Series ([ 31 , 33 , 34 , 35 , 36 , 38 , 40 , 41 , 44 ], name = "salary (thousands)" ) with_owner = pd . concat ([ team , pd . Series ([ 400 ])], ignore_index = True ) print ( "Team only: mean" , round ( team . mean (), 1 ), "| median" , team . median ()) print ( "With owner: mean" , round ( with_owner . mean (), 1 ), "| median" , with_owner . median ()) Team only: mean 36.9 | median 36.0 With owner: mean 73.2 | median 37.0 One extreme value dragged the mean far away from every real team member, while the median barely moved. The median resists extreme values; statisticians call this being robust . The mean is not wrong. If the question is "what will the payroll cost?", the mean (times the head count) gives the total. If the question is "what does a typical person earn?", the median is the honest answer. The mode ¶ For a category, the only sensible "typical value" is the most frequent one. value_counts() lists every category with its count; mode() returns the most frequent: print ( df [ "ship_mode" ] . value_counts ()) print ( "Mode:" , df [ "ship_mode" ] . mode ()[ 0 ]) ship_mode Standard Class 4171 Second Class 1313 First Class 972 Same Day 359 Name: count, dtype: int64 Mode: Standard Class Check your understanding 1 A manager says "our average customer spends a lot". Which two questions would you ask before believing it? Why can you not compute a mean or a median of ship_mode ? Which level of measurement from Session 2 explains this? Part 2: Spread — how different are the values? ¶ Two delivery services can have the same average delivery time and still feel very different to customers. Here are two simulated services, each with 500 deliveries: steady = pd . Series ( rng . normal ( loc = 4 , scale = 0.5 , size = 500 )) . clip ( lower = 0 ) erratic = pd . Series ( rng . normal ( loc = 4 , scale = 2.0 , size = 500 )) . clip ( lower = 0 ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 9 , 3.2 ), sharex = True , sharey = True ) for ax , data , title in zip ( axes , [ steady , erratic ], [ "Steady service" , "Erratic service" ]): ax . hist ( data , bins = 30 ) ax . axvline ( data . mean (), color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 ) ax . set_title ( title ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Delivery time (days)" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Deliveries" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () The orange line is the mean. It sits in nearly the same place for both. The difference is the spread . Four ways to measure it: Measure Meaning Resists extreme values? Range Largest minus smallest No: one value changes it IQR (interquartile range) Width of the middle half: 75th percentile minus 25th percentile Yes Standard deviation Typical distance of a value from the mean No Percentiles The value below which a given share of the data falls Yes, apart from the most extreme ones def spread ( s ): return pd . Series ({ "mean" : s . mean (), "range" : s . max () - s . min (), "IQR" : s . quantile ( 0.75 ) - s . quantile ( 0.25 ), "std" : s . std (), "90th percentile" : s . quantile ( 0.90 ), }) pd . DataFrame ({ "steady" : spread ( steady ), "erratic" : spread ( erratic )}) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } steady erratic mean 3.99 3.94 range 2.74 10.36 IQR 0.63 2.64 std 0.48 1.96 90th percentile 4.60 6.55 Read the table column by column. The means agree; every spread measure tells you the erratic service is less predictable. Percentiles speak the language of service promises. "90% of deliveries arrive within X days" is the 90th percentile. A customer cares far more about that than about the average. Check your understanding 2 Why does the range depend on just two deliveries? If you had to promise customers a delivery time, would you quote the mean or a high percentile? Why? Part 3: Shape — skew and long tails ¶ A distribution's shape is how its values are spread out: piled up evenly around the middle, or bunched on one side with a long tail on the other. Shape What it looks like Typical business example Symmetric Mirror image around the middle Weights of packaged goods, measurement errors Right-skewed Most values small, a long tail of large ones Order values, incomes, house prices, claim sizes Left-skewed Most values high, a tail of small ones Scores on an easy test, product lifetimes with early failures Predict, then reveal In a right-skewed distribution, is the mean above or below the median? Decide, then run the next cell. The orange line is the mean, the dark line the median. shapes = { "Symmetric" : pd . Series ( rng . normal ( 50 , 10 , 2000 )), "Right-skewed" : pd . Series ( rng . lognormal ( mean = 3.5 , sigma = 0.7 , size = 2000 )), "Left-skewed" : pd . Series ( 100 - rng . lognormal ( mean = 2.5 , sigma = 0.6 , size = 2000 )), } fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 3 , figsize = ( 11 , 3.2 )) for ax , ( title , data ) in zip ( axes , shapes . items ()): ax . hist ( data , bins = 40 ) ax . axvline ( data . mean (), color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 , label = "mean" ) ax . axvline ( data . median (), color = "#333333" , linewidth = 2 , linestyle = "--" , label = "median" ) ax . set_title ( title ) axes [ 0 ] . legend () plt . tight_layout () plt . show () for title , data in shapes . items (): print ( f " { title : 13 } mean { data . mean () : 6.1f } | median { data . median () : 6.1f } | skew { data . skew () : 5.2f } " ) Symmetric mean 49.8 | median 50.0 | skew -0.03 Right-skewed mean 41.9 | median 32.7 | skew 2.98 Left-skewed mean 85.0 | median 87.8 | skew -2.01 The long tail pulls the mean towards it . So a quick check needs no chart at all: mean clearly above median → right skew (long tail of large values); mean clearly below median → left skew; mean close to median → roughly symmetric. pandas' .skew() turns this into one number: near 0 for symmetric data, positive for a right tail, negative for a left tail. Use it as a signal to look at the chart, not as a replacement for it. Check your understanding 3 A report says "average house price: 420,000; median house price: 350,000". Without a chart, describe the shape of the distribution and say which number better describes a typical house. Part 4: Three pictures of one distribution ¶ Each chart type answers a different question, and each can hide something. Chart Answers Watch out for Histogram Where do values pile up? The number of bins changes the story Box plot Where are the middle half, the median and the unusual values? Hides gaps and double peaks ECDF (empirical cumulative distribution) What share of values is at or below x ? Unfamiliar to many readers: label it well Here are all three for the right-skewed sample from Part 3: data = shapes [ "Right-skewed" ] fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 3 , figsize = ( 11 , 3.4 )) axes [ 0 ] . hist ( data , bins = 40 ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Histogram" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_xlabel ( "Value" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Count" ) axes [ 1 ] . boxplot ( data ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Box plot" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_ylabel ( "Value" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_xticks ([]) ecdf_x = np . sort ( data ) ecdf_y = np . arange ( 1 , len ( data ) + 1 ) / len ( data ) axes [ 2 ] . plot ( ecdf_x , ecdf_y ) axes [ 2 ] . axhline ( 0.9 , color = "#eb6834" , linestyle = "--" , linewidth = 1 ) axes [ 2 ] . set_title ( "ECDF" ) axes [ 2 ] . set_xlabel ( "Value" ) axes [ 2 ] . set_ylabel ( "Share at or below" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () print ( "90th percentile:" , round ( data . quantile ( 0.9 ), 1 )) 90th percentile: 78.7 How to read them: Histogram: bars show how many values fall in each interval. The tall bars on the left and the thin tail on the right are the right skew. Box plot: read it from bottom to top. The box spans the 25th to 75th percentiles (the IQR), the line inside is the median, the "whiskers" reach to the furthest values within 1.5 × IQR of the box, and the circles beyond them are values the IQR rule flags (Part 6). ECDF: go up to a share on the vertical axis, across to the line, and down to the value. The dashed line at 0.9 crosses the curve at the 90th percentile printed above. Predict, then reveal: the number of bins ¶ Predict, then reveal Will the same data look different with 5 bins and with 100 bins? Run the cell. fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 9 , 3 ), sharey = False ) for ax , bins in zip ( axes , [ 5 , 100 ]): ax . hist ( data , bins = bins ) ax . set_title ( f " { bins } bins" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Value" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () With too few bins the shape disappears; with too many, random noise looks like structure. Try a few bin counts before choosing one, and never draw conclusions from a single setting. Part 5: z-scores and the normal curve as a reference ¶ A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is from the mean: z = (value − mean) ÷ standard deviation A z-score of +2 means "two standard deviations above the mean". It lets you compare values measured in different units, such as a delivery time and an order value. The normal distribution is the familiar symmetric bell curve. For data that really are normal, about 68% of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within 2 and 99.7% within 3. Many people apply this rule to any data. Let us test it on a symmetric and a skewed sample. def share_within ( s , k ): z = ( s - s . mean ()) / s . std () return ( z . abs () <= k ) . mean () table = pd . DataFrame ({ "normal reference" : [ 0.683 , 0.954 , 0.997 ], "symmetric sample" : [ share_within ( shapes [ "Symmetric" ], k ) for k in ( 1 , 2 , 3 )], "right-skewed sample" : [ share_within ( shapes [ "Right-skewed" ], k ) for k in ( 1 , 2 , 3 )], }, index = [ "within 1 sd" , "within 2 sd" , "within 3 sd" ]) ( table * 100 ) . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } normal reference symmetric sample right-skewed sample within 1 sd 68.30 68.50 87.30 within 2 sd 95.40 95.20 95.60 within 3 sd 99.70 100.00 98.30 The symmetric sample follows the reference closely. The skewed sample does not: its shares differ, and the extreme values sit on one side only. The normal curve is a reference, not an assumption Compare your data with the normal curve to learn how it differs. Do not assume business data are normal: order values, waiting times and incomes almost never are. Rules built on the normal curve, such as "anything beyond 3 standard deviations is an outlier", can mislead on skewed data. Check your understanding 4 An order has a z-score of 4. Is it necessarily an error? What would you check? Part 6: Unusual values — flag, do not delete ¶ The IQR rule marks a value as unusual if it lies more than 1.5 × IQR below the 25th percentile or above the 75th percentile. These limits are called fences . It is the rule box plots use, and it works on skewed data because quartiles resist extreme values. def iqr_fences ( s ): q1 , q3 = s . quantile ( 0.25 ), s . quantile ( 0.75 ) iqr = q3 - q1 return q1 - 1.5 * iqr , q3 + 1.5 * iqr for title , data in shapes . items (): low , high = iqr_fences ( data ) flagged = (( data < low ) | ( data > high )) . mean () print ( f " { title : 13 } fences { low : 7.1f } to { high : 7.1f } | flagged { flagged : .1% } " ) Symmetric fences 22.9 to 76.7 | flagged 0.9% Right-skewed fences -25.3 to 96.8 | flagged 6.0% Left-skewed fences 65.2 to 107.6 | flagged 4.7% In the right-skewed sample, the rule flags a noticeable share of values, and all of them are genuine draws from the same process. In skewed business data, big orders and long waits are often real and often the most important records. What to do with a flagged value: Finding Action It is impossible (negative quantity, ship date before order date) Treat as a data error: correct it from the source or exclude it, and record the change in the preparation log It is possible but rare (a very large order) Keep it. Report robust statistics (median, IQR), and look at the large cases separately You cannot tell Keep it, flag it, and ask the data owner Check your understanding 5 A colleague deletes every order above the upper IQR fence "to clean the data" and then reports total sales. What has gone wrong? Part 7: Worked case — Superstore orders ¶ The retail table has one row per order line . Questions about "a typical order" need one row per order . We build that table first and check our grain claim. # One row per ORDER: add up the lines of each order. # Segment, ship mode and ship days are the same on every line of an order, so we take the first. orders = df . groupby ( "order_id" ) . agg ( order_value = ( "sales" , "sum" ), segment = ( "segment" , "first" ), ship_mode = ( "ship_mode" , "first" ), ship_days = ( "order_to_ship_days" , "first" ), ) # Check that claim before relying on it: each should be 1. per_order = df . groupby ( "order_id" )[[ "segment" , "ship_mode" , "order_to_ship_days" ]] . nunique () print ( "Most different values inside one order:" ) print ( per_order . max ()) print ( "Orders:" , len ( orders )) Most different values inside one order: segment 1 ship_mode 1 order_to_ship_days 1 dtype: int64 Orders: 3388 Every maximum is 1: each order has one segment, one ship mode and one ship-days value, so taking the first line is safe. Step 1: Predict, then reveal — is order value skewed? ¶ Predict, then reveal Will the mean order value be close to the median, or far above it? Run the cell. ov = orders [ "order_value" ] print ( "Mean: " , round ( ov . mean (), 2 )) print ( "Median:" , round ( ov . median (), 2 )) print ( "Skew: " , round ( ov . skew (), 2 )) ov . quantile ([ 0.10 , 0.25 , 0.50 , 0.75 , 0.90 , 0.99 ]) . to_frame ( "order value" ) Mean: 466.64 Median: 151.46 Skew: 8.86 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } order value 0.10 12.96 0.25 38.33 0.50 151.46 0.75 531.66 0.90 1,181.29 0.99 4,256.06 The mean is far above the median and the skew is strongly positive: a few very large orders pull the mean up. Look at how the percentiles grow faster and faster towards the top. Step 2: Picture it ¶ A histogram on an ordinary axis squeezes most orders into the first bar. A second histogram with logarithmic bins (each bin a fixed multiple wider than the last) spreads the small and large orders out so the shape is visible. The axis labels still show ordinary values. fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 10 , 3.4 )) axes [ 0 ] . hist ( ov , bins = 50 ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Ordinary bins" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_xlabel ( "Order value (source monetary units)" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Orders" ) log_bins = np . logspace ( np . log10 ( ov . min ()), np . log10 ( ov . max ()), 40 ) axes [ 1 ] . hist ( ov , bins = log_bins ) axes [ 1 ] . set_xscale ( "log" ) axes [ 1 ] . axvline ( ov . median (), color = "#333333" , linestyle = "--" , label = "median" ) axes [ 1 ] . axvline ( ov . mean (), color = "#eb6834" , label = "mean" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Logarithmic bins" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_xlabel ( "Order value (source monetary units, log scale)" ) axes [ 1 ] . legend () plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Step 3: Ship days — a different shape ¶ Ship days take only a few whole-number values, so a bar per value works better than a histogram. sd = orders [ "ship_days" ] sd . value_counts () . sort_index () . plot ( kind = "bar" , title = "Days from order to shipment, one bar per value" ) plt . xlabel ( "Days" ) plt . ylabel ( "Orders" ) plt . xticks ( rotation = 0 ) plt . show () print ( "Mean:" , round ( sd . mean (), 2 ), "| median:" , sd . median (), "| mode:" , sd . mode ()[ 0 ]) print ( "90th percentile:" , sd . quantile ( 0.9 )) Mean: 3.97 | median: 4.0 | mode: 4 90th percentile: 6.0 Here the mean and median are close, so either is a fair "typical" value. Look carefully at the right end of the chart: is there a value far from all the others? That is a candidate for a flag, and for a question to the operations team, not for deletion. Step 4: One summary table for the report ¶ def describe_shape ( s ): q1 , q3 = s . quantile ( 0.25 ), s . quantile ( 0.75 ) low , high = q1 - 1.5 * ( q3 - q1 ), q3 + 1.5 * ( q3 - q1 ) return pd . Series ({ "count" : s . count (), "mean" : s . mean (), "median" : s . median (), "std" : s . std (), "IQR" : q3 - q1 , "90th pct" : s . quantile ( 0.9 ), "skew" : s . skew (), "flagged by IQR rule" : (( s < low ) | ( s > high )) . sum (), }) summary = pd . DataFrame ({ "order value (per order)" : describe_shape ( orders [ "order_value" ]), "ship days (per order)" : describe_shape ( orders [ "ship_days" ]), }) summary .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } order value (per order) ship days (per order) count 3,388.00 3,388.00 mean 466.64 3.97 median 151.46 4.00 std 975.36 1.73 IQR 493.33 2.00 90th pct 1,181.29 6.00 skew 8.86 -0.42 flagged by IQR rule 305.00 1.00 Reading the table: Order value is strongly right-skewed: report the median with the IQR (or percentiles), and mention that a small number of large orders exist. Ship days is close to symmetric with a few whole-number values: the mean or median both work, with the 90th percentile for service promises. The grain is in the column names on purpose. "Order value per order" and "sales per order line" are different variables with different distributions. Summary ¶ Variable looks like… Centre to report Spread to report Roughly symmetric, no extreme values Mean (median is similar) Standard deviation Skewed or with extreme values Median IQR or chosen percentiles Categories Mode (and the share in each category) Shares of each category A service level or promise — A high percentile (90th, 95th) Always say what one row is before you summarise, always look at the shape , and flag unusual values instead of deleting them. Quiz ¶ Answer these at the start of the next lecture. Write short answers. Give one business variable where the median is a better "typical value" than the mean, and explain why. A dataset's mean is 120 and its median is 80. What does this suggest about its shape? Which spread measures resist extreme values, and which do not? What does "the 90th percentile of delivery time is 6 days" mean in plain words? Name one thing a box plot hides that a histogram can show. A value has a z-score of −2.5. What does that mean? Why is "beyond 3 standard deviations = outlier" risky for skewed data? State the IQR rule and say what you should do with a value it flags. Lab briefing ¶ In the Lab you: Build the order-level table and describe order value and ship days. Compare distributions across segments and ship modes with box plots. Explore the long tail of negative profits. Use US Census house prices to see the mean–median gap over four decades. Flag unusual orders with the IQR rule and write a distribution summary table. Debug a colleague's "average order value". Open the Session 4 lab .

docs.text: When the mean , the median or the mode is the right "typical value". How range , IQR , standard deviation and percentiles describe spread, and which ones resist extreme values. What skew and a long tail are, and how to spot them from the mean and median alone. How to read a histogram , a box plot and an ECDF , and what each can hide. What a z-score says, and why the normal curve is a reference , not an assumption. How the IQR rule flags unusual values, and why we flag them instead of deleting them. This lecture builds on How statistics can mislead , especially the section on averages. In the Lab you apply every idea to the retail orders and to US house prices. How to use the questions in this notebook Predict, then reveal boxes ask you to guess before running the next cell. Write your guess down first. Check your understanding boxes are short questions to answer in your own words. Run the setup cell first. Later we also use numpy , Python's library for numbers, to simulate small example datasets. A fixed seed makes the "random" numbers the same every time you run the notebook, so your output matches everyone else's. # Course data setup. Run this cell first; you do not need to understand it yet. # It downloads the Superstore sample from Tableau's website, checks it is the # exact version this course was written for, and prepares the order-lines table. import hashlib import os import urllib.request import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd SOURCE_URL = "https://public.tableau.com/app/sample-data/sample_-_superstore.xls" EXPECTED_SHA256 = "5045ed4fec49cae2cc0dfc5ab0d204ba09efa767fe00c996822499e8cc42fbbd" SOURCE_FILE = os . environ . get ( "COURSE_XLS_PATH" , "sample_-_superstore.xls" ) try : import xlrd # noqa: F401 (needed to read .xls files) except ImportError : import subprocess import sys subprocess . check_call ([ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-q" , "xlrd" ]) if not os . path . exists ( SOURCE_FILE ): urllib . request . urlretrieve ( SOURCE_URL , SOURCE_FILE ) with open ( SOURCE_FILE , "rb" ) as f : digest = hashlib . sha256 ( f . read ()) . hexdigest () if digest != EXPECTED_SHA256 : print ( "WARNING: Tableau has changed this sample file since the course was written." ) print ( "Your numbers will differ from the lesson. docs.text: There are three common answers to "what is a typical value?": Measure How it is found Good for Mean (average) Add all values, divide by how many Totals and planning: mean × count = total Median The middle value once values are sorted "A typical case" when a few values are extreme Mode The most frequent value Categories, and counts with few possible values

docs.text: A small team has nine salaries. Then the company owner, who pays themself far more, is added to the list. Predict, then reveal When the owner is added, which moves more: the mean or the median ? Write down your guess, then run the next cell. team = pd . Series ([ 31 , 33 , 34 , 35 , 36 , 38 , 40 , 41 , 44 ], name = "salary (thousands)" ) with_owner = pd . concat ([ team , pd . Series ([ 400 ])], ignore_index = True ) print ( "Team only: mean" , round ( team . mean (), 1 ), "| median" , team . median ()) print ( "With owner: mean" , round ( with_owner . mean (), 1 ), "| median" , with_owner . median ()) Team only: mean 36.9 | median 36.0 With owner: mean 73.2 | median 37.0 One extreme value dragged the mean far away from every real team member, while the median barely moved. The median resists extreme values; statisticians call this being robust . The mean is not wrong. If the question is "what will the payroll cost?", the mean (times the head count) gives the total. If the question is "what does a typical person earn?", the median is the honest answer.
