docs.text: A distribution's shape is how its values are spread out: piled up evenly around the middle, or bunched on one side with a long tail on the other. Shape What it looks like Typical business example Symmetric Mirror image around the middle Weights of packaged goods, measurement errors Right-skewed Most values small, a long tail of large ones Order values, incomes, house prices, claim sizes Left-skewed Most values high, a tail of small ones Scores on an easy test, product lifetimes with early failures Predict, then reveal In a right-skewed distribution, is the mean above or below the median? Decide, then run the next cell. The orange line is the mean, the dark line the median. shapes = { "Symmetric" : pd . Series ( rng . normal ( 50 , 10 , 2000 )), "Right-skewed" : pd . Series ( rng . lognormal ( mean = 3.5 , sigma = 0.7 , size = 2000 )), "Left-skewed" : pd . Series ( 100 - rng . lognormal ( mean = 2.5 , sigma = 0.6 , size = 2000 )), } fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 3 , figsize = ( 11 , 3.2 )) for ax , ( title , data ) in zip ( axes , shapes . items ()): ax . hist ( data , bins = 40 ) ax . axvline ( data . mean (), color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 , label = "mean" ) ax . axvline ( data . median (), color = "#333333" , linewidth = 2 , linestyle = "--" , label = "median" ) ax . set_title ( title ) axes [ 0 ] . legend () plt . tight_layout () plt . show () for title , data in shapes . items (): print ( f " { title : 13 } mean { data . mean () : 6.1f } | median { data . median () : 6.1f } | skew { data . skew () : 5.2f } " ) Symmetric mean 49.8 | median 50.0 | skew -0.03 Right-skewed mean 41.9 | median 32.7 | skew 2.98 Left-skewed mean 85.0 | median 87.8 | skew -2.01 The long tail pulls the mean towards it . So a quick check needs no chart at all: mean clearly above median → right skew (long tail of large values); mean clearly below median → left skew; mean close to median → roughly symmetric. pandas' .skew() turns this into one number: near 0 for symmetric data, positive for a right tail, negative for a left tail. Use it as a signal to look at the chart, not as a replacement for it. Check your understanding 3 A report says "average house price: 420,000; median house price: 350,000". Without a chart, describe the shape of the distribution and say which number better describes a typical house.
docs.title: Part 3: Shape — skew and long tails

docs.text: Each chart type answers a different question, and each can hide something. Chart Answers Watch out for Histogram Where do values pile up? The number of bins changes the story Box plot Where are the middle half, the median and the unusual values? Hides gaps and double peaks ECDF (empirical cumulative distribution) What share of values is at or below x ? Unfamiliar to many readers: label it well Here are all three for the right-skewed sample from Part 3: data = shapes [ "Right-skewed" ] fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 3 , figsize = ( 11 , 3.4 )) axes [ 0 ] . hist ( data , bins = 40 ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Histogram" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_xlabel ( "Value" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Count" ) axes [ 1 ] . boxplot ( data ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Box plot" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_ylabel ( "Value" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_xticks ([]) ecdf_x = np . sort ( data ) ecdf_y = np . arange ( 1 , len ( data ) + 1 ) / len ( data ) axes [ 2 ] . plot ( ecdf_x , ecdf_y ) axes [ 2 ] . axhline ( 0.9 , color = "#eb6834" , linestyle = "--" , linewidth = 1 ) axes [ 2 ] . set_title ( "ECDF" ) axes [ 2 ] . set_xlabel ( "Value" ) axes [ 2 ] . set_ylabel ( "Share at or below" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () print ( "90th percentile:" , round ( data . quantile ( 0.9 ), 1 )) 90th percentile: 78.7 How to read them: Histogram: bars show how many values fall in each interval. The tall bars on the left and the thin tail on the right are the right skew. Box plot: read it from bottom to top. The box spans the 25th to 75th percentiles (the IQR), the line inside is the median, the "whiskers" reach to the furthest values within 1.5 × IQR of the box, and the circles beyond them are values the IQR rule flags (Part 6). ECDF: go up to a share on the vertical axis, across to the line, and down to the value. The dashed line at 0.9 crosses the curve at the 90th percentile printed above.
docs.title: Part 4: Three pictures of one distribution

docs.text: Predict, then reveal Will the same data look different with 5 bins and with 100 bins? Run the cell. fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 9 , 3 ), sharey = False ) for ax , bins in zip ( axes , [ 5 , 100 ]): ax . hist ( data , bins = bins ) ax . set_title ( f " { bins } bins" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Value" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () With too few bins the shape disappears; with too many, random noise looks like structure. Try a few bin counts before choosing one, and never draw conclusions from a single setting.
docs.title: Predict, then reveal: the number of bins

docs.text: A z-score says how many standard deviations a value is from the mean: z = (value − mean) ÷ standard deviation A z-score of +2 means "two standard deviations above the mean". It lets you compare values measured in different units, such as a delivery time and an order value. The normal distribution is the familiar symmetric bell curve. For data that really are normal, about 68% of values lie within 1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within 2 and 99.7% within 3. Many people apply this rule to any data. Let us test it on a symmetric and a skewed sample. def share_within ( s , k ): z = ( s - s . mean ()) / s . std () return ( z . abs () <= k ) . mean () table = pd . DataFrame ({ "normal reference" : [ 0.683 , 0.954 , 0.997 ], "symmetric sample" : [ share_within ( shapes [ "Symmetric" ], k ) for k in ( 1 , 2 , 3 )], "right-skewed sample" : [ share_within ( shapes [ "Right-skewed" ], k ) for k in ( 1 , 2 , 3 )], }, index = [ "within 1 sd" , "within 2 sd" , "within 3 sd" ]) ( table * 100 ) . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } normal reference symmetric sample right-skewed sample within 1 sd 68.30 68.50 87.30 within 2 sd 95.40 95.20 95.60 within 3 sd 99.70 100.00 98.30 The symmetric sample follows the reference closely. The skewed sample does not: its shares differ, and the extreme values sit on one side only. The normal curve is a reference, not an assumption Compare your data with the normal curve to learn how it differs. Do not assume business data are normal: order values, waiting times and incomes almost never are. Rules built on the normal curve, such as "anything beyond 3 standard deviations is an outlier", can mislead on skewed data. Check your understanding 4 An order has a z-score of 4. Is it necessarily an error? What would you check?
docs.title: Part 5: z-scores and the normal curve as a reference

docs.text: The IQR rule marks a value as unusual if it lies more than 1.5 × IQR below the 25th percentile or above the 75th percentile. These limits are called fences . It is the rule box plots use, and it works on skewed data because quartiles resist extreme values. def iqr_fences ( s ): q1 , q3 = s . quantile ( 0.25 ), s . quantile ( 0.75 ) iqr = q3 - q1 return q1 - 1.5 * iqr , q3 + 1.5 * iqr for title , data in shapes . items (): low , high = iqr_fences ( data ) flagged = (( data < low ) | ( data > high )) . mean () print ( f " { title : 13 } fences { low : 7.1f } to { high : 7.1f } | flagged { flagged : .1% } " ) Symmetric fences 22.9 to 76.7 | flagged 0.9% Right-skewed fences -25.3 to 96.8 | flagged 6.0% Left-skewed fences 65.2 to 107.6 | flagged 4.7% In the right-skewed sample, the rule flags a noticeable share of values, and all of them are genuine draws from the same process. In skewed business data, big orders and long waits are often real and often the most important records. What to do with a flagged value: Finding Action It is impossible (negative quantity, ship date before order date) Treat as a data error: correct it from the source or exclude it, and record the change in the preparation log It is possible but rare (a very large order) Keep it. Report robust statistics (median, IQR), and look at the large cases separately You cannot tell Keep it, flag it, and ask the data owner Check your understanding 5 A colleague deletes every order above the upper IQR fence "to clean the data" and then reports total sales. What has gone wrong?
docs.title: Part 6: Unusual values — flag, do not delete

docs.text: The retail table has one row per order line . Questions about "a typical order" need one row per order . We build that table first and check our grain claim. # One row per ORDER: add up the lines of each order. # Segment, ship mode and ship days are the same on every line of an order, so we take the first. orders = df . groupby ( "order_id" ) . agg ( order_value = ( "sales" , "sum" ), segment = ( "segment" , "first" ), ship_mode = ( "ship_mode" , "first" ), ship_days = ( "order_to_ship_days" , "first" ), ) # Check that claim before relying on it: each should be 1. per_order = df . groupby ( "order_id" )[[ "segment" , "ship_mode" , "order_to_ship_days" ]] . nunique () print ( "Most different values inside one order:" ) print ( per_order . max ()) print ( "Orders:" , len ( orders )) Most different values inside one order: segment 1 ship_mode 1 order_to_ship_days 1 dtype: int64 Orders: 3388 Every maximum is 1: each order has one segment, one ship mode and one ship-days value, so taking the first line is safe.
docs.title: Part 7: Worked case — Superstore orders

A second histogram with logarithmic bins (each bin a fixed multiple wider than the last) spreads the small and large orders out so the shape is visible. docs.text: Ship days take only a few whole-number values, so a bar per value works better than a histogram. sd = orders [ "ship_days" ] sd . value_counts () . sort_index () . plot ( kind = "bar" , title = "Days from order to shipment, one bar per value" ) plt . xlabel ( "Days" ) plt . ylabel ( "Orders" ) plt . xticks ( rotation = 0 ) plt . show () print ( "Mean:" , round ( sd . mean (), 2 ), "| median:" , sd . median (), "| mode:" , sd . mode ()[ 0 ]) print ( "90th percentile:" , sd . quantile ( 0.9 )) Mean: 3.97 | median: 4.0 | mode: 4 90th percentile: 6.0 Here the mean and median are close, so either is a fair "typical" value. DataFrame ({ "order value (per order)" : describe_shape ( orders [ "order_value" ]), "ship days (per order)" : describe_shape ( orders [ "ship_days" ]), }) summary .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } order value (per order) ship days (per order) count 3,388.00 3,388.00 mean 466.64 3.97 median 151.46 4.00 std 975.36 1.73 IQR 493.33 2.00 90th pct 1,181.29 6.00 skew 8.86 -0.42 flagged by IQR rule 305.00 1.00 Reading the table: Order value is strongly right-skewed: report the median with the IQR (or percentiles), and mention that a small number of large orders exist. docs.text: Session 5 lab: Which segment deserves a closer look? ¶ Compare the three customer segments using five measures, calculate each one correctly, check that the numbers add up, write a metric contract, and make a careful recommendation. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . The business decision ¶ The retail head has one analyst free next month and asks: "Which customer segment should we investigate first, and what should we check before we change any promotions?" A big Sales total alone is not enough to decide. A segment can sell a lot and still earn little profit, or have many small orders. In this lab you build a fair comparison. About the data The Superstore sample describes a fictitious company. Sales and Profit are in source monetary units : the currency is not stated, so never add a currency symbol. The source does not explain how Profit is calculated, so we say profit ratio , never "margin". The Berkeley admissions counts are the published figures for the six largest departments in 1973 (Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell, 1975, Science ). How this lab works ¶ Part What you do Tasks Guided practice Follow along step by step, everyone together G1–G5 Independent tasks Same skills, new questions, on your own or in pairs I1–I7 Challenge Harder reasoning and debugging C1–C2 Each task has a level: Core : everyone completes it; it is enough for your portfolio. Stretch : for when you finish the core tasks early. Challenge : optional, harder reasoning. What you will be able to do ¶ Define five measures precisely: Sales, Orders, Average order value, Profit and Profit ratio. Calculate them in pandas, for the whole table and for each segment. Calculate ratios from totals , not by averaging other ratios. Check that segment results reconcile with the overall total. Explain how a filter changes every measure. Write a metric contract and explain Simpson's paradox with real data. Write a short, evidence-based recommendation with one limitation. Evidence you keep: a segment KPI table, a metric contract, a validation checklist, a Berkeley explanation and a five-sentence recommendation. Before you start, read the Session 5 lecture and have your grain statement from the Session 2 lab ready. Guided practice ¶ G1 (Core): Agree the measures ¶ Every measure uses the same rows : all order lines in the table, unless you deliberately apply a filter. Measure What it means pandas Sales Total reported Sales df["sales"].sum() Orders Number of different orders df["order_id"].nunique() AOV (average order value) Sales per order Sales ÷ Orders Profit Total reported Profit (can be negative) df["profit"].sum() Profit ratio Profit per unit of Sales Profit ÷ Sales Totals first, then divide AOV and Profit ratio are always calculated from the totals of whatever you are looking at. Never average the ratios of individual rows or of segments. You will see why in C1. When there is nothing to divide by If a filter leaves no orders or no Sales, the ratio is not available . pandas shows this as NaN ("not a number"). Read it as "not available" , never as 0%. Predict first ¶ Before you run the next cells, write down your answers: Will AOV be larger or smaller than Sales divided by the number of rows ? Why? Can Profit ratio be negative? When? Run the setup cell, then load the table. # Course data setup. Run this cell first; you do not need to understand it yet. # It downloads the Superstore sample from Tableau's website, checks it is the # exact version this course was written for, and prepares the order-lines table. import hashlib import os import urllib.request import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd SOURCE_URL = "https://public.tableau.com/app/sample-data/sample_-_superstore.xls" EXPECTED_SHA256 = "5045ed4fec49cae2cc0dfc5ab0d204ba09efa767fe00c996822499e8cc42fbbd" SOURCE_FILE = os . environ . get ( "COURSE_XLS_PATH" , "sample_-_superstore.xls" ) try : import xlrd # noqa: F401 (needed to read .xls files) except ImportError : import subprocess import sys subprocess . check_call ([ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-q" , "xlrd" ]) if not os . path . exists ( SOURCE_FILE ): urllib . request . urlretrieve ( SOURCE_URL , SOURCE_FILE ) with open ( SOURCE_FILE , "rb" ) as f : digest = hashlib . sha256 ( f . read ()) . hexdigest () if digest != EXPECTED_SHA256 : print ( "WARNING: Tableau has changed this sample file since the course was written." ) print ( "Your numbers will differ from the lesson. Ask your facilitator for the course copy." ) def load_orders (): """Return one row per order line, orders placed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31.""" raw = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Orders" ) returns = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Returns" ) # Orders with more than one Customer ID (a known data issue), found before filtering. ids_per_order = raw . groupby ( "Order ID" )[ "Customer ID" ] . nunique () conflict_orders = set ( ids_per_order [ ids_per_order > 1 ] . index ) in_scope = ( raw [ "Order Date" ] >= "2023-01-01" ) & ( raw [ "Order Date" ] < "2026-01-01" ) df = raw . loc [ in_scope ] . copy () df = df . rename ( columns = { "Row ID" : "row_id" , "Order ID" : "order_id" , "Order Date" : "order_date" , "Ship Date" : "ship_date" , "Ship Mode" : "ship_mode" , "Customer ID" : "customer_id" , "Segment" : "segment" , "Country/Region" : "country_region" , "Region" : "region" , "Category" : "category" , "Sub-Category" : "sub_category" , "Product ID" : "product_id" , "Product Name" : "product_name" , "Sales" : "sales" , "Quantity" : "quantity" , "Discount" : "discount" , "Profit" : "profit" , }) df [ "returned_order_flag" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( set ( returns [ "Order ID" ])) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( conflict_orders ) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_analysis_eligible" ] = 1 - df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] df [ "order_to_ship_days" ] = ( df [ "ship_date" ] - df [ "order_date" ]) . dt . days df [ "order_month" ] = df [ "order_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "M" ) . dt . to_timestamp () columns = [ "row_id" , "order_id" , "order_date" , "ship_date" , "ship_mode" , "customer_id" , "segment" , "country_region" , "region" , "category" , "sub_category" , "product_id" , "product_name" , "sales" , "quantity" , "discount" , "profit" , "returned_order_flag" , "customer_analysis_eligible" , "customer_order_conflict" , "order_to_ship_days" , "order_month" , ] return df [ columns ] . sort_values ( "row_id" ) . reset_index ( drop = True ) pd . set_option ( "display.float_format" , " {:,.2f} " . format ) plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 8 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.prop_cycle" : plt . cycler ( color = [ "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]), "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) print ( "Setup complete." ) Setup complete. df = load_orders () print ( "Order lines (rows):" , len ( df )) Order lines (rows): 6815 G2 (Core): The five measures for the whole table ¶ Read each line: it matches one row of the table in G1. total_sales = df [ "sales" ] . sum () total_orders = df [ "order_id" ] . nunique () total_profit = df [ "profit" ] . sum () aov = total_sales / total_orders profit_ratio = total_profit / total_sales print ( "Sales: " , round ( total_sales , 2 )) print ( "Orders: " , total_orders ) print ( "AOV: " , round ( aov , 2 )) print ( "Profit: " , round ( total_profit , 2 )) print ( "Profit ratio (%):" , round ( profit_ratio * 100 , 1 )) Sales: 1580966.82 Orders: 3388 AOV: 466.64 Profit: 196370.47 Profit ratio (%): 12.4 round(x, 2) keeps two decimal places, just for display. We multiply the profit ratio by 100 to show it as a percentage. Check your predictions Compare the number of rows with the number of orders above. Does that change your answer to prediction 1? G3 (Core): The segment KPI table ¶ Step 1: totals for each segment ¶ In the Session 1 lab you used groupby with one sum. .agg lets you calculate several totals at once. Each line inside reads as new column name = (column to use, how to summarise it) . segment_kpis = df . groupby ( "segment" ) . agg ( sales = ( "sales" , "sum" ), orders = ( "order_id" , "nunique" ), profit = ( "profit" , "sum" ), ) segment_kpis .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } sales orders profit segment Consumer 835,747.86 1738 90,101.17 Corporate 467,562.02 1044 65,842.38 Home Office 277,656.95 606 40,426.92 Step 2: the two ratios, from each segment's totals ¶ segment_kpis [ "aov" ] = segment_kpis [ "sales" ] / segment_kpis [ "orders" ] segment_kpis [ "profit_ratio_pct" ] = segment_kpis [ "profit" ] / segment_kpis [ "sales" ] * 100 segment_kpis .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } sales orders profit aov profit_ratio_pct segment Consumer 835,747.86 1738 90,101.17 480.87 10.78 Corporate 467,562.02 1044 65,842.38 447.86 14.08 Home Office 277,656.95 606 40,426.92 458.18 14.56 Step 3: add an overall row ¶ The overall row uses the totals from G2. Its AOV and profit ratio are recalculated from totals , not added up or averaged from the rows above. segment_kpis . loc [ "All" ] = [ total_sales , total_orders , total_profit , aov , profit_ratio * 100 ] segment_kpis [ "orders" ] = segment_kpis [ "orders" ] . astype ( int ) segment_kpis = segment_kpis [[ "sales" , "orders" , "aov" , "profit" , "profit_ratio_pct" ]] segment_kpis . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } sales orders aov profit profit_ratio_pct segment Consumer 835,747.86 1738 480.87 90,101.17 10.78 Corporate 467,562.02 1044 447.86 65,842.38 14.08 Home Office 277,656.95 606 458.18 40,426.92 14.56 All 1,580,966.82 3388 466.64 196,370.47 12.42 The second line keeps orders as whole numbers. The third line puts the columns in the same order as the table in G1. Give the table a clear title in your evidence log, for example "Segment comparison, orders placed 2023–2025 (source monetary units)" . A picture of the profit ratio ¶ The dashed line is the overall profit ratio from the All row. by_segment = segment_kpis . drop ( "All" ) by_segment [ "profit_ratio_pct" ] . sort_values () . plot ( kind = "barh" , title = "Profit ratio by segment, orders placed 2023–2025" , label = "Segment" ) plt . axvline ( profit_ratio * 100 , color = "#444444" , linestyle = "--" , label = "All segments" ) plt . xlabel ( "Profit ratio ( % o f Sales)" ) plt . ylabel ( "" ) plt . legend () plt . show () Read the chart Which segment is above the line and which is below? Now look back at the Sales column. Is the segment with the most Sales also the one with the highest profit ratio? G4 (Core): Check that it reconciles ¶ A table you cannot reconcile is a table you cannot trust. by_segment is the table without the All row. print ( "Sales: segments add up to" , round ( by_segment [ "sales" ] . sum (), 2 ), "| overall" , round ( total_sales , 2 )) print ( "Profit: segments add up to" , round ( by_segment [ "profit" ] . sum (), 2 ), "| overall" , round ( total_profit , 2 )) print ( "Orders: segments add up to" , by_segment [ "orders" ] . sum (), "| overall" , total_orders ) Sales: segments add up to 1580966.82 | overall 1580966.82 Profit: segments add up to 196370.47 | overall 196370.47 Orders: segments add up to 3388 | overall 3388 Orders can only add up if every order belongs to exactly one segment. Check it: count the different segments inside each order and look at the largest count. segments_per_order = df . groupby ( "order_id" )[ "segment" ] . nunique () print ( "Largest number of segments in one order:" , segments_per_order . max ()) Largest number of segments in one order: 1 Tick each check in your evidence log: The segment Sales add up to the overall total. docs.text: The retail head has one analyst free next month and asks: "Which customer segment should we investigate first, and what should we check before we change any promotions?" A big Sales total alone is not enough to decide. A segment can sell a lot and still earn little profit, or have many small orders. In this lab you build a fair comparison. About the data The Superstore sample describes a fictitious company. Sales and Profit are in source monetary units : the currency is not stated, so never add a currency symbol. The source does not explain how Profit is calculated, so we say profit ratio , never "margin". The Berkeley admissions counts are the published figures for the six largest departments in 1973 (Bickel, Hammel and O'Connell, 1975, Science ).

docs.text: Session 5 lecture: Metrics and KPIs ¶ A metric is only as good as its definition. This lecture shows what makes a metric useful, how to write it down so everyone calculates the same number, and the traps that make honest totals and averages tell the wrong story. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . Recap quiz ¶ Before we start, answer the quiz at the end of the Session 4 lecture . Write short answers; we discuss them together. What you will be able to explain ¶ What makes a metric actionable , defined and comparable , and how a KPI differs from any other metric. What goes into a metric contract : grain, numerator, denominator, scope, zero and missing rules, owner. Why a ratio of sums is not the mean of ratios , and how the overall rate is a weighted average of group rates. Why distinct counts do not add up across groups or periods. How Simpson's paradox can reverse a comparison when groups are combined. Why a metric that becomes a target can stop measuring what you wanted ( Goodhart's law ). This lecture builds on How statistics can mislead , especially Simpson's paradox and the averages traps. A KPI (key performance indicator) is a metric that a team has agreed to watch because it is tied to a goal. A good metric is: Quality Question to ask Weak example Better example Actionable If it moves, does someone know what to do? Total page views Share of visitors who reach checkout Defined Would two analysts get the same number? "Average order" Sales ÷ distinct orders, orders placed in the period Comparable Can we compare groups or periods fairly? Total sales by region (regions differ in size) Sales per order, profit ratio Timely Is it available when the decision is made? Annual survey for a weekly decision Weekly order count Hard to game Can it improve while the business gets worse? Number of calls closed Calls closed and repeat calls within 7 days Vanity metrics A vanity metric goes up and looks good, but does not help a decision: total registered users, all-time downloads, total impressions. They almost always grow. Ask: "What would we do differently if this number fell?" If there is no answer, it is not a KPI. Check your understanding 1 A manager wants to track "total sales" to compare four regional teams. Which quality is weakest, and what metric would you suggest alongside it? Part 2: Metric contracts ¶ A metric contract is a short written definition that removes every choice an analyst could make differently. Without one, two people can both be "right" and still report different numbers. Field Question it answers Example: average order value (AOV) Name What do we call it? Average order value Purpose Which decision does it inform? Compare how much customers spend per order across segments Grain What is one row in the data? One order line Numerator What is added up on top? Sum of sales Denominator What is counted below? Number of distinct order_id Scope and filters Which rows and dates count? Orders placed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31; no other filters Zero and missing rules What if the denominator is 0 or values are missing? No orders → "not available" ( NaN ), never 0 Unit and display How is it shown? Source monetary units, 2 decimals, no currency symbol Owner Who decides if the definition changes? Retail analytics lead Predict, then reveal: one name, two numbers ¶ Two analysts are both asked for "average order value". One divides Sales by the number of rows ; the other divides by the number of distinct orders . Predict, then reveal Which answer is larger, and roughly by how much? Think about how many lines a typical order has. sales = df [ "sales" ] . sum () per_row = sales / len ( df ) per_order = sales / df [ "order_id" ] . nunique () print ( "Analyst 1, Sales per row (order line):" , round ( per_row , 2 )) print ( "Analyst 2, Sales per distinct order: " , round ( per_order , 2 )) print ( "Ratio of the two: " , round ( per_order / per_row , 2 )) Analyst 1, Sales per row (order line): 231.98 Analyst 2, Sales per distinct order: 466.64 Ratio of the two: 2.01 Both analysts calculated something correctly. Only one calculated what the name promises. The ratio of the two is exactly the average number of lines per order. A contract that states the denominator prevents this argument. A contract can also live in code, next to the calculation, so the definition travels with the number: aov_contract = { "name" : "Average order value (AOV)" , "purpose" : "Compare spend per order across customer segments" , "grain" : "One order line" , "numerator" : "Sum of sales" , "denominator" : "Number of distinct order_id" , "scope" : "Orders placed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31" , "zero_rule" : "No orders in scope -> not available (NaN), never 0" , "unit" : "Source monetary units, 2 decimals, no currency symbol" , "owner" : "Retail analytics lead" , } pd . Series ( aov_contract , name = "definition" ) . to_frame () .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } definition name Average order value (AOV) purpose Compare spend per order across customer segments grain One order line numerator Sum of sales denominator Number of distinct order_id scope Orders placed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31 zero_rule No orders in scope -> not available (NaN), nev... unit Source monetary units, 2 decimals, no currency... owner Retail analytics lead Check your understanding 2 A report shows "Return rate: 4%". Write three questions you would need answered (three contract fields) before you could reproduce that number. Part 3: Ratio of sums versus mean of ratios ¶ Many KPIs are ratios : profit ÷ sales, conversions ÷ visits, late deliveries ÷ deliveries. When you combine groups, there are two tempting ways to get an overall ratio: Ratio of sums: add up all numerators, add up all denominators, then divide. Mean of ratios: calculate each group's ratio, then average them. Predict, then reveal: a big store and a tiny store ¶ Two stores report their profit ratio. Store A is large; Store B is a small kiosk. Store Sales Profit A 10,000 1,000 B 100 50 Predict, then reveal What is the company's overall profit ratio? Is it closer to Store A's ratio or to the simple average of the two ratios? stores = pd . DataFrame ({ "sales" : [ 10_000 , 100 ], "profit" : [ 1_000 , 50 ]}, index = [ "A" , "B" ]) stores [ "profit_ratio" ] = stores [ "profit" ] / stores [ "sales" ] mean_of_ratios = stores [ "profit_ratio" ] . mean () ratio_of_sums = stores [ "profit" ] . sum () / stores [ "sales" ] . sum () print ( stores ) print () print ( "Mean of the two ratios:" , f " { mean_of_ratios : .1% } " ) print ( "Ratio of the sums: " , f " { ratio_of_sums : .1% } " ) sales profit profit_ratio A 10000 1000 0.10 B 100 50 0.50 Mean of the two ratios: 30.0% Ratio of the sums: 10.4% The kiosk's high ratio counts as much as the big store's in the simple mean, even though it sold a hundred times less. The ratio of sums is what the company actually earned per unit of sales. The overall ratio is a weighted average ¶ The ratio of sums is not a mysterious new number. It is the average of the group ratios, weighted by each group's share of the denominator . Here the weights are each store's share of Sales: weights = stores [ "sales" ] / stores [ "sales" ] . sum () weighted = ( weights * stores [ "profit_ratio" ]) . sum () print ( "Sales share (weights):" ) print ( weights . round ( 4 )) print () print ( "Weighted average of ratios:" , f " { weighted : .1% } " ) print ( "Ratio of sums: " , f " { ratio_of_sums : .1% } " ) Sales share (weights): A 0.99 B 0.01 Name: sales, dtype: float64 Weighted average of ratios: 10.4% Ratio of sums: 10.4% The two printed numbers are identical. This gives you a rule you can use everywhere: Totals first, then divide To get a ratio for any combination of groups, add up the numerator and the denominator over those groups, then divide. A simple mean of group ratios is only correct when every group has the same denominator. Check your understanding 3 A website reports a conversion rate for each of 30 days. Your manager wants "the conversion rate for the month". What should you calculate, and when would the simple average of the 30 daily rates give the same answer? Part 4: Weighted rates in practice ¶ The same idea applies whenever a rate is compared across groups of different sizes. Here, three warehouses report their on-time delivery rate. warehouses = pd . DataFrame ({ "deliveries" : [ 5_000 , 800 , 200 ], "on_time" : [ 4_500 , 760 , 196 ], }, index = [ "Central" , "North" , "Island" ]) warehouses [ "on_time_rate" ] = warehouses [ "on_time" ] / warehouses [ "deliveries" ] print ( warehouses ) print () print ( "Simple mean of rates: " , f " { warehouses [ 'on_time_rate' ] . mean () : .1% } " ) print ( "Company on-time rate (sums):" , f " { warehouses [ 'on_time' ] . sum () / warehouses [ 'deliveries' ] . sum () : .1% } " ) deliveries on_time on_time_rate Central 5000 4500 0.90 North 800 760 0.95 Island 200 196 0.98 Simple mean of rates: 94.3% Company on-time rate (sums): 90.9% The small warehouses have the best rates, so the simple mean makes the company look better than its customers experience. Customers experience deliveries , so deliveries are the right weight. Which weight? The weight is always the denominator of the rate: Sales for a profit ratio, orders for an order-level rate, visits for a conversion rate, employees for a turnover rate. If you are unsure, write the rate as a fraction and look at the bottom. There is one case where an unweighted mean of rates is right: when the question is about the groups themselves , for example "How does a typical warehouse perform?" Then each warehouse counts once. Say so explicitly in the metric contract. Part 5: Distinct counts do not add up ¶ Sums add up across groups: the Sales of three segments add up to total Sales. Distinct counts often do not, because the same item can appear in several groups. Predict, then reveal: customers per year ¶ We count distinct customers in each year and add them up. Then we count distinct customers over all three years. Predict, then reveal Will the sum of the yearly counts be larger, smaller or equal to the three-year count? Why? Customer counts use only the lines marked customer_analysis_eligible == 1 , which excludes the few orders that carry two different customer IDs (Session 2). We disclose that exclusion every time we count customers. eligible = df [ df [ "customer_analysis_eligible" ] == 1 ] print ( "Lines excluded from customer counts:" , len ( df ) - len ( eligible )) by_year = eligible . groupby ( eligible [ "order_date" ] . dt . year )[ "customer_id" ] . nunique () print ( by_year ) print () print ( "Sum of yearly distinct customers:" , by_year . sum ()) print ( "Distinct customers, 2023-2025: " , eligible [ "customer_id" ] . nunique ()) Lines excluded from customer counts: 4 order_date 2023 605 2024 577 2025 649 Name: customer_id, dtype: int64 Sum of yearly distinct customers: 1831 Distinct customers, 2023-2025: 789 Most customers bought in more than one year, so they are counted once per year in the yearly totals but only once in the three-year count. Non-additive measures Distinct counts (customers, orders across categories, products), medians and percentiles, and ratios are non-additive : you cannot add the group values to get the total. Always recalculate them from the underlying rows for the total. Sums and plain counts of rows are additive . Check your understanding 4 A dashboard shows distinct orders for each product category and a "Total" row that is the sum of the category values. Why is the total wrong, and would it be too high or too low? Part 6: Simpson's paradox ¶ Simpson's paradox happens when a comparison holds in every group, but reverses (or disappears) when the groups are combined. It is the weighted-average idea from Part 3 with a twist: the two things being compared have different mixes across the groups. UC Berkeley graduate admissions, 1973 ¶ The Foundations page told the story: across all departments, a higher share of men than women were admitted. DataFrame ({ "department" : [ "A" , "B" , "C" , "D" , "E" , "F" ], "men_applied" : [ 825 , 560 , 325 , 417 , 191 , 373 ], "men_admitted" : [ 512 , 353 , 120 , 138 , 53 , 22 ], "women_applied" : [ 108 , 25 , 593 , 375 , 393 , 341 ], "women_admitted" : [ 89 , 17 , 202 , 131 , 94 , 24 ], }) . set_index ( "department" ) berkeley [ "men_rate" ] = berkeley [ "men_admitted" ] / berkeley [ "men_applied" ] berkeley [ "women_rate" ] = berkeley [ "women_admitted" ] / berkeley [ "women_applied" ] berkeley [[ "men_applied" , "men_rate" , "women_applied" , "women_rate" ]] . round ( 3 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } men_applied men_rate women_applied women_rate department A 825 0.62 108 0.82 B 560 0.63 25 0.68 C 325 0.37 593 0.34 D 417 0.33 375 0.35 E 191 0.28 393 0.24 F 373 0.06 341 0.07 Predict, then reveal In how many of the six departments is the women's admission rate higher? Now predict: when we add the six departments together, which group will have the higher overall rate? men_overall = berkeley [ "men_admitted" ] . sum () / berkeley [ "men_applied" ] . sum () women_overall = berkeley [ "women_admitted" ] . sum () / berkeley [ "women_applied" ] . sum () print ( "Departments where women's rate is higher:" , ( berkeley [ "women_rate" ] > berkeley [ "men_rate" ]) . sum (), "of 6" ) print ( "Six departments combined, men: " , f " { men_overall : .1% } " ) print ( "Six departments combined, women:" , f " { women_overall : .1% } " ) Departments where women's rate is higher: 4 of 6 Six departments combined, men: 44.5% Six departments combined, women: 30.4% Why it reverses: different application mixes ¶ The overall rate for each group is a weighted average of the department rates, weighted by where that group applied . Look at the share of each group's applications that went to each department, next to how hard each department was to get into. mix = pd . DataFrame ({ "share_of_men_applying" : berkeley [ "men_applied" ] / berkeley [ "men_applied" ] . sum (), "share_of_women_applying" : berkeley [ "women_applied" ] / berkeley [ "women_applied" ] . sum (), "dept_admit_rate_all" : ( berkeley [ "men_admitted" ] + berkeley [ "women_admitted" ]) / ( berkeley [ "men_applied" ] + berkeley [ "women_applied" ]), }) mix . round ( 3 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } share_of_men_applying share_of_women_applying dept_admit_rate_all department A 0.31 0.06 0.64 B 0.21 0.01 0.63 C 0.12 0.32 0.35 D 0.15 0.20 0.34 E 0.07 0.21 0.25 F 0.14 0.19 0.06 fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4 )) x = range ( len ( berkeley )) ax . bar ([ i - 0.2 for i in x ], mix [ "share_of_men_applying" ] * 100 , width = 0.4 , label = "Men" , color = "#4C78A8" ) ax . bar ([ i + 0.2 for i in x ], mix [ "share_of_women_applying" ] * 100 , width = 0.4 , label = "Women" , color = "#F58518" ) ax . set_xticks ( list ( x ), [ f "Dept { d } \n (admits { r : .0% } )" for d , r in mix [ "dept_admit_rate_all" ] . items ()]) ax . set_ylabel ( "Share of the group's applications (%)" ) ax . set_title ( "Women applied mostly to the departments that admitted fewest applicants" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) ax . spines [[ "top" , "right" ]] . set_visible ( False ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Most men applied to departments A and B, which admitted most applicants. Most women applied to C to F, which admitted few applicants of either sex. So the combined rate mostly reflects which departments people applied to , not how each department treated men and women. What Simpson's paradox does and does not prove The department-level view removes one explanation (department choice). It does not prove there was no bias anywhere: why women applied to more competitive departments is a separate question. Splitting data is a way to ask better questions, not a way to make awkward results disappear. Explain how this can happen in two sentences. Part 7: Goodhart's law ¶ "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." (a common summary of economist Charles Goodhart's 1975 observation) Once people are rewarded for a number, they find ways to move the number that do not move the goal: Target Easy way to hit it What gets worse Average call handling time below 4 minutes End calls early Problems not solved, repeat calls On-time delivery rate above 95% Promise later delivery dates Customers wait longer Average order value up 10% Stop small orders with high minimum basket Fewer customers, fewer orders Profit ratio up Stop selling low-margin items Total profit can fall The defence is to pair every target with a guardrail metric that would get worse if the target were gamed, and to keep the metric contract public so changes in definition are visible. Part 8: Worked case — a segment KPI table that reconciles ¶ The retail head wants to compare the three customer segments. We apply everything above to the Superstore orders. Step 1: Totals for each segment, then divide ¶ Every ratio is calculated from the segment's totals . Orders use nunique . seg = df . groupby ( "segment" ) . agg ( sales = ( "sales" , "sum" ), orders = ( "order_id" , "nunique" ), profit = ( "profit" , "sum" ), ) seg [ "aov" ] = seg [ "sales" ] / seg [ "orders" ] seg [ "profit_ratio" ] = seg [ "profit" ] / seg [ "sales" ] # Show the ratio as a percentage for reading; keep the fraction for calculations below. seg . assign ( profit_ratio_pct = seg [ "profit_ratio" ] * 100 ) . drop ( columns = "profit_ratio" ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } sales orders profit aov profit_ratio_pct segment Consumer 835,747.86 1738 90,101.17 480.87 10.78 Corporate 467,562.02 1044 65,842.38 447.86 14.08 Home Office 277,656.95 606 40,426.92 458.18 14.56 Step 2: Predict, then reveal — the overall profit ratio ¶ Predict, then reveal Will the simple mean of the three segment profit ratios be above or below the true overall profit ratio? Look at which segment has the most Sales and where its ratio sits. overall_ratio = df [ "profit" ] . sum () / df [ "sales" ] . sum () simple_mean = seg [ "profit_ratio" ] . mean () sales_share = seg [ "sales" ] / seg [ "sales" ] . sum () weighted_mean = ( sales_share * seg [ "profit_ratio" ]) . sum () print ( "True overall profit ratio (sums): " , f " { overall_ratio : .2% } " ) print ( "Simple mean of segment ratios: " , f " { simple_mean : .2% } " ) print ( "Sales-weighted mean of segment ratios:" , f " { weighted_mean : .2% } " ) print () print ( "Each segment's share of Sales (the weights):" ) print ( sales_share . round ( 3 )) True overall profit ratio (sums): 12.42% Simple mean of segment ratios: 13.14% Sales-weighted mean of segment ratios: 12.42% Each segment's share of Sales (the weights): segment Consumer 0.53 Corporate 0.30 Home Office 0.18 Name: sales, dtype: float64 The weighted mean matches the true ratio exactly; the simple mean does not. The segment with the largest Sales share pulls the true overall ratio towards its own value. Step 3: Does it reconcile? ¶ Additive measures must add up to the overall total. Orders add up only because every order belongs to exactly one segment, which we check rather than assume. print ( "Sales add up: " , bool ( abs ( seg [ "sales" ] . sum () - df [ "sales" ] . sum ()) < 1e-6 )) print ( "Profit adds up:" , bool ( abs ( seg [ "profit" ] . sum () - df [ "profit" ] . sum ()) < 1e-6 )) print ( "Orders add up: " , seg [ "orders" ] . sum () == df [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) print ( "Max segments in one order:" , df . groupby ( "order_id" )[ "segment" ] . nunique () . max ()) Sales add up: True Profit adds up: True Orders add up: True Max segments in one order: 1 Step 4: The same check for category ¶ Now group by product category, where one order can contain several categories. cat_orders = df . groupby ( "category" )[ "order_id" ] . nunique () print ( cat_orders ) print () print ( "Category orders added up:" , cat_orders . sum ()) print ( "Distinct orders overall: " , df [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) category Furniture 1235 Office Supplies 2516 Technology 1028 Name: order_id, dtype: int64 Category orders added up: 4779 Distinct orders overall: 3388 The category order counts add up to more than the true number of orders, because an order with a chair and some paper is counted in both Furniture and Office Supplies. A "Total" row that sums them would be wrong. This is the non-additive trap from Part 5 inside a real table. Summary ¶ Situation Do this Not this Any shared metric Write a contract: grain, numerator, denominator, scope, zero rule, owner Rely on the metric's name Combining a ratio across groups Sum numerators and denominators, then divide Average the group ratios Comparing rates of groups with different sizes Weight by the rate's denominator Treat each group as equal (unless the question is about groups) Distinct counts, medians, ratios in a total row Recalculate from rows Add up the group values A comparison that changes when you split or combine Check the mix of each group across subgroups (Simpson) Report only the combined number A metric becomes a target Pair it with a guardrail Reward the single number Quiz ¶ Answer these at the start of the next lecture. docs.text: A metric is a number calculated the same way every time, so you can compare it over time or across groups. A KPI (key performance indicator) is a metric that a team has agreed to watch because it is tied to a goal. A good metric is: Quality Question to ask Weak example Better example Actionable If it moves, does someone know what to do? Total page views Share of visitors who reach checkout Defined Would two analysts get the same number? "Average order" Sales ÷ distinct orders, orders placed in the period Comparable Can we compare groups or periods fairly? Total sales by region (regions differ in size) Sales per order, profit ratio Timely Is it available when the decision is made? Annual survey for a weekly decision Weekly order count Hard to game Can it improve while the business gets worse? Number of calls closed Calls closed and repeat calls within 7 days Vanity metrics A vanity metric goes up and looks good, but does not help a decision: total registered users, all-time downloads, total impressions. They almost always grow. Ask: "What would we do differently if this number fell?" If there is no answer, it is not a KPI. Check your understanding 1 A manager wants to track "total sales" to compare four regional teams. Which quality is weakest, and what metric would you suggest alongside it?

docs.text: A metric contract is a short written definition that removes every choice an analyst could make differently. Without one, two people can both be "right" and still report different numbers. Field Question it answers Example: average order value (AOV) Name What do we call it? Average order value Purpose Which decision does it inform? Compare how much customers spend per order across segments Grain What is one row in the data? One order line Numerator What is added up on top? Sum of sales Denominator What is counted below? Number of distinct order_id Scope and filters Which rows and dates count? Orders placed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31; no other filters Zero and missing rules What if the denominator is 0 or values are missing? No orders → "not available" ( NaN ), never 0 Unit and display How is it shown? Source monetary units, 2 decimals, no currency symbol Owner Who decides if the definition changes? Retail analytics lead
docs.title: Part 2: Metric contracts

docs.text: Two analysts are both asked for "average order value". One divides Sales by the number of rows ; the other divides by the number of distinct orders . Predict, then reveal Which answer is larger, and roughly by how much? Think about how many lines a typical order has. sales = df [ "sales" ] . sum () per_row = sales / len ( df ) per_order = sales / df [ "order_id" ] . nunique () print ( "Analyst 1, Sales per row (order line):" , round ( per_row , 2 )) print ( "Analyst 2, Sales per distinct order: " , round ( per_order , 2 )) print ( "Ratio of the two: " , round ( per_order / per_row , 2 )) Analyst 1, Sales per row (order line): 231.98 Analyst 2, Sales per distinct order: 466.64 Ratio of the two: 2.01 Both analysts calculated something correctly. Only one calculated what the name promises. The ratio of the two is exactly the average number of lines per order. A contract that states the denominator prevents this argument. A contract can also live in code, next to the calculation, so the definition travels with the number: aov_contract = { "name" : "Average order value (AOV)" , "purpose" : "Compare spend per order across customer segments" , "grain" : "One order line" , "numerator" : "Sum of sales" , "denominator" : "Number of distinct order_id" , "scope" : "Orders placed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31" , "zero_rule" : "No orders in scope -> not available (NaN), never 0" , "unit" : "Source monetary units, 2 decimals, no currency symbol" , "owner" : "Retail analytics lead" , } pd . Series ( aov_contract , name = "definition" ) . to_frame () .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } definition name Average order value (AOV) purpose Compare spend per order across customer segments grain One order line numerator Sum of sales denominator Number of distinct order_id scope Orders placed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31 zero_rule No orders in scope -> not available (NaN), nev... unit Source monetary units, 2 decimals, no currency... owner Retail analytics lead Check your understanding 2 A report shows "Return rate: 4%". docs.text: Many KPIs are ratios : profit ÷ sales, conversions ÷ visits, late deliveries ÷ deliveries. When you combine groups, there are two tempting ways to get an overall ratio: Ratio of sums: add up all numerators, add up all denominators, then divide. Mean of ratios: calculate each group's ratio, then average them.
docs.title: Part 3: Ratio of sums versus mean of ratios

docs.text: Two stores report their profit ratio. Store A is large; Store B is a small kiosk. Store Sales Profit A 10,000 1,000 B 100 50 Predict, then reveal What is the company's overall profit ratio? Is it closer to Store A's ratio or to the simple average of the two ratios? stores = pd . DataFrame ({ "sales" : [ 10_000 , 100 ], "profit" : [ 1_000 , 50 ]}, index = [ "A" , "B" ]) stores [ "profit_ratio" ] = stores [ "profit" ] / stores [ "sales" ] mean_of_ratios = stores [ "profit_ratio" ] . mean () ratio_of_sums = stores [ "profit" ] . sum () / stores [ "sales" ] . sum () print ( stores ) print () print ( "Mean of the two ratios:" , f " { mean_of_ratios : .1% } " ) print ( "Ratio of the sums: " , f " { ratio_of_sums : .1% } " ) sales profit profit_ratio A 10000 1000 0.10 B 100 50 0.50 Mean of the two ratios: 30.0% Ratio of the sums: 10.4% The kiosk's high ratio counts as much as the big store's in the simple mean, even though it sold a hundred times less. The ratio of sums is what the company actually earned per unit of sales.
docs.title: Predict, then reveal: a big store and a tiny store

docs.text: The ratio of sums is not a mysterious new number. It is the average of the group ratios, weighted by each group's share of the denominator . Here the weights are each store's share of Sales: weights = stores [ "sales" ] / stores [ "sales" ] . sum () weighted = ( weights * stores [ "profit_ratio" ]) . sum () print ( "Sales share (weights):" ) print ( weights . round ( 4 )) print () print ( "Weighted average of ratios:" , f " { weighted : .1% } " ) print ( "Ratio of sums: " , f " { ratio_of_sums : .1% } " ) Sales share (weights): A 0.99 B 0.01 Name: sales, dtype: float64 Weighted average of ratios: 10.4% Ratio of sums: 10.4% The two printed numbers are identical. This gives you a rule you can use everywhere: Totals first, then divide To get a ratio for any combination of groups, add up the numerator and the denominator over those groups, then divide. A simple mean of group ratios is only correct when every group has the same denominator. Check your understanding 3 A website reports a conversion rate for each of 30 days. Your manager wants "the conversion rate for the month". What should you calculate, and when would the simple average of the 30 daily rates give the same answer?
docs.title: The overall ratio is a weighted average

docs.text: The same idea applies whenever a rate is compared across groups of different sizes. Here, three warehouses report their on-time delivery rate. warehouses = pd . DataFrame ({ "deliveries" : [ 5_000 , 800 , 200 ], "on_time" : [ 4_500 , 760 , 196 ], }, index = [ "Central" , "North" , "Island" ]) warehouses [ "on_time_rate" ] = warehouses [ "on_time" ] / warehouses [ "deliveries" ] print ( warehouses ) print () print ( "Simple mean of rates: " , f " { warehouses [ 'on_time_rate' ] . mean () : .1% } " ) print ( "Company on-time rate (sums):" , f " { warehouses [ 'on_time' ] . sum () / warehouses [ 'deliveries' ] . sum () : .1% } " ) deliveries on_time on_time_rate Central 5000 4500 0.90 North 800 760 0.95 Island 200 196 0.98 Simple mean of rates: 94.3% Company on-time rate (sums): 90.9% The small warehouses have the best rates, so the simple mean makes the company look better than its customers experience. Customers experience deliveries , so deliveries are the right weight. Which weight? The weight is always the denominator of the rate: Sales for a profit ratio, orders for an order-level rate, visits for a conversion rate, employees for a turnover rate. If you are unsure, write the rate as a fraction and look at the bottom. There is one case where an unweighted mean of rates is right: when the question is about the groups themselves , for example "How does a typical warehouse perform?" Then each warehouse counts once. Say so explicitly in the metric contract.
docs.title: Part 4: Weighted rates in practice

docs.text: Sums add up across groups: the Sales of three segments add up to total Sales. Distinct counts often do not, because the same item can appear in several groups.
docs.title: Part 5: Distinct counts do not add up

docs.text: We count distinct customers in each year and add them up. Then we count distinct customers over all three years. Predict, then reveal Will the sum of the yearly counts be larger, smaller or equal to the three-year count? Why? Customer counts use only the lines marked customer_analysis_eligible == 1 , which excludes the few orders that carry two different customer IDs (Session 2). We disclose that exclusion every time we count customers. eligible = df [ df [ "customer_analysis_eligible" ] == 1 ] print ( "Lines excluded from customer counts:" , len ( df ) - len ( eligible )) by_year = eligible . groupby ( eligible [ "order_date" ] . dt . year )[ "customer_id" ] . nunique () print ( by_year ) print () print ( "Sum of yearly distinct customers:" , by_year . sum ()) print ( "Distinct customers, 2023-2025: " , eligible [ "customer_id" ] . nunique ()) Lines excluded from customer counts: 4 order_date 2023 605 2024 577 2025 649 Name: customer_id, dtype: int64 Sum of yearly distinct customers: 1831 Distinct customers, 2023-2025: 789 Most customers bought in more than one year, so they are counted once per year in the yearly totals but only once in the three-year count. Non-additive measures Distinct counts (customers, orders across categories, products), medians and percentiles, and ratios are non-additive : you cannot add the group values to get the total. Always recalculate them from the underlying rows for the total. Sums and plain counts of rows are additive . Check your understanding 4 A dashboard shows distinct orders for each product category and a "Total" row that is the sum of the category values. Why is the total wrong, and would it be too high or too low?

docs.text: Simpson's paradox happens when a comparison holds in every group, but reverses (or disappears) when the groups are combined. It is the weighted-average idea from Part 3 with a twist: the two things being compared have different mixes across the groups.

docs.text: Every ratio is calculated from the segment's totals . docs.text: Predict, then reveal Will the simple mean of the three segment profit ratios be above or below the true overall profit ratio? Look at which segment has the most Sales and where its ratio sits. overall_ratio = df [ "profit" ] . sum () / df [ "sales" ] . sum () simple_mean = seg [ "profit_ratio" ] . mean () sales_share = seg [ "sales" ] / seg [ "sales" ] . sum () weighted_mean = ( sales_share * seg [ "profit_ratio" ]) . sum () print ( "True overall profit ratio (sums): " , f " { overall_ratio : .2% } " ) print ( "Simple mean of segment ratios: " , f " { simple_mean : .2% } " ) print ( "Sales-weighted mean of segment ratios:" , f " { weighted_mean : .2% } " ) print () print ( "Each segment's share of Sales (the weights):" ) print ( sales_share . round ( 3 )) True overall profit ratio (sums): 12.42% Simple mean of segment ratios: 13.14% Sales-weighted mean of segment ratios: 12.42% Each segment's share of Sales (the weights): segment Consumer 0.53 Corporate 0.30 Home Office 0.18 Name: sales, dtype: float64 The weighted mean matches the true ratio exactly; the simple mean does not. The segment with the largest Sales share pulls the true overall ratio towards its own value.

docs.text: Additive measures must add up to the overall total. Orders add up only because every order belongs to exactly one segment, which we check rather than assume. print ( "Sales add up: " , bool ( abs ( seg [ "sales" ] . sum () - df [ "sales" ] . sum ()) < 1e-6 )) print ( "Profit adds up:" , bool ( abs ( seg [ "profit" ] . sum () - df [ "profit" ] . sum ()) < 1e-6 )) print ( "Orders add up: " , seg [ "orders" ] . sum () == df [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) print ( "Max segments in one order:" , df . groupby ( "order_id" )[ "segment" ] . nunique () . max ()) Sales add up: True Profit adds up: True Orders add up: True Max segments in one order: 1

docs.text: Now group by product category, where one order can contain several categories. cat_orders = df . groupby ( "category" )[ "order_id" ] . nunique () print ( cat_orders ) print () print ( "Category orders added up:" , cat_orders . sum ()) print ( "Distinct orders overall: " , df [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) category Furniture 1235 Office Supplies 2516 Technology 1028 Name: order_id, dtype: int64 Category orders added up: 4779 Distinct orders overall: 3388 The category order counts add up to more than the true number of orders, because an order with a chair and some paper is counted in both Furniture and Office Supplies. A "Total" row that sums them would be wrong. This is the non-additive trap from Part 5 inside a real table.

docs.text: Session 6 lab: From default charts to decision charts ¶ Take charts that technically work but mislead or tire the reader, and rebuild them so the important comparison is obvious, honest and labelled. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . The business decision ¶ The head of the retail business says: "I get charts every week and I can never tell what I am supposed to see. Next month I want one page that shows me where we lose money and whether discounting is the reason." Today you build the habits that make that page possible: every chart has a task, one highlight, honest axes and a title that states the finding. About the data We use the Superstore sample published by Tableau. It describes a fictitious company. Sales and Profit are in source monetary units ; the currency is not stated. How this lab works ¶ Part What you do Tasks Guided practice Follow along step by step, everyone together G1–G5 Independent tasks Same skills, new charts, on your own or in pairs I1–I5 Challenge A decision chart and a debugging task C1–C2 Each task has a level: Core : everyone completes it; it is enough for your portfolio. Stretch : for when you finish the core tasks early. Challenge : optional, harder reasoning. What you will be able to do ¶ Write and reuse a small style helper for message titles and quiet axes. Redesign a crowded pie , a truncated bar axis and a rainbow line spaghetti . Draw a histogram , a scatter plot and small multiples and say what each shows. Choose sequential or diverging colour for a heatmap. Write a short critique for every before/after pair. Evidence you keep: three before/after chart pairs with critiques, your one-, two- and many-variable views, and a critique log. Before you start, work through the Session 6 lecture . Guided practice ¶ G1 (Core): Load the data and build a style helper ¶ Run the setup cell first. # Course data setup. Run this cell first; you do not need to understand it yet. # It downloads the Superstore sample from Tableau's website, checks it is the # exact version this course was written for, and prepares the order-lines table. import hashlib import os import urllib.request import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd SOURCE_URL = "https://public.tableau.com/app/sample-data/sample_-_superstore.xls" EXPECTED_SHA256 = "5045ed4fec49cae2cc0dfc5ab0d204ba09efa767fe00c996822499e8cc42fbbd" SOURCE_FILE = os . environ . get ( "COURSE_XLS_PATH" , "sample_-_superstore.xls" ) try : import xlrd # noqa: F401 (needed to read .xls files) except ImportError : import subprocess import sys subprocess . check_call ([ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-q" , "xlrd" ]) if not os . path . exists ( SOURCE_FILE ): urllib . request . urlretrieve ( SOURCE_URL , SOURCE_FILE ) with open ( SOURCE_FILE , "rb" ) as f : digest = hashlib . sha256 ( f . read ()) . hexdigest () if digest != EXPECTED_SHA256 : print ( "WARNING: Tableau has changed this sample file since the course was written." ) print ( "Your numbers will differ from the lesson. Ask your facilitator for the course copy." ) def load_orders (): """Return one row per order line, orders placed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31.""" raw = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Orders" ) returns = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Returns" ) # Orders with more than one Customer ID (a known data issue), found before filtering. ids_per_order = raw . groupby ( "Order ID" )[ "Customer ID" ] . nunique () conflict_orders = set ( ids_per_order [ ids_per_order > 1 ] . index ) in_scope = ( raw [ "Order Date" ] >= "2023-01-01" ) & ( raw [ "Order Date" ] < "2026-01-01" ) df = raw . loc [ in_scope ] . copy () df = df . rename ( columns = { "Row ID" : "row_id" , "Order ID" : "order_id" , "Order Date" : "order_date" , "Ship Date" : "ship_date" , "Ship Mode" : "ship_mode" , "Customer ID" : "customer_id" , "Segment" : "segment" , "Country/Region" : "country_region" , "Region" : "region" , "Category" : "category" , "Sub-Category" : "sub_category" , "Product ID" : "product_id" , "Product Name" : "product_name" , "Sales" : "sales" , "Quantity" : "quantity" , "Discount" : "discount" , "Profit" : "profit" , }) df [ "returned_order_flag" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( set ( returns [ "Order ID" ])) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( conflict_orders ) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_analysis_eligible" ] = 1 - df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] df [ "order_to_ship_days" ] = ( df [ "ship_date" ] - df [ "order_date" ]) . dt . days df [ "order_month" ] = df [ "order_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "M" ) . dt . to_timestamp () columns = [ "row_id" , "order_id" , "order_date" , "ship_date" , "ship_mode" , "customer_id" , "segment" , "country_region" , "region" , "category" , "sub_category" , "product_id" , "product_name" , "sales" , "quantity" , "discount" , "profit" , "returned_order_flag" , "customer_analysis_eligible" , "customer_order_conflict" , "order_to_ship_days" , "order_month" , ] return df [ columns ] . sort_values ( "row_id" ) . reset_index ( drop = True ) pd . set_option ( "display.float_format" , " {:,.2f} " . format ) plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 8 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.prop_cycle" : plt . cycler ( color = [ "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]), "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) print ( "Setup complete." ) Setup complete. Every chart in this lab uses the same two small functions: finish(ax, title, subtitle, xlabel, ylabel) writes a bold message title , a smaller subtitle for scope and units, and the axis labels. highlight(labels, focus) returns one colour per label: orange for the label(s) in focus , grey for the rest. Writing them once means every chart gets the same look, and you can copy them into later sessions. import numpy as np from matplotlib.colors import TwoSlopeNorm df = load_orders () GREY , HIGHLIGHT , INK , BLUE = "#c9c7c1" , "#eb6834" , "#55534e" , "#2a78d6" rng = np . random . default_rng ( 6 ) # fixed seed for the small random jitter used in G4 def finish ( ax , title , subtitle = "" , xlabel = "" , ylabel = "" ): """Course chart style: message title, scope subtitle, axis labels, quiet frame.""" extra_lines = subtitle . count ( " \n " ) ax . set_title ( title , loc = "left" , fontsize = 12 , fontweight = "bold" , pad = ( 24 + 12 * extra_lines ) if subtitle else 8 ) if subtitle : ax . text ( 0 , 1.02 , subtitle , transform = ax . transAxes , fontsize = 9 , color = INK , va = "bottom" ) ax . set_xlabel ( xlabel ) ax . set_ylabel ( ylabel ) for side in ( "top" , "right" ): ax . spines [ side ] . set_visible ( False ) return ax def highlight ( labels , focus ): """One colour per label: HIGHLIGHT for the label(s) in focus, GREY for the rest.""" focus = [ focus ] if isinstance ( focus , str ) else list ( focus ) return [ HIGHLIGHT if label in focus else GREY for label in labels ] print ( "Order lines:" , len ( df ), "| distinct orders:" , df [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) Order lines: 6815 | distinct orders: 3388 G2 (Core): Bad chart 1, the crowded pie ¶ A colleague wants to show "which sub-categories are in the most orders". Their chart: orders_by_sub = df . groupby ( "sub_category" )[ "order_id" ] . nunique () orders_by_sub . plot ( kind = "pie" , figsize = ( 7 , 7 ), title = "Orders by sub-category" , textprops = { "fontsize" : 8 }) plt . ylabel ( "" ) plt . show () print ( "Slices add up to:" , orders_by_sub . sum (), "| distinct orders:" , df [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) Slices add up to: 6232 | distinct orders: 3388 Read the printed line. The slices add up to more than the number of orders, because one order can contain several sub-categories (you met this overlap in Session 2). A pie says "these parts make one whole", so here it is not just hard to read; it is wrong . Problems: Seventeen slices: angles of similar size cannot be compared. Alphabetical order around the circle: the ranking is hidden. The parts overlap, so a part-of-a-whole chart misstates the data. The redesign: the share of orders that contain each sub-category, as sorted bars, with the largest highlighted. The subtitle warns that shares add up to more than 100%. share = ( orders_by_sub / df [ "order_id" ] . nunique () * 100 ) . sort_values () fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 6 )) ax . barh ( share . index , share , color = highlight ( share . index , share . idxmax ())) for name , value in share . items (): ax . text ( value + 0.3 , name , f " { value : .0f } %" , va = "center" , fontsize = 8 , color = INK ) ax . set_xlim ( 0 , share . max () * 1.1 ) ax . grid ( False ) ax . set_xticks ([]) ax . spines [ "bottom" ] . set_visible ( False ) finish ( ax , f " { share . idxmax () } is in more orders than any other sub-category" , "Share of orders containing each sub-category, orders placed 2023–2025. \n " "An order can contain several sub-categories, so the shares add up to more than 100%." ) plt . show () Write your critique In your evidence log, write two or three sentences: what was wrong with the pie, which principle each change applies (task, encoding, highlight, honest framing), and what a reader can now see in seconds. G3 (Core): One variable, a histogram ¶ How big is a typical order? First add up Sales per order (an order has several lines), then look at the distribution . order_value = df . groupby ( "order_id" )[ "sales" ] . sum () fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 4 )) ax1 . hist ( order_value , bins = 40 , color = BLUE ) ax1 . grid ( axis = "x" , visible = False ) finish ( ax1 , "A few very large orders stretch the axis" , "Sales per order, all orders" , xlabel = "Order value" ) bins = np . geomspace ( order_value . min (), order_value . max (), 40 ) ax2 . hist ( order_value , bins = bins , color = BLUE ) ax2 . set_xscale ( "log" ) ax2 . axvline ( order_value . median (), color = HIGHLIGHT , linewidth = 2 ) ax2 . text ( order_value . median () * 1.15 , ax2 . get_ylim ()[ 1 ] * 0.97 , f "median { order_value . median () : ,.0f } " , color = HIGHLIGHT , fontsize = 9 , va = "top" , bbox = { "facecolor" : "white" , "linewidth" : 0 , "pad" : 1 }) ax2 . xaxis . set_major_formatter ( " {x:,.0f} " ) ax2 . grid ( axis = "x" , visible = False ) finish ( ax2 , "On a log scale the typical order is visible" , "Same data, logarithmic x-axis" , xlabel = "Order value (log scale)" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () print ( f "Median order value: { order_value . median () : ,.2f } | mean: { order_value . mean () : ,.2f } " ) Median order value: 151.46 | mean: 466.64 The left histogram is squeezed against the axis by a long right tail. On a log scale each step to the right multiplies the value, so the bulk of orders spreads out. The mean is pulled above the median by the large orders: Session 4 goes deeper into this. A first scatter plot of every order line: fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) ax . scatter ( df [ "discount" ], df [ "profit" ], s = 10 ) finish ( ax , "Discount vs profit" , xlabel = "Discount" , ylabel = "Profit" ) plt . show () Thousands of points sit on top of each other in a few vertical stripes (the discount levels), and a handful of huge values set the scale. Add the total profit ratio at each discount level (a ratio of sums, as in Session 5) and a zero line. line_ratio = df [ "profit" ] / df [ "sales" ] * 100 jitter = rng . normal ( 0 , 0.6 , len ( df )) by_discount = df . groupby ( "discount" ) . agg ( sales = ( "sales" , "sum" ), profit = ( "profit" , "sum" ), lines = ( "row_id" , "count" )) by_discount [ "profit_ratio_pct" ] = by_discount [ "profit" ] / by_discount [ "sales" ] * 100 losing = by_discount . index [ by_discount [ "profit_ratio_pct" ] < 0 ] first_loss = losing . min () all_after_lose = ( by_discount . loc [ by_discount . index >= first_loss , "profit_ratio_pct" ] < 0 ) . all () if all_after_lose : title = f "From a { first_loss : .0% } discount upward, every discount level loses money overall" else : title = f "Some discount levels from { first_loss : .0% } upward lose money overall" fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 9 , 4.5 )) ax . scatter ( df [ "discount" ] * 100 + jitter , line_ratio , s = 8 , color = GREY , alpha = 0.25 , linewidth = 0 ) ax . scatter ( by_discount . index * 100 , by_discount [ "profit_ratio_pct" ], s = 70 , color = HIGHLIGHT , zorder = 3 , label = "Total profit ratio at that discount" ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = INK , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "lower left" , fontsize = 9 ) finish ( ax , title , "Grey: each order line (jittered sideways). docs.text: The head of the retail business says: "I get charts every week and I can never tell what I am supposed to see. Next month I want one page that shows me where we lose money and whether discounting is the reason." Today you build the habits that make that page possible: every chart has a task, one highlight, honest axes and a title that states the finding. About the data We use the Superstore sample published by Tableau. It describes a fictitious company. Sales and Profit are in source monetary units ; the currency is not stated.

docs.text: Run the setup cell first. # Course data setup. Run this cell first; you do not need to understand it yet. # It downloads the Superstore sample from Tableau's website, checks it is the # exact version this course was written for, and prepares the order-lines table. import hashlib import os import urllib.request import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd SOURCE_URL = "https://public.tableau.com/app/sample-data/sample_-_superstore.xls" EXPECTED_SHA256 = "5045ed4fec49cae2cc0dfc5ab0d204ba09efa767fe00c996822499e8cc42fbbd" SOURCE_FILE = os . environ . get ( "COURSE_XLS_PATH" , "sample_-_superstore.xls" ) try : import xlrd # noqa: F401 (needed to read .xls files) except ImportError : import subprocess import sys subprocess . check_call ([ sys . executable , "-m" , "pip" , "install" , "-q" , "xlrd" ]) if not os . path . exists ( SOURCE_FILE ): urllib . request . urlretrieve ( SOURCE_URL , SOURCE_FILE ) with open ( SOURCE_FILE , "rb" ) as f : digest = hashlib . sha256 ( f . read ()) . hexdigest () if digest != EXPECTED_SHA256 : print ( "WARNING: Tableau has changed this sample file since the course was written." ) print ( "Your numbers will differ from the lesson. Ask your facilitator for the course copy." ) def load_orders (): """Return one row per order line, orders placed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31.""" raw = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Orders" ) returns = pd . read_excel ( SOURCE_FILE , sheet_name = "Returns" ) # Orders with more than one Customer ID (a known data issue), found before filtering. ids_per_order = raw . groupby ( "Order ID" )[ "Customer ID" ] . nunique () conflict_orders = set ( ids_per_order [ ids_per_order > 1 ] . index ) in_scope = ( raw [ "Order Date" ] >= "2023-01-01" ) & ( raw [ "Order Date" ] < "2026-01-01" ) df = raw . loc [ in_scope ] . copy () df = df . rename ( columns = { "Row ID" : "row_id" , "Order ID" : "order_id" , "Order Date" : "order_date" , "Ship Date" : "ship_date" , "Ship Mode" : "ship_mode" , "Customer ID" : "customer_id" , "Segment" : "segment" , "Country/Region" : "country_region" , "Region" : "region" , "Category" : "category" , "Sub-Category" : "sub_category" , "Product ID" : "product_id" , "Product Name" : "product_name" , "Sales" : "sales" , "Quantity" : "quantity" , "Discount" : "discount" , "Profit" : "profit" , }) df [ "returned_order_flag" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( set ( returns [ "Order ID" ])) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] = df [ "order_id" ] . isin ( conflict_orders ) . astype ( int ) df [ "customer_analysis_eligible" ] = 1 - df [ "customer_order_conflict" ] df [ "order_to_ship_days" ] = ( df [ "ship_date" ] - df [ "order_date" ]) . dt . days df [ "order_month" ] = df [ "order_date" ] . dt . to_period ( "M" ) . dt . to_timestamp () columns = [ "row_id" , "order_id" , "order_date" , "ship_date" , "ship_mode" , "customer_id" , "segment" , "country_region" , "region" , "category" , "sub_category" , "product_id" , "product_name" , "sales" , "quantity" , "discount" , "profit" , "returned_order_flag" , "customer_analysis_eligible" , "customer_order_conflict" , "order_to_ship_days" , "order_month" , ] return df [ columns ] . sort_values ( "row_id" ) . reset_index ( drop = True ) pd . set_option ( "display.float_format" , " {:,.2f} " . format ) plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 8 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.prop_cycle" : plt . cycler ( color = [ "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]), "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) print ( "Setup complete." ) Setup complete. Every chart in this lab uses the same two small functions: finish(ax, title, subtitle, xlabel, ylabel) writes a bold message title , a smaller subtitle for scope and units, and the axis labels. highlight(labels, focus) returns one colour per label: orange for the label(s) in focus , grey for the rest. Writing them once means every chart gets the same look, and you can copy them into later sessions. import numpy as np from matplotlib.colors import TwoSlopeNorm df = load_orders () GREY , HIGHLIGHT , INK , BLUE = "#c9c7c1" , "#eb6834" , "#55534e" , "#2a78d6" rng = np . random . default_rng ( 6 ) # fixed seed for the small random jitter used in G4 def finish ( ax , title , subtitle = "" , xlabel = "" , ylabel = "" ): """Course chart style: message title, scope subtitle, axis labels, quiet frame.""" extra_lines = subtitle . count ( " \n " ) ax . set_title ( title , loc = "left" , fontsize = 12 , fontweight = "bold" , pad = ( 24 + 12 * extra_lines ) if subtitle else 8 ) if subtitle : ax . text ( 0 , 1.02 , subtitle , transform = ax . transAxes , fontsize = 9 , color = INK , va = "bottom" ) ax . set_xlabel ( xlabel ) ax . set_ylabel ( ylabel ) for side in ( "top" , "right" ): ax . spines [ side ] . set_visible ( False ) return ax def highlight ( labels , focus ): """One colour per label: HIGHLIGHT for the label(s) in focus, GREY for the rest.""" focus = [ focus ] if isinstance ( focus , str ) else list ( focus ) return [ HIGHLIGHT if label in focus else GREY for label in labels ] print ( "Order lines:" , len ( df ), "| distinct orders:" , df [ "order_id" ] . nunique ()) Order lines: 6815 | distinct orders: 3388
