docs.title: G2 (Core): Segments and seasons

docs.text: Growth type Compares each month with pandas Month-on-month (MoM) the previous calendar month pct_change() Year-on-year (YoY) the same month one year earlier pct_change(periods=12) Both use the same formula: (this month − comparison month) ÷ comparison month . Only on a complete monthly series pct_change compares each row with the row above it (or 12 rows above). That only means "previous month" or "same month last year" because we checked that all 36 months are present and in order. To see what is being compared, the table below also keeps the comparison values. shift(1) moves each value down one row; shift(12) moves it down twelve rows. growth = pd . DataFrame ({ "sales" : monthly }) growth [ "previous_month" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . shift ( 1 ) growth [ "mom_growth" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . pct_change () growth [ "same_month_last_year" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . shift ( 12 ) growth [ "yoy_growth" ] = growth [ "sales" ] . pct_change ( periods = 12 ) # A comparison month with zero Sales gives no fair growth figure: treat it as blank. growth [ "mom_growth" ] = growth [ "mom_growth" ] . where ( growth [ "previous_month" ] != 0 ) growth [ "yoy_growth" ] = growth [ "yoy_growth" ] . where ( growth [ "same_month_last_year" ] != 0 ) The full table has 36 rows. To keep it readable we show a few months and format growth as percentages. as_pct writes a blank growth value as the words "no comparison". def as_pct ( value ): if pd . isna ( value ): return "no comparison" return f " { value : +.1% } " def growth_table ( table , months ): rows = table . loc [ months ] return pd . DataFrame ({ "Sales" : rows [ "sales" ] . map ( " {:,.0f} " . format ), "MoM growth" : rows [ "mom_growth" ] . map ( as_pct ), "YoY growth" : rows [ "yoy_growth" ] . map ( as_pct ), }, index = rows . index . strftime ( "%b %Y" )) growth_table ( growth , [ "2023-01-01" , "2023-02-01" , "2023-03-01" , "2024-01-01" , "2025-01-01" , "2025-12-01" ]) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Sales MoM growth YoY growth Jan 2023 14,518 no comparison no comparison Feb 2023 4,520 -68.9% no comparison Mar 2023 56,934 +1159.6% no comparison Jan 2024 18,462 -74.4% +27.2% Jan 2025 18,830 -75.1% +2.0% Dec 2025 97,502 +22.8% +29.1% Read the output above row by row: January 2023 is the first month in the file, so it has no previous month and no month a year earlier. Every 2023 month has no year-earlier month in the file, so its YoY growth is blank. Look at March 2023 . A very large MoM figure often just means the previous month was small, not that something remarkable happened. Compare January 2025 MoM with January 2025 YoY. Do they tell the same story?

docs.text: Suppose you only care about 2025. There are two orders of work: Filter, then compute: keep only 2025 rows, then calculate growth. Compute, then filter: calculate growth on all 36 months, then show only 2025. Run both and compare January and February 2025. # 1. Filter first, then compute growth only_2025 = df [ df [ "order_date" ] . dt . year == 2025 ] monthly_2025 = only_2025 . groupby ( "order_month" )[ "sales" ] . sum () filter_first = pd . DataFrame ({ "mom_growth" : monthly_2025 . pct_change (), "yoy_growth" : monthly_2025 . pct_change ( periods = 12 ), }) # 2. Compute growth on all months first, then keep 2025 compute_first = growth . loc [ "2025" , [ "mom_growth" , "yoy_growth" ]] check_months = [ "2025-01-01" , "2025-02-01" ] pd . DataFrame ({ "MoM, filter first" : filter_first . loc [ check_months , "mom_growth" ] . map ( as_pct ), "MoM, compute first" : compute_first . loc [ check_months , "mom_growth" ] . map ( as_pct ), "YoY, filter first" : filter_first . loc [ check_months , "yoy_growth" ] . map ( as_pct ), "YoY, compute first" : compute_first . loc [ check_months , "yoy_growth" ] . map ( as_pct ), }, index = pd . DatetimeIndex ( check_months ) . strftime ( "%b %Y" )) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } MoM, filter first MoM, compute first YoY, filter first YoY, compute first Jan 2025 no comparison -75.1% no comparison +2.0% Feb 2025 +22.0% +22.0% no comparison +92.3% In the output above, filtering first leaves January 2025 with no row above it, so its MoM growth becomes blank. And because the filtered series holds only 12 months, every YoY value becomes blank: December 2024 and all of 2024 were removed before the calculation could see them. Rule Compute growth on the complete monthly series first. Filter or highlight the period you want to show afterwards. If you must filter first, say clearly that the comparison months were removed. Filtering by segment or region is different: it changes which lines count, and it applies equally to both months being compared. That is fine, as long as you build the full 36-month series for that group and state the filter.
docs.title: G4 (Core): Filtering can remove the comparison

docs.text: From the Session 2 lab, returned_order_flag is 1 when an order appears on the source's returns list . It is an order-level flag: every line of a listed order has 1. So we count distinct orders , never lines. returned = df [ df [ "returned_order_flag" ] == 1 ] returns_by_segment = pd . DataFrame ({ "orders" : df . groupby ( "segment" )[ "order_id" ] . nunique (), "orders_on_returns_list" : returned . groupby ( "segment" )[ "order_id" ] . nunique (), }) returns_by_segment . loc [ "All segments" ] = [ df [ "order_id" ] . nunique (), returned [ "order_id" ] . nunique (), ] returns_by_segment [ "share_on_list" ] = ( returns_by_segment [ "orders_on_returns_list" ] / returns_by_segment [ "orders" ] ) . map ( " {:.1%} " . format ) returns_by_segment .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } orders orders_on_returns_list share_on_list segment Consumer 1738 99 5.7% Corporate 1044 61 5.8% Home Office 606 31 5.1% All segments 3388 191 5.6% The All segments row is calculated from the whole table, not by adding the segment rows. Check that the segment counts add up to it: if an order appeared in two segments it would be counted twice. What the returns list cannot tell you When an order was returned, or how many items. How much money was refunded. Whether an order not on the list was definitely kept. So call it "share of orders on the returns list" , not "return rate", and do not subtract anything from Sales because of it.
docs.title: G5 (Core): The returns list

docs.text: In Python, a simple dashboard is one figure with several charts (called subplots ). plt.subplots(3, 1) creates three charts stacked vertically; each one has its own ax to draw on. The code is wrapped in a function , draw_dashboard , so you can redraw the whole dashboard for one region later by changing a single line. That is the Python version of one filter that controls every view. The function: builds a segment KPI table (Sales and share of orders on the returns list); builds a complete 36-month Sales series, putting 0 in any month where the selection has no lines; computes YoY growth on the full series before anything is hidden; draws three panels with message titles and a scope note. def draw_dashboard ( data , scope ): # 1. Segment KPIs kpis = pd . docs.text: Write five sentences to the commercial lead: The test: one specific change to try, in one segment. Evidence: one measure from the trend or growth views. Evidence: one measure from the segment table, including the returns-list share. Limitation: for example, the trend shows when sales change, not why ; the returns list has no refund amounts; the data is a fictitious sample. How to measure success: the measure and comparison you would use to judge the test, such as YoY Sales for the same months, or the same months in a similar group that did not get the change. Why a test? Past data shows patterns, not causes. A segment growing at the same time as something else happened is an association , not proof that one caused the other. A small, well-measured test, compared fairly with the same months last year or with an untouched group, is how you find out whether a change actually works.

docs.text: Session 7 lecture: Time series and trends ¶ A number on its own says little; the same number compared with the right earlier period says a lot. This lecture shows how to read a series over time, pick a fair comparison, smooth out the noise and avoid the traps that make ordinary months look like disasters. Open this notebook in Google Colab with the button above, then run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Save your own copy with File → Save a copy in Drive . Recap quiz ¶ Before we start, answer the quiz at the end of the Session 6 lecture . Write short answers; we discuss them together. What you will be able to explain ¶ The three components of a time series: trend, seasonality and noise. When month-on-month and when year-on-year growth is the fair comparison. How a rolling average smooths a series, and the difference between trailing and centred windows. How index numbers (base = 100) let you compare series of very different sizes. What a seasonally adjusted series is, and why official statistics publish one. Why incomplete and missing periods break comparisons, and how to guard against them. Why growth must be computed before you filter to a period. This lecture builds on the section on cherry-picked time windows in How statistics can mislead . In the Lab you apply every idea to the retail orders and to official US construction spending. Most business series are a mix of three parts: Component What it is Example Trend The slow, long-run direction A shop growing a little every year Seasonality A pattern that repeats at the same time every year (or week, or day) Busy Novembers and Decembers, quiet Januaries Noise Irregular ups and downs with no pattern A delivery delay, one big one-off order The cell below builds a series from these three parts, so we know exactly what is inside it. Real data never tells you its parts; you have to infer them. rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 7 ) months = pd . date_range ( "2021-01-01" , "2024-12-01" , freq = "MS" ) t = np . arange ( len ( months )) trend = 100 + 1.5 * t # grows steadily every month season_by_month = [ - 25 , - 20 , - 5 , 0 , 5 , 0 , - 5 , 0 , 10 , 5 , 15 , 20 ] # same shape every year seasonal = np . array ([ season_by_month [ m . month - 1 ] for m in months ]) noise = rng . normal ( 0 , 5 , len ( months )) demo = pd . DataFrame ({ "trend" : trend , "seasonal" : seasonal , "noise" : noise }, index = months ) demo [ "sales" ] = demo [ "trend" ] + demo [ "seasonal" ] + demo [ "noise" ] fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 4 , 1 , figsize = ( 9 , 8 ), sharex = True ) for ax , col , colour in zip ( axes , [ "sales" , "trend" , "seasonal" , "noise" ], [ "#2a78d6" , "#555555" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]): ax . plot ( demo . index , demo [ col ], color = colour ) ax . set_title ( col . capitalize () if col != "sales" else "Sales = trend + seasonal + noise" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Predict, then reveal Look only at the top panel. Between December and January of each year, does the series go up or down? Is that the trend changing, or something else? Now look at the three panels underneath and check. The top line drops every January even though the trend never stops rising. A manager looking only at the latest two months would see a "fall" that is entirely seasonal. Check your understanding 1 Name one business series you know and describe its likely trend, its seasonality and one source of noise. Part 2: Month-on-month versus year-on-year ¶ Growth always compares two values: (this period − comparison period) ÷ comparison period . The question is which comparison period. Growth type Compares with pandas Month-on-month (MoM) the previous month pct_change() Year-on-year (YoY) the same month a year earlier pct_change(periods=12) Predict, then reveal In the simulated series, the trend rises a little every month. What do you expect January's MoM growth to look like? And January's YoY growth? demo [ "mom" ] = demo [ "sales" ] . pct_change () demo [ "yoy" ] = demo [ "sales" ] . pct_change ( periods = 12 ) fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 2 , 1 , figsize = ( 9 , 5.5 ), sharex = True ) ax1 . bar ( demo . index , demo [ "mom" ] * 100 , width = 20 ) ax1 . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax1 . set_title ( "Month-on-month growth: big swings driven by the seasons" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "MoM (%)" ) ax2 . bar ( demo . index , demo [ "yoy" ] * 100 , width = 20 , color = "#eb6834" ) ax2 . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax2 . set_title ( "Year-on-year growth: steady, close to the real trend (first year has no comparison)" ) ax2 . set_ylabel ( "YoY (%)" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () def as_pct ( value ): return "no comparison" if pd . isna ( value ) else f " { value : +.1% } " januaries = demo [ demo . index . month == 1 ][[ "sales" , "mom" , "yoy" ]] januaries . assign ( mom = januaries [ "mom" ] . map ( as_pct ), yoy = januaries [ "yoy" ] . map ( as_pct )) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } sales mom yoy 2021-01-01 75.01 no comparison no comparison 2022-01-01 93.53 -32.4% +24.7% 2023-01-01 111.78 -28.3% +19.5% 2024-01-01 128.84 -23.5% +15.3% Read the table above. Every January has a large negative MoM figure, while YoY stays positive. The first January has no comparison at all: pandas stores it as NaN ( not a number ), and our as_pct helper prints it as "no comparison", never as zero. Use… When… Watch out for… MoM You need to spot a sudden change quickly, and the series is not strongly seasonal Seasonal swings that look like booms and crashes YoY The business is seasonal and you want like-for-like A one-off event in the same month last year; it reacts slowly to new changes Blank is not zero A growth value with no comparison period is not available . It is not 0%. Never fill it with 0. Check your understanding 2 A colleague reports "Sales up 40% month-on-month in November". What extra comparison would you ask for before celebrating, and why? Part 3: Rolling averages, trailing and centred ¶ A rolling average (or moving average) replaces each value with the average of a window of neighbouring values. A 12-month window covers exactly one full year, so every month of the season appears once and the seasonal pattern cancels out. Window Uses Good for Cost Trailing this month and the 11 before it Dashboards: only uses data you already have It lags : it turns late Centred about 6 months either side Seeing exactly when the trend turned Needs future data, so the last months are blank We add a sudden step : from mid-2023, sales jump by 40 and stay there. stepped = demo [ "sales" ] + np . where ( demo . index >= "2023-07-01" , 40 , 0 ) smooth = pd . DataFrame ({ "monthly" : stepped , "trailing 12" : stepped . rolling ( 12 ) . mean (), "centred 12" : stepped . rolling ( 12 , center = True ) . mean (), }) ax = smooth [ "monthly" ] . plot ( color = "#b8b6b0" , label = "Monthly value" ) smooth [ "trailing 12" ] . plot ( ax = ax , color = "#2a78d6" , linewidth = 2.5 , label = "Trailing 12-month average" ) smooth [ "centred 12" ] . plot ( ax = ax , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2.5 , linestyle = "--" , label = "Centred 12-month average" ) ax . axvline ( pd . Timestamp ( "2023-07-01" ), color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax . set_title ( "A level change in July 2023: the trailing average reacts late" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (simulated)" ) ax . legend () plt . show () print ( "Blank trailing values:" , smooth [ "trailing 12" ] . isna () . sum (), "| blank centred values:" , smooth [ "centred 12" ] . isna () . sum ()) Blank trailing values: 11 | blank centred values: 11 Predict, then reveal Before reading the chart: which line will finish its climb closer to the vertical line in July 2023, the trailing or the centred average? Where will each line be blank? The trailing average needs 11 earlier months, so it is blank at the start . The centred average needs months on both sides, so it is blank at both ends , including the most recent months a manager usually cares about most. Check your understanding 3 You are building a monthly dashboard that updates on the first day of each month. Which rolling average can you show for the latest month, and what will it hide? Part 4: Index numbers (base = 100) ¶ Two series of very different sizes are hard to compare on one chart: the big one squashes the small one flat. An index divides every value by the value in a chosen base period and multiplies by 100. index = value ÷ base value × 100 So the base period is 100 for every series, and 120 later means "20% above the base period". We add up each segment's Sales by year and use 2023 as the base year. A whole year as the base means one unusual month cannot distort it. seg_monthly = df . groupby ([ "order_month" , "segment" ])[ "sales" ] . sum () . unstack () seg_yearly = seg_monthly . groupby ( seg_monthly . index . year ) . sum () base = seg_yearly . loc [ 2023 ] index = seg_yearly / base * 100 fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 10 , 3.8 )) seg_yearly . plot ( ax = ax1 , marker = "o" , title = "Yearly Sales by segment" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "Sales (source monetary units)" ) ax1 . set_xticks ( seg_yearly . index ) ax1 . set_xlabel ( "Year of order" ) index . plot ( ax = ax2 , marker = "o" , title = "Indexed: 2023 = 100" , legend = False ) ax2 . axhline ( 100 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax2 . set_ylabel ( "Index (2023 = 100)" ) ax2 . set_xticks ( index . index ) ax2 . set_xlabel ( "Year of order" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () index . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } segment Consumer Corporate Home Office order_month 2023 100.00 100.00 100.00 2024 99.50 98.70 81.00 2025 111.50 158.80 112.70 On the left, the largest segment dominates. On the right, every segment starts at 100, so you compare growth paths , not sizes. Check your understanding 4 An index reads 85 in the latest year with base year 2023 = 100. Say in plain words what happened. Does the index tell you which segment is the largest? Part 5: Seasonally adjusted series ¶ National statistics offices publish many series twice: Not seasonally adjusted (NSA): the actual amount in each month. Seasonally adjusted (SA): the same series with the usual seasonal pattern taken out, so one month can be compared directly with the month before. Official agencies use detailed methods (for example, the US Census Bureau uses a program called X-13ARIMA-SEATS). The core idea is simple enough to build by hand: Estimate the trend with a centred 12-month average. For each month, see how far the actual value sits above or below that trend. Average those gaps by calendar month: that is the seasonal factor for January, February and so on. Subtract each month's seasonal factor from the actual value. sales = demo [ "sales" ] trend_est = sales . rolling ( 12 , center = True ) . mean () gap = sales - trend_est seasonal_factor = gap . groupby ( gap . index . month ) . mean () adjusted = sales - seasonal_factor . reindex ( sales . index . month ) . values ax = sales . plot ( color = "#b8b6b0" , label = "Not adjusted (actual)" ) adjusted . plot ( ax = ax , color = "#2a78d6" , linewidth = 2.5 , label = "Seasonally adjusted (our estimate)" ) demo [ "trend" ] . plot ( ax = ax , color = "black" , linestyle = ":" , label = "True trend (known only because we built it)" ) ax . set_title ( "Removing the seasonal pattern leaves trend plus noise" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (simulated)" ) ax . legend () plt . show () pd . DataFrame ({ "estimated factor" : seasonal_factor . round ( 1 ), "true factor" : season_by_month }, index = pd . Index ( range ( 1 , 13 ), name = "month" )) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } estimated factor true factor month 1 -22.00 -25 2 -17.60 -20 3 -7.30 -5 4 2.80 0 5 5.70 5 6 2.30 0 7 -8.30 -5 8 2.30 0 9 7.40 10 10 5.20 5 11 18.30 15 12 22.40 20 The estimated seasonal factors come out close to the true ones we built in, and the adjusted line follows the trend plus noise. Annual rates Some official monthly series are published as a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) : the adjusted monthly value multiplied up to a full year. A SAAR of 1,200 means "if every month were like this one, the year would total about 1,200". Divide by 12 to compare it with a monthly amount, and never add up annual-rate values across months. Check your understanding 5 A news report says spending "fell 8% in January". Which would you rather see: the adjusted or the unadjusted series? Why? Part 6: Incomplete and missing periods ¶ Two quiet traps. An incomplete last period. If data were pulled on the 10th of a month, that month holds about a third of its orders. On a chart it looks like a collapse. cut = demo [ "sales" ] . copy () cut . iloc [ - 1 ] = cut . iloc [ - 1 ] * 10 / 31 # data pulled on the 10th of the last month ax = cut . plot ( marker = "o" , markersize = 3 ) ax . annotate ( "Only 10 of 31 days \n loaded so far" , xy = ( cut . index [ - 1 ], cut . iloc [ - 1 ]), xytext = ( - 130 , - 10 ), textcoords = "offset points" , arrowprops = { "arrowstyle" : "->" }) ax . set_title ( "An incomplete last month looks like a crash" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (simulated)" ) plt . show () print ( "Last month MoM growth:" , f " { cut . pct_change () . iloc [ - 1 ] : +.1% } " ) Last month MoM growth: -67.3% A missing month. pct_change() compares each row with the row above. If a month is missing, "the row above" is two months earlier, and nothing warns you. The fix is to line the series up against the full calendar first. gappy = demo [ "sales" ] . drop ( pd . Timestamp ( "2024-06-01" )) print ( "Rows:" , len ( gappy ), "| months in the calendar:" , len ( months )) wrong = gappy . pct_change () . loc [ "2024-07-01" ] safe = gappy . reindex ( months ) . pct_change ( fill_method = None ) . loc [ "2024-07-01" ] print ( "July 2024 MoM, missing June ignored: " , f " { wrong : +.1% } <- silently compared with May" ) print ( "July 2024 MoM, after reindex: " , safe , " <- no comparison available" ) Rows: 47 | months in the calendar: 48 July 2024 MoM, missing June ignored: -8.3% <- silently compared with May July 2024 MoM, after reindex: nan <- no comparison available Rules for periods Check the first and last date, and whether the last period is complete. Build the full calendar with pd.date_range and reindex against it, so gaps show as blanks. Compare like with like : a part-year only with the same part of earlier years (for example January–September with January–September). Check your understanding 6 A file has nine months of 2016 and twelve months of every earlier year. A colleague compares yearly totals and reports that 2016 was the weakest year. What should you check, and what fair comparison would you make instead? Part 7: Growth after filtering, the trap ¶ You want a table of 2025 only. If you filter first , the earlier months the growth formula needs are gone. monthly = df . groupby ( "order_month" )[ "sales" ] . sum () filter_first = monthly . loc [ "2025" ] . pct_change ( periods = 12 ) compute_first = monthly . pct_change ( periods = 12 ) . loc [ "2025" ] pd . DataFrame ({ "YoY, filter then compute" : filter_first . map ( as_pct ), "YoY, compute then filter" : compute_first . map ( as_pct )}) . head ( 4 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } YoY, filter then compute YoY, compute then filter order_month 2025-01-01 no comparison +2.0% 2025-02-01 no comparison +92.3% 2025-03-01 no comparison +32.6% 2025-04-01 no comparison +13.6% Predict, then reveal Before running the cell above: how many of the twelve 2025 months will have a YoY value when you filter first? Filtering to one year leaves only twelve rows, so no row has a partner twelve rows above it. Every YoY value becomes blank ("no comparison"). Rule Compute growth on the complete series first, then filter or highlight the period you want to show. Filtering by a group such as a segment is fine, because it applies to both months in the comparison; build that group's complete series first. Part 8: Worked case — Superstore monthly Sales ¶ We put the pieces together on the retail orders. Step 1: Check the calendar ¶ all_months = pd . date_range ( "2023-01-01" , "2025-12-01" , freq = "MS" ) print ( "First order month:" , monthly . index . min () . date (), "| last:" , monthly . index . max () . date ()) print ( "Months expected:" , len ( all_months ), "| months present:" , len ( monthly ), "| missing:" , len ( all_months . difference ( monthly . index ))) monthly = monthly . reindex ( all_months ) First order month: 2023-01-01 | last: 2025-12-01 Months expected: 36 | months present: 36 | missing: 0 Step 2: Trend and seasonality in one view ¶ A light line for the actual months, a strong line for the trailing 12-month average, and a year-overlay chart for the season. rolling_12 = monthly . rolling ( 12 ) . mean () fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 11 , 3.8 )) ax1 . plot ( monthly . index , monthly , color = "#b8b6b0" , label = "Monthly Sales" ) ax1 . plot ( rolling_12 . index , rolling_12 , color = "#2a78d6" , linewidth = 2.5 , label = "Trailing 12-month average" ) ax1 . set_title ( "Underlying level, without the season" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "Sales (source monetary units)" ) ax1 . legend ( fontsize = 8 ) overlay = pd . DataFrame ({ "year" : monthly . index . year , "month" : monthly . index . month , "sales" : monthly . values }) overlay . pivot ( index = "month" , columns = "year" , values = "sales" ) . plot ( ax = ax2 , marker = "o" , markersize = 3 ) ax2 . set_title ( "The same seasonal shape every year" ) ax2 . set_xlabel ( "Month of the year" ) ax2 . set_xticks ( range ( 1 , 13 )) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Step 3: Which comparison is fair for January 2025? ¶ jan = pd . Timestamp ( "2025-01-01" ) print ( "January 2025 Sales:" , f " { monthly [ jan ] : ,.0f } " ) print ( "MoM (vs December 2024):" , f " { monthly . pct_change ()[ jan ] : +.1% } " ) print ( "YoY (vs January 2024): " , f " { monthly . pct_change ( periods = 12 )[ jan ] : +.1% } " ) January 2025 Sales: 18,830 MoM (vs December 2024): -75.1% YoY (vs January 2024): +2.0% Read the two growth figures above alongside the year-overlay chart. The month-on-month figure repeats the usual January drop; the year-on-year figure compares January with January. For a seasonal business, the YoY figure is the fair headline, and the trailing average shows whether the underlying level is rising. Summary ¶ Question Tool Trap to avoid Is there a pattern by time of year? Year-overlay chart Reading one month in isolation Did this month grow? YoY for seasonal series; MoM for non-seasonal Calling a seasonal dip a crash What is the underlying level? Trailing 12-month average Forgetting it lags When exactly did it turn? Centred average (on history) Expecting it for the latest months How do different-sized series compare? Index, base = 100 Choosing an unusual base period Is this month normal for the season? Seasonally adjusted series Adding up annual-rate values Can I trust the comparison? Full calendar, complete periods Missing months, part-years, filtering first Quiz ¶ Answer these at the start of the next lecture. Write short answers. Name the three components of a time series and give a one-line example of each. Why can month-on-month growth mislead for a seasonal business? What does year-on-year growth compare, and when can it still mislead? A trailing and a centred 12-month average are drawn on the same series. Which turns later after a sudden change, and which is blank for the latest months? An index with base year 2023 = 100 reads 112 in 2025. What does that mean? What does a seasonally adjusted series remove, and why do official agencies publish one? Why should you never fill a blank growth value with 0%? You filter a monthly table to one year and then compute YoY growth. What happens, and what should you do instead? Lab briefing ¶ In the Lab you: Build the monthly Superstore series, check it is complete and read its seasons. Calculate MoM and YoY growth and see how filtering removes the comparison. Measure the share of orders on the returns list and build a three-panel dashboard. Select one consistent series from official US construction spending, read its seasons and compare part-years fairly. Debug a "75% crash" and a "weakest year ever" claim. Write a five-sentence test recommendation for the commercial lead. Open the Session 7 lab .

docs.text: A number on its own says little; the same number compared with the right earlier period says a lot. This lecture shows how to read a series over time, pick a fair comparison, smooth out the noise and avoid the traps that make ordinary months look like disasters. docs.text: The three components of a time series: trend, seasonality and noise. When month-on-month and when year-on-year growth is the fair comparison. How a rolling average smooths a series, and the difference between trailing and centred windows. How index numbers (base = 100) let you compare series of very different sizes. What a seasonally adjusted series is, and why official statistics publish one. Why incomplete and missing periods break comparisons, and how to guard against them. Why growth must be computed before you filter to a period. This lecture builds on the section on cherry-picked time windows in How statistics can mislead . In the Lab you apply every idea to the retail orders and to official US construction spending. docs.text: A time series is one measure recorded at regular intervals: Sales per month, visitors per day, spending per quarter. Most business series are a mix of three parts: Component What it is Example Trend The slow, long-run direction A shop growing a little every year Seasonality A pattern that repeats at the same time every year (or week, or day) Busy Novembers and Decembers, quiet Januaries Noise Irregular ups and downs with no pattern A delivery delay, one big one-off order The cell below builds a series from these three parts, so we know exactly what is inside it. Real data never tells you its parts; you have to infer them. rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 7 ) months = pd . date_range ( "2021-01-01" , "2024-12-01" , freq = "MS" ) t = np . arange ( len ( months )) trend = 100 + 1.5 * t # grows steadily every month season_by_month = [ - 25 , - 20 , - 5 , 0 , 5 , 0 , - 5 , 0 , 10 , 5 , 15 , 20 ] # same shape every year seasonal = np . array ([ season_by_month [ m . month - 1 ] for m in months ]) noise = rng . normal ( 0 , 5 , len ( months )) demo = pd . DataFrame ({ "trend" : trend , "seasonal" : seasonal , "noise" : noise }, index = months ) demo [ "sales" ] = demo [ "trend" ] + demo [ "seasonal" ] + demo [ "noise" ] fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 4 , 1 , figsize = ( 9 , 8 ), sharex = True ) for ax , col , colour in zip ( axes , [ "sales" , "trend" , "seasonal" , "noise" ], [ "#2a78d6" , "#555555" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" ]): ax . plot ( demo . index , demo [ col ], color = colour ) ax . set_title ( col . capitalize () if col != "sales" else "Sales = trend + seasonal + noise" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Predict, then reveal Look only at the top panel. Between December and January of each year, does the series go up or down? Is that the trend changing, or something else? Now look at the three panels underneath and check. The top line drops every January even though the trend never stops rising. A manager looking only at the latest two months would see a "fall" that is entirely seasonal. Check your understanding 1 Name one business series you know and describe its likely trend, its seasonality and one source of noise.
docs.title: Part 1: The three components of a series

docs.text: Growth always compares two values: (this period − comparison period) ÷ comparison period . The question is which comparison period. Growth type Compares with pandas Month-on-month (MoM) the previous month pct_change() Year-on-year (YoY) the same month a year earlier pct_change(periods=12) Predict, then reveal In the simulated series, the trend rises a little every month. What do you expect January's MoM growth to look like? And January's YoY growth? demo [ "mom" ] = demo [ "sales" ] . pct_change () demo [ "yoy" ] = demo [ "sales" ] . pct_change ( periods = 12 ) fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 2 , 1 , figsize = ( 9 , 5.5 ), sharex = True ) ax1 . bar ( demo . index , demo [ "mom" ] * 100 , width = 20 ) ax1 . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax1 . set_title ( "Month-on-month growth: big swings driven by the seasons" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "MoM (%)" ) ax2 . bar ( demo . index , demo [ "yoy" ] * 100 , width = 20 , color = "#eb6834" ) ax2 . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax2 . set_title ( "Year-on-year growth: steady, close to the real trend (first year has no comparison)" ) ax2 . set_ylabel ( "YoY (%)" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () def as_pct ( value ): return "no comparison" if pd . isna ( value ) else f " { value : +.1% } " januaries = demo [ demo . index . month == 1 ][[ "sales" , "mom" , "yoy" ]] januaries . assign ( mom = januaries [ "mom" ] . map ( as_pct ), yoy = januaries [ "yoy" ] . map ( as_pct )) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } sales mom yoy 2021-01-01 75.01 no comparison no comparison 2022-01-01 93.53 -32.4% +24.7% 2023-01-01 111.78 -28.3% +19.5% 2024-01-01 128.84 -23.5% +15.3% Read the table above. Every January has a large negative MoM figure, while YoY stays positive. The first January has no comparison at all: pandas stores it as NaN ( not a number ), and our as_pct helper prints it as "no comparison", never as zero. Use… When… Watch out for… MoM You need to spot a sudden change quickly, and the series is not strongly seasonal Seasonal swings that look like booms and crashes YoY The business is seasonal and you want like-for-like A one-off event in the same month last year; it reacts slowly to new changes Blank is not zero A growth value with no comparison period is not available . It is not 0%. Never fill it with 0. Check your understanding 2 A colleague reports "Sales up 40% month-on-month in November". What extra comparison would you ask for before celebrating, and why?
docs.title: Part 2: Month-on-month versus year-on-year

docs.text: A rolling average (or moving average) replaces each value with the average of a window of neighbouring values. A 12-month window covers exactly one full year, so every month of the season appears once and the seasonal pattern cancels out. Window Uses Good for Cost Trailing this month and the 11 before it Dashboards: only uses data you already have It lags : it turns late Centred about 6 months either side Seeing exactly when the trend turned Needs future data, so the last months are blank We add a sudden step : from mid-2023, sales jump by 40 and stay there. stepped = demo [ "sales" ] + np . where ( demo . index >= "2023-07-01" , 40 , 0 ) smooth = pd . DataFrame ({ "monthly" : stepped , "trailing 12" : stepped . rolling ( 12 ) . mean (), "centred 12" : stepped . rolling ( 12 , center = True ) . mean (), }) ax = smooth [ "monthly" ] . plot ( color = "#b8b6b0" , label = "Monthly value" ) smooth [ "trailing 12" ] . plot ( ax = ax , color = "#2a78d6" , linewidth = 2.5 , label = "Trailing 12-month average" ) smooth [ "centred 12" ] . plot ( ax = ax , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2.5 , linestyle = "--" , label = "Centred 12-month average" ) ax . axvline ( pd . Timestamp ( "2023-07-01" ), color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax . set_title ( "A level change in July 2023: the trailing average reacts late" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (simulated)" ) ax . legend () plt . show () print ( "Blank trailing values:" , smooth [ "trailing 12" ] . isna () . sum (), "| blank centred values:" , smooth [ "centred 12" ] . isna () . sum ()) Blank trailing values: 11 | blank centred values: 11 Predict, then reveal Before reading the chart: which line will finish its climb closer to the vertical line in July 2023, the trailing or the centred average? Where will each line be blank? The trailing average needs 11 earlier months, so it is blank at the start . The centred average needs months on both sides, so it is blank at both ends , including the most recent months a manager usually cares about most. Check your understanding 3 You are building a monthly dashboard that updates on the first day of each month. Which rolling average can you show for the latest month, and what will it hide?
docs.title: Part 3: Rolling averages, trailing and centred

docs.text: Two series of very different sizes are hard to compare on one chart: the big one squashes the small one flat. An index divides every value by the value in a chosen base period and multiplies by 100. index = value ÷ base value × 100 So the base period is 100 for every series, and 120 later means "20% above the base period". We add up each segment's Sales by year and use 2023 as the base year. A whole year as the base means one unusual month cannot distort it. seg_monthly = df . groupby ([ "order_month" , "segment" ])[ "sales" ] . sum () . unstack () seg_yearly = seg_monthly . groupby ( seg_monthly . index . year ) . sum () base = seg_yearly . loc [ 2023 ] index = seg_yearly / base * 100 fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 10 , 3.8 )) seg_yearly . plot ( ax = ax1 , marker = "o" , title = "Yearly Sales by segment" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "Sales (source monetary units)" ) ax1 . set_xticks ( seg_yearly . index ) ax1 . set_xlabel ( "Year of order" ) index . plot ( ax = ax2 , marker = "o" , title = "Indexed: 2023 = 100" , legend = False ) ax2 . axhline ( 100 , color = "black" , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax2 . set_ylabel ( "Index (2023 = 100)" ) ax2 . set_xticks ( index . index ) ax2 . set_xlabel ( "Year of order" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () index . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } segment Consumer Corporate Home Office order_month 2023 100.00 100.00 100.00 2024 99.50 98.70 81.00 2025 111.50 158.80 112.70 On the left, the largest segment dominates. On the right, every segment starts at 100, so you compare growth paths , not sizes. Check your understanding 4 An index reads 85 in the latest year with base year 2023 = 100. Say in plain words what happened. Does the index tell you which segment is the largest?
docs.title: Part 4: Index numbers (base = 100)

docs.text: National statistics offices publish many series twice: Not seasonally adjusted (NSA): the actual amount in each month. Seasonally adjusted (SA): the same series with the usual seasonal pattern taken out, so one month can be compared directly with the month before. Official agencies use detailed methods (for example, the US Census Bureau uses a program called X-13ARIMA-SEATS). The core idea is simple enough to build by hand: Estimate the trend with a centred 12-month average. For each month, see how far the actual value sits above or below that trend. Average those gaps by calendar month: that is the seasonal factor for January, February and so on. Subtract each month's seasonal factor from the actual value. sales = demo [ "sales" ] trend_est = sales . rolling ( 12 , center = True ) . mean () gap = sales - trend_est seasonal_factor = gap . groupby ( gap . index . month ) . mean () adjusted = sales - seasonal_factor . reindex ( sales . index . month ) . values ax = sales . plot ( color = "#b8b6b0" , label = "Not adjusted (actual)" ) adjusted . plot ( ax = ax , color = "#2a78d6" , linewidth = 2.5 , label = "Seasonally adjusted (our estimate)" ) demo [ "trend" ] . plot ( ax = ax , color = "black" , linestyle = ":" , label = "True trend (known only because we built it)" ) ax . set_title ( "Removing the seasonal pattern leaves trend plus noise" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (simulated)" ) ax . legend () plt . show () pd . DataFrame ({ "estimated factor" : seasonal_factor . round ( 1 ), "true factor" : season_by_month }, index = pd . Index ( range ( 1 , 13 ), name = "month" )) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } estimated factor true factor month 1 -22.00 -25 2 -17.60 -20 3 -7.30 -5 4 2.80 0 5 5.70 5 6 2.30 0 7 -8.30 -5 8 2.30 0 9 7.40 10 10 5.20 5 11 18.30 15 12 22.40 20 The estimated seasonal factors come out close to the true ones we built in, and the adjusted line follows the trend plus noise. Annual rates Some official monthly series are published as a seasonally adjusted annual rate (SAAR) : the adjusted monthly value multiplied up to a full year. A SAAR of 1,200 means "if every month were like this one, the year would total about 1,200". Divide by 12 to compare it with a monthly amount, and never add up annual-rate values across months. Check your understanding 5 A news report says spending "fell 8% in January". Which would you rather see: the adjusted or the unadjusted series? Why?
docs.title: Part 5: Seasonally adjusted series

docs.text: Two quiet traps. An incomplete last period. If data were pulled on the 10th of a month, that month holds about a third of its orders. On a chart it looks like a collapse. cut = demo [ "sales" ] . copy () cut . iloc [ - 1 ] = cut . iloc [ - 1 ] * 10 / 31 # data pulled on the 10th of the last month ax = cut . plot ( marker = "o" , markersize = 3 ) ax . annotate ( "Only 10 of 31 days \n loaded so far" , xy = ( cut . index [ - 1 ], cut . iloc [ - 1 ]), xytext = ( - 130 , - 10 ), textcoords = "offset points" , arrowprops = { "arrowstyle" : "->" }) ax . set_title ( "An incomplete last month looks like a crash" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (simulated)" ) plt . show () print ( "Last month MoM growth:" , f " { cut . pct_change () . iloc [ - 1 ] : +.1% } " ) Last month MoM growth: -67.3% A missing month. pct_change() compares each row with the row above. If a month is missing, "the row above" is two months earlier, and nothing warns you. The fix is to line the series up against the full calendar first. gappy = demo [ "sales" ] . drop ( pd . Timestamp ( "2024-06-01" )) print ( "Rows:" , len ( gappy ), "| months in the calendar:" , len ( months )) wrong = gappy . pct_change () . loc [ "2024-07-01" ] safe = gappy . reindex ( months ) . pct_change ( fill_method = None ) . loc [ "2024-07-01" ] print ( "July 2024 MoM, missing June ignored: " , f " { wrong : +.1% } <- silently compared with May" ) print ( "July 2024 MoM, after reindex: " , safe , " <- no comparison available" ) Rows: 47 | months in the calendar: 48 July 2024 MoM, missing June ignored: -8.3% <- silently compared with May July 2024 MoM, after reindex: nan <- no comparison available Rules for periods Check the first and last date, and whether the last period is complete. Build the full calendar with pd.date_range and reindex against it, so gaps show as blanks. Compare like with like : a part-year only with the same part of earlier years (for example January–September with January–September). Check your understanding 6 A file has nine months of 2016 and twelve months of every earlier year. A colleague compares yearly totals and reports that 2016 was the weakest year. What should you check, and what fair comparison would you make instead?
docs.title: Part 6: Incomplete and missing periods

docs.text: You want a table of 2025 only. If you filter first , the earlier months the growth formula needs are gone. monthly = df . groupby ( "order_month" )[ "sales" ] . sum () filter_first = monthly . loc [ "2025" ] . pct_change ( periods = 12 ) compute_first = monthly . pct_change ( periods = 12 ) . loc [ "2025" ] pd . DataFrame ({ "YoY, filter then compute" : filter_first . map ( as_pct ), "YoY, compute then filter" : compute_first . map ( as_pct )}) . head ( 4 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } YoY, filter then compute YoY, compute then filter order_month 2025-01-01 no comparison +2.0% 2025-02-01 no comparison +92.3% 2025-03-01 no comparison +32.6% 2025-04-01 no comparison +13.6% Predict, then reveal Before running the cell above: how many of the twelve 2025 months will have a YoY value when you filter first? Filtering to one year leaves only twelve rows, so no row has a partner twelve rows above it. Every YoY value becomes blank ("no comparison"). Rule Compute growth on the complete series first, then filter or highlight the period you want to show. Filtering by a group such as a segment is fine, because it applies to both months in the comparison; build that group's complete series first.
docs.title: Part 7: Growth after filtering, the trap

docs.text: We put the pieces together on the retail orders.

DataFrame ({ "year" : monthly . index . year , "month" : monthly . index . month , "sales" : monthly . values }) overlay . pivot ( index = "month" , columns = "year" , values = "sales" ) . plot ( ax = ax2 , marker = "o" , markersize = 3 ) ax2 . set_title ( "The same seasonal shape every year" ) ax2 . set_xlabel ( "Month of the year" ) ax2 . set_xticks ( range ( 1 , 13 )) fig . tight_layout () plt . show ()

docs.text: jan = pd . Timestamp ( "2025-01-01" ) print ( "January 2025 Sales:" , f " { monthly [ jan ] : ,.0f } " ) print ( "MoM (vs December 2024):" , f " { monthly . pct_change ()[ jan ] : +.1% } " ) print ( "YoY (vs January 2024): " , f " { monthly . pct_change ( periods = 12 )[ jan ] : +.1% } " ) January 2025 Sales: 18,830 MoM (vs December 2024): -75.1% YoY (vs January 2024): +2.0% Read the two growth figures above alongside the year-overlay chart. The month-on-month figure repeats the usual January drop; the year-on-year figure compares January with January. For a seasonal business, the YoY figure is the fair headline, and the trailing average shows whether the underlying level is rising.

docs.text: Tableau Lesson 1: From decision to evidence ¶ Turn a vague business request into a clear question, open your first dataset in Tableau, and build a first chart you can explain. Draft lesson: Tableau section (coming later) The course currently teaches this lesson in Python: see Session 2 lab . This Tableau version will be completed in the later Tableau section. The Tableau steps on this page have not yet been rehearsed on the course version of Tableau. Menu names may differ slightly on your computer. Your facilitator will confirm them in class. The business decision ¶ The head of a retail business says: "Sales feel uneven across our customer groups. I need to know where to look first." This is not yet a question you can answer with data. Today you will turn it into one, and then take a first look at the evidence. About the data We use a fictitious retail sample published by Tableau (the "Superstore" sample), prepared for this course. It is not a real company. Sales and Profit are in the file's own monetary units; the currency is not stated, so we never label it as dollars, rupees or anything else. What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of this lesson you will be able to: Write a business question that names a decision, a population and a time period. Connect Tableau to a CSV file and recognise dimensions and measures. Build a simple bar chart and add a filter. Explain the difference between one row and one order in this file. Save your workbook on your computer and reopen it. Evidence you keep: your written question, a saved first chart and a one-sentence explanation of what a row means. Before you start ¶ Read the Foundations pages. They explain why the habits in this lesson matter. Install Tableau Desktop Public Edition (see Setup and practice ). Complete the smoke test: open a CSV, create a sum, save, close and reopen. Get the course file order_lines.csv (release superstore-retail-v1 ) from your facilitator. Save it in a folder you can find again, for example Documents/DataAnalytics/data . If Tableau will not install or open Tell your facilitator before the session. You can follow the demonstration, pair with a classmate and still write your question and notes. You will build your own chart later. Part 1: From request to question ¶ A good analytical question answers four things: Part Ask yourself Example Decision What will someone do differently? Choose one customer segment to investigate next month Population Which records count? All order lines in the course file Period Which dates? Orders placed in 2023, 2024 and 2025 Measure What will we compare? Sales by customer segment Putting it together: "Which customer segment had the highest Sales for orders placed in 2023–2025, so we can choose one segment to investigate next month?" Your turn Rewrite the head's request as your own question. Use the four parts in the table. Keep it to one sentence. Part 2: Watch the demonstration ¶ Your facilitator will connect to the file and build a first chart while you watch. Before each step, predict what you think will happen. Things to notice: How Tableau reads each column (text, number or date). Which fields appear as dimensions (things you group by) and which as measures (numbers you add up). What happens to a number when you drag it into the view. Part 3: Guided practice ¶ Follow along step by step. Connect to the file ¶ Open Tableau Desktop Public Edition. In the Connect pane on the left, under To a File , choose Text file . Find and open order_lines.csv . Tableau opens the Data Source page with a preview of the rows. Check the column types ¶ Look at the small icon above each column in the preview: Icon Meaning Examples in this file Abc Text order_id, segment, region # Number sales, profit, quantity Calendar Date order_date, ship_date Check the IDs order_id and row_id are identifiers, not amounts. Adding them up means nothing. If an ID shows as a number, note it in your log. Tableau may tidy column names for display, for example showing order_id as Order Id . It is the same field. Build a first chart ¶ Click the Sheet 1 tab at the bottom. In the Data pane, find Segment and drag it to Rows . Find Sales and drag it to Columns . You should see one bar per segment. Tableau shows this as SUM(Sales) . Add a filter ¶ Drag Region to the Filters card. Tick one region and click OK . Watch how the bars change. Then clear the filter so all regions are included again. Write it down Every time you filter, record it. A chart without its filters written down is easy to misread later. Save and reopen ¶ Choose File → Save As and save the workbook in your course folder, for example class01_first_view . Close Tableau, open it again and open your saved workbook. Check that the chart and your filter settings are still there. Part 4: Rows versus orders ¶ Open the Data Source page again and look at a few rows that share the same order_id . One row in this file is one order line : one product within an order. One order can have several lines. So the number of rows is not the number of orders. Quick check In the Data pane, Tableau lists a field named after the file with (Count) at the end. Drag it to the view. Is that counting rows or orders? Write your answer in one sentence. You will measure orders properly in Lesson 2 . Part 5: Independent work ¶ On a new sheet, build one more simple view on your own: Choose a different grouping: Region or Category . Show Sales for each group. Add a title that says what the chart shows and for which period. Write one sentence describing what the chart shows. Do not explain why yet. Part 6: Challenge ¶ A colleague says: "The biggest bar is the best segment, so we should invest there." In two or three sentences, explain why a bigger Sales bar alone does not tell us where to invest. What else would you want to see? Exit ticket ¶ Before you finish, write: Your one-sentence business question. What one row in order_lines.csv represents. One thing you are still unsure about. After the lesson ¶ Fix anything that did not work during setup. Read the Analytical workflow page. Start your evidence log (see Setup and practice ) with today's question, file name and filters.

Adding them up means nothing. If an ID shows as a number, note it in your log. Tableau may tidy column names for display, for example showing order_id as Order Id . It is the same field.

docs.text: Click the Sheet 1 tab at the bottom. In the Data pane, find Segment and drag it to Rows . Find Sales and drag it to Columns . You should see one bar per segment. Tableau shows this as SUM(Sales) .

Drag it to the view. Is that counting rows or orders? Write your answer in one sentence. You will measure orders properly in Lesson 2 .

docs.text: Tableau Lesson 2: Can we trust the sales table? ¶ Before comparing anything, find out exactly what the retail file contains: what a row is, which columns can be added up, and how to count orders correctly. Draft lesson: Tableau section (coming later) The course currently teaches this lesson in Python: see Session 2 lab . This Tableau version will be completed in the later Tableau section. The Tableau steps on this page have not yet been rehearsed on the course version of Tableau. Menu names may differ slightly on your computer. The business decision ¶ The retail head now asks: "Before you show me any chart, can I trust these numbers? How many orders did we actually have?" A wrong count at this stage spoils every later chart. Today is about building trust in the data. What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of this lesson you will be able to: State the grain of the file: what one row represents. Tell which columns are identifiers, categories, dates or amounts. Count orders correctly with a distinct count. Explain what the returns flag does and does not tell you. Check a small slice of data by hand. Record what you changed in a short preparation log . Evidence you keep: a grain statement, a short quality checklist, a preparation log and one checked order. Before you start ¶ Bring your saved Lesson 1 workbook and your evidence log. Keep the original order_lines.csv untouched. If you ever need to experiment, work on a copy. Part 1: Meet the data dictionary ¶ Every column has a job. Knowing that job tells you how to use it. Column What it is Can you add it up? row_id Unique number for each order line No, it is an identifier order_id Order identifier; repeats across that order's lines No, count it distinctly order_date , ship_date Calendar dates No order_month First day of the order's month, for monthly grouping No ship_mode Shipping service chosen No customer_id Fictitious customer identifier No segment Customer group: Consumer, Corporate or Home Office No, use it to group country_region , region Location labels No, use them to group category , sub_category Product groups No, use them to group product_id , product_name Product identifier and name No sales Sales reported for the line, in the file's own monetary units Yes quantity Number of items on the line Yes , but it counts items, not orders profit Profit reported for the line (can be negative) Yes discount Discount value as given in the source No, its exact definition is not documented returned_order_flag 1 if the order appears on the source's returns list, otherwise 0 Not on line rows (see Part 4) order_to_ship_days Days between order date and ship date No, not without care customer_analysis_eligible , customer_order_conflict Flags for a small data issue with customer IDs Used only for customer analysis later Scope of this file The file contains orders placed from 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2025 . A few orders placed late in 2025 shipped in early 2026; they are kept because the order date is what defines the period. Part 2: Find the grain ¶ Grain means: what does one row represent? Open your workbook and go to the Data Source page. Sort or scan the preview by order_id . Find an order that appears on more than one row . Compare those rows. What is the same? What is different? Write your grain statement Complete this sentence in your log: "One row in order_lines.csv represents one _ _ , identified by ____ ." Part 3: Count orders correctly ¶ Demonstration ¶ Your facilitator will show two numbers side by side: the number of rows (the field ending in (Count) ) the number of distinct orders Predict before you see them: will the two numbers be equal, or which will be larger? Guided practice ¶ On a new sheet, drag the (Count) field to the view. This counts rows. Drag Order Id into the view as well. Right-click it and choose Measure → Count (Distinct) . This counts orders. Put both numbers in a small table and label them clearly. Write one sentence explaining why they differ. A reusable calculation You can also create a calculated field named Orders with the formula: COUNTD([Order Id]) Use this whenever a chart needs a number of orders. Part 4: What the returns flag means ¶ returned_order_flag is 1 when an order appears on the source's returns list . Be careful with what it does not tell you: It has no return date, quantity or refund amount. A 0 means not on the list . It does not prove the order was never returned. The flag repeats on every line of a listed order. A common mistake Adding up returned_order_flag across lines counts lines of returned orders, not returned orders . To count returned orders, count distinct order_id values where the flag is 1. Part 5: Check one order by hand ¶ Pick one order with several lines. Filter the view to that single order_id . Show each line's sales and profit in a table. Add up the lines yourself on paper or in a spreadsheet. Compare with Tableau's total for that order. Do they match? Record the order ID, your hand total and Tableau's total in your log. Part 6: Keep a preparation log ¶ Write down every change you make to how the data is read or shaped, even small ones. Date What I changed Why How I checked it example Created calculated field Orders = COUNTD([Order Id]) Rows are order lines, not orders Compared with the row count; checked one order by hand The original file is never edited. Every change lives in Tableau or in your log. Part 7: Independent work ¶ For each Segment , build a small table showing: the number of rows, the number of distinct orders, total sales . Then answer in your log: Do the segment order counts add up to the overall order count? Why might that be true for Segment? Try the same with Category . Do category order counts add up to the overall total? Why not? Think about it Can one order contain products from more than one category? Can one order belong to more than one segment? Part 8: Debugging challenge ¶ A colleague sends this summary: "We had [row count] orders, and [sum of returned_order_flag] of them were returned." Which two mistakes are in this sentence? What should each number be counting instead? How would you check your corrected numbers? Write your corrected sentence. You do not need to share the numbers with anyone yet. Exit ticket ¶ Your grain statement. Why rows and orders differ in this file. One thing the returns flag cannot tell you. After the lesson ¶ Finish the Segment and Category tables from Part 7. Complete your preparation log and one hand-checked order. Keep your workbook for Lesson 3 , where we compare segments using Sales, Profit and average order value.

docs.text: Tableau Lesson 3: Which segment deserves a closer look? ¶ Compare the three customer segments using five measures, calculate each one correctly, check that the numbers add up, and make a careful recommendation. Draft lesson: Tableau section (coming later) The course currently teaches this lesson in Python: see Session 5 lab . This Tableau version will be completed in the later Tableau section. The Tableau steps on this page have not yet been rehearsed on the course version of Tableau. Menu names may differ slightly on your computer. The business decision ¶ The retail head has one analyst free next month and asks: "Which customer segment should we investigate first, and what should we check before we change any promotions?" A big Sales total alone is not enough to decide. A segment can sell a lot and still earn little profit, or have many small orders. Today you build a fair comparison. What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of this lesson you will be able to: Define five measures precisely: Sales, Orders, Average order value, Profit and Profit ratio. Build them in Tableau as calculated fields. Calculate ratios from totals , not by averaging other ratios. Check that segment results reconcile with the overall total. Explain how a filter changes every measure. Write a short, evidence-based recommendation with one limitation. Evidence you keep: a segment KPI table, your metric definitions, a validation checklist and a five-sentence recommendation. Before you start ¶ Open your workbook from Lesson 2 , with the Orders calculated field. Have your grain statement and evidence log ready. Re-read the averages and percentages traps in Foundations. Part 1: Agree the measures ¶ Every measure uses the same rows : all order lines in the file, unless you deliberately apply a filter. Measure What it means How to calculate it Sales Total reported Sales Add up sales Orders Number of different orders Count distinct order_id Average order value (AOV) Typical Sales per order Sales ÷ Orders Profit Total reported Profit (can be negative) Add up profit Profit ratio Profit earned per unit of Sales Profit ÷ Sales About the money Sales and Profit are in the file's own monetary units. The currency is not stated, so do not add a currency symbol. The source does not explain exactly how Profit is calculated, so call it profit ratio , not "gross margin". Totals first, then divide AOV and Profit ratio must be calculated from the totals for whatever you are looking at. Never average the ratios of individual rows or of segments. You will see why in Part 6. Part 2: Watch the demonstration ¶ Your facilitator builds the five measures for the whole file and shows them as a small table. Before each number appears, predict : Will AOV be larger or smaller than Sales divided by the number of rows ? Why? Can Profit ratio be negative? When? Part 3: Guided practice — build the calculations ¶ Create each calculated field ( Analysis → Create Calculated Field ). Type the name and formula exactly. Sales SUM([Sales]) Orders (from Lesson 2) COUNTD([Order Id]) AOV IF COUNTD([Order Id]) > 0 THEN SUM([Sales]) / COUNTD([Order Id]) END Profit SUM([Profit]) Profit ratio IF SUM([Sales]) <> 0 THEN SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) END Why the IF? If a filter leaves no orders or no Sales, dividing would be undefined. The IF makes Tableau show a blank instead of an error or a misleading zero. A blank here means "not available" , never 0%. Format the results: Sales, Profit and AOV: number with two decimal places, no currency symbol. Profit ratio: percentage with one decimal place. Part 4: Guided practice — the segment table ¶ Start a new sheet. Drag Segment to Rows . Drag Measure Names to Columns and Measure Values to the table area. Keep only your five measures. Turn on totals: Analysis → Totals → Show Column Grand Totals . Give the sheet a clear title, for example "Segment comparison, orders placed 2023–2025 (source monetary units)" . Check that it reconciles ¶ Tick each check in your evidence log: The three segment Sales add up to the grand total. The three segment Profit values add up to the grand total. The three segment Orders add up to the grand total. (They should, because every order belongs to exactly one segment.) The grand total AOV equals total Sales ÷ total Orders. It is not the average of the three segment AOVs. The grand total Profit ratio equals total Profit ÷ total Sales. It is not the average of the three segment ratios. If a total looks wrong Check that every measure uses the same filters, and that the grand total is recalculated, not summed. Right-click the measure and check which aggregation the total uses. Part 5: Independent work ¶ A. Filter by region ¶ Duplicate your segment sheet. Add Region to Filters and choose one region. Record all five measures for each segment in that region. Write two sentences: does the ranking of segments change inside this region? B. Look at a category ¶ Duplicate the sheet again and filter to one Category . Notice that AOV now means "Sales of this category's lines per order that contains this category" , not full basket value. Rename the column to say so. Remove the filter and put Category on Rows instead of Segment. Do the category Orders add up to the overall total? Explain why not, in one sentence. Part 6: Debugging challenge ¶ A colleague sends you this summary: "Our overall profit ratio is the average of the three segment ratios. And our average order value is total Sales divided by the number of rows." Calculate the colleague's two numbers from your own table. Compare them with your correct grand totals. Explain each mistake in one sentence. Which segment has the most influence on the correct overall profit ratio, and why? Think about weights A segment with much more Sales should pull the overall ratio more strongly than a small segment. Does a simple average of the three ratios allow that? Part 7: Make a recommendation ¶ Write five sentences to the retail head: Recommendation: which segment to investigate first. Evidence 1: one measure, with its value and how it compares. Evidence 2: a second, different measure. Limitation: one thing this data cannot tell you. For example, it shows which segment looks different; it does not show why , and it does not prove a discount or promotion caused anything. Next check: one specific piece of evidence to request before changing promotions. Association, not cause If a segment with more discounts has a lower profit ratio, that is a pattern worth investigating. It is not proof that the discounts caused it. Other differences between segments, such as product mix, could explain it. Validation checklist ¶ Before submitting, confirm: Every measure uses the same filters and date scope. Orders are counted distinctly, not as rows. AOV and Profit ratio are calculated from totals. Segment Sales, Profit and Orders reconcile with the grand totals. Money is labelled "source monetary units", with no currency symbol. The recommendation names a limitation and a next check. Exit ticket ¶ Why is the average of three segment ratios not the overall ratio? What does a blank AOV or Profit ratio mean? One question you would want answered before acting on your recommendation. After the lesson ¶ Finish the region and category work from Part 5. Correct the colleague's summary in Part 6 and add it to your evidence log. Keep your workbook for Lesson 4 , where we look at monthly trends and the returns list, and build a dashboard.

docs.text: Tableau Lesson 4: Trends, returns and a decision dashboard ¶ Add time to your segment comparison, read growth figures without being fooled by seasons, use the returns list carefully, and bring it all together in one dashboard with a recommendation. Draft lesson: Tableau section (coming later) The course currently teaches this lesson in Python: see Session 7 lab . This Tableau version will be completed in the later Tableau section. The Tableau steps on this page have not yet been rehearsed on the course version of Tableau. Menu names may differ slightly on your computer. The business decision ¶ The commercial lead asks: "Before we test any change, show me how sales have moved over time, whether returns differ between segments, and which one test you would run first." A single snapshot cannot answer this. A month can look like a crash or a boom simply because of the time of year. What you will be able to do ¶ By the end of this lesson you will be able to: Build a monthly Sales trend and recognise seasonal patterns. Calculate month-on-month and year-on-year growth, and explain when each is fair. Measure the share of orders on the returns list, and state what it cannot tell you. Combine views into a dashboard with one shared filter. Write a recommendation for a test, with an honest limitation. Evidence you keep: a retail dashboard, your growth and returns definitions, and a short recommendation. This dashboard is your retail portfolio checkpoint . Before you start ¶ Open your workbook from Lesson 3 with the segment KPI table. Re-read cherry-picked time windows and storytelling with data . Part 1: The monthly trend ¶ Start a new sheet. Drag Order Month to Columns . Right-click it and choose the continuous Month option (green pill), so every month from January 2023 to December 2025 appears in order. Drag your Sales measure to Rows . You now have a line chart. Add Segment to Color to see one line per segment. Then remove it again for the overall view. What do you notice? Write down three observations. Look at the same months in different years. Are some months always high? Are January and February always low? Use the month field order_month is the first day of each order's month. Using it keeps every order in the right calendar month and makes year-on-year comparisons simple. Part 2: Two kinds of growth ¶ Month-on-month growth ¶ Compares each month with the previous month. IF LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1) <> 0 THEN (SUM([Sales]) - LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1)) / LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1) END Year-on-year growth ¶ Compares each month with the same month one year earlier . IF LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -12) <> 0 THEN (SUM([Sales]) - LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -12)) / LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -12) END To use them: Create both as calculated fields and format them as percentages with one decimal place. Put Order Month (continuous month) on Columns and one growth measure on Rows. Right-click the growth measure, choose Compute Using , and select Order Month . Blank is correct sometimes January 2023 has no previous month in this file, so its month-on-month growth is blank. All of 2023 has no year-earlier month, so its year-on-year growth is blank. Blank means "no comparison available" , never 0%. Filters can remove the comparison LOOKUP compares with the previous month shown in the view . If you filter the view to only 2025, January 2025 can no longer see December 2024 and becomes blank. Keep all months in the view and highlight the period you care about instead of filtering it away. Which one is fair? ¶ Growth type Good for Can mislead when Month-on-month Spotting sudden changes The business is seasonal: January after a busy December always looks like a crash Year-on-year Comparing like with like across seasons A one-off event happened in the same month last year Part 3: The returns list ¶ From Lesson 2, you know the returns flag marks orders that appear on the source's returns list . Create two measures: Orders on returns list COUNTD(IF [Returned Order Flag] = 1 THEN [Order Id] END) Share of orders on returns list IF COUNTD([Order Id]) > 0 THEN COUNTD(IF [Returned Order Flag] = 1 THEN [Order Id] END) / COUNTD([Order Id]) END Add the share to your segment table. What the returns list cannot tell you When an order was returned, or how many items. How much money was refunded. Whether an order not on the list was definitely kept. So call it "share of orders on the returns list" , not "return rate", and do not subtract anything from Sales because of it. A separate synthetic exercise will cover refund amounts later. Part 4: Guided practice — build the dashboard ¶ Create a new dashboard ( Dashboard → New Dashboard ). Drag in three sheets: your segment KPI table from Lesson 3, with the returns share added the monthly Sales trend the year-on-year growth chart Add a Region filter. Click its menu and choose Apply to Worksheets → All Using This Data Source , so every view responds together. Give each sheet a message title that says what to notice, for example in the form "[Segment] sales [rose / fell] most in [period]" , filled in with what your chart actually shows. Add one short text box stating the scope: "Orders placed 2023–2025. Source monetary units. Fictitious sample data." Design checks ¶ Use what you learned in Designing clear visuals : The most important view is at the top left. Colour is used only where it means something, and each segment keeps the same colour everywhere. Every chart has labelled axes with units. Nothing can be understood only by colour; labels or a table are available too. When you change the Region filter, all views change together and the totals still reconcile. Part 5: Independent work ¶ Choose one segment . Using your dashboard, describe its trend over the three years in three sentences. Compare the same quarter across years for that segment. Is it growing, flat or falling? Add one annotation to the trend chart marking something a manager should notice ( right-click a point → Annotate → Mark ). Part 6: Debugging challenge ¶ A colleague posts this in a team chat: "Disaster! Sales fell about 75% in January 2025. And I filtered the dashboard to 2025 to check, but now January's growth is blank. Something is broken." Is January's fall a real problem, or a seasonal pattern? Which growth measure would you show instead, and what does it say? Why did January's month-on-month growth become blank after filtering to 2025? Rewrite the colleague's message so it is accurate. Part 7: Recommend a test ¶ Write five sentences to the commercial lead: The test: one specific change to try, in one segment. Evidence: one measure from the trend or growth views. Evidence: one measure from the segment table, including the returns share. Limitation: for example, the trend shows when sales change, not why ; the returns list has no refund amounts; the data is a fictitious sample. How to measure success: the measure and comparison period you would use to judge the test, such as year-on-year Sales and profit ratio for the same months. Why a test? Past data shows patterns, not causes. A small, well-measured test, compared fairly with the same months last year or with an untouched group, is how you find out whether a change actually works. Validation checklist ¶ The trend shows all 36 months with no gaps. Growth measures compute along Order Month, and blanks appear only where no comparison exists. Returns are counted as distinct orders, not lines. The dashboard filter changes every view, and segment totals still reconcile with the overall total. Titles state messages; scope and units are written on the dashboard. Exit ticket ¶ Why can month-on-month growth mislead for a seasonal business? What is one thing the returns list cannot tell you? What would you measure to judge whether your proposed test worked? After the lesson ¶ Finish your dashboard and recommendation. Together they form your retail portfolio checkpoint . Save the workbook locally with a clear name, and record the file name in your evidence log.
